name: A. O. Dennis Willows
text:
A. O. Dennis Willows is a neurobiologist and professor emeritus of biology at the University of Washington who directed Friday Harbor Laboratories from 1971 to 2005. In 1964 he spent a summer at FHL with his PhD advisor Graham Hoyle, a University of Oregon neurobiologist, and there found that the brain of the nudibranch Tritonia has large neurons, many of them individually identifiable. He earned his PhD in 1967 and joined the UW faculty in 1968. He also served as director of the Neurobiology Program of the US National Science Foundation. FHL has a Dennis Willows Director's Endowed Professorship, and a January 2024 conference at FHL honoring his work led to a 2025 review of Tritonia neuroscience in the Journal of Neurophysiology. The census lists 46 FHL-connected papers, 1973–2011, and the report's network records Hoyle as his teacher through a 1973 co-authorship.

Willows's research asks how nervous systems are wired to produce coherent behavior. In Tritonia diomedea (now T. exsulans) he found that stimulating single identified neurons could produce specific movements, and a 1978 paper showed single central neurons controlling a fixed action pattern. His group traced the neural control of feeding, crawling, gut motility and ciliary beating, and the roles of serotonin and of neuropeptides from identified neurons. A second line of work, combining field observation with electrophysiology, asked how the slugs orient to water flow, odors and the Earth's magnetic field; representative papers report lunar-modulated geomagnetic orientation (1987), a neuron that responds to Earth-strength magnetic fields (1991) and daily tracking of slugs in the field (2011). He also worked on Phestilla, Clione and sea hares, and with engineers on instruments for recording from neurons. His trainee Peter Getting studied central pattern generators, including early realistic modeling of neural circuits.

name: AWE Galloway
text:
Aaron W. E. Galloway (listed here as "AWE Galloway") is a marine ecologist and associate professor of biology at the University of Oregon's Oregon Institute of Marine Biology. He joined the faculty in 2015 and leads the Coastal Trophic Ecology Lab. He holds a B.A. from The Evergreen State College (1999), an M.S. in resource management from Central Washington University (2004) and a Ph.D. in aquatic and fishery sciences from the University of Washington (2013). His dissertation dealt with food web biomarkers. Postdoctoral positions followed at the University of Eastern Finland, Stockholm University and Washington State University. At FHL he held the Richard and Megumi Strathmann and the Alan and Marian Kohn fellowships in 2012, and he taught summer courses there in 2015 and 2018 with a scientific diving option. The papers under this name form date from 2013 to 2021.

Galloway studies trophic links in coastal seafloor food webs, especially between seaweeds and invertebrates in kelp forests. He uses fatty acids as dietary tracers, with scuba, experiments and modelling, on the northeast Pacific coast and in Antarctica. A 2013 paper led by Megan N. Dethier showed that variation in the stable isotopes and fatty acids of seaweeds and seagrasses among sites and dates can confound food web conclusions. Another 2013 paper assessed fatty acids of 37 freshwater microalgal strains as biomarkers. In 2014 he led a study using feeding trials and a Bayesian fatty acid mixing model to estimate diets of the isopod Idotea wosnesenskii in Puget Sound. A 2014 study with Wendel W. Raymond and Alexander T. Lowe found that degraded kelp diets changed the fatty acids, but not the size, of red sea urchin gonads. A 2021 paper led by Raymond examined how sea otters affect seagrass food webs in southeast Alaska.

name: Aaron W. E. Galloway
text:
Aaron W. E. Galloway is an associate professor of biology at the University of Oregon's Oregon Institute of Marine Biology, where he leads the Coastal Trophic Ecology Lab. He holds a BA in environmental science and policy from The Evergreen State College (1999), an MS in resource management (wildlife biology) from Central Washington University (2004), with a thesis on ungulate surveys by students along school bus routes, and a PhD in aquatic and fishery sciences from the University of Washington (2013). From 2007 to 2013 he was a graduate research assistant based at Friday Harbor Laboratories, with Kenneth Sebens and Michael Brett among his supervisors. At FHL he held Strathmann and Kohn fellowships (2012), was an NSF GK-12 teaching fellow in Friday Harbor schools and was scheduled to teach a summer course in 2015. Postdoctoral posts followed at the University of Eastern Finland, Stockholm University and Washington State University.

Galloway studies the base of coastal food webs, especially links between algae and their invertebrate grazers. He uses fatty acids and stable isotopes as dietary markers, with field diving, experiments and modelling. His FHL-connected papers examined how habitat and depth shape the distribution of drift seaweeds and their invertebrates (2011), showed that fatty acid signatures distinguish marine macrophytes by order and family (2012) and traced microbe-linked differences between shallow and deep benthic food webs (2013). Others followed the declining food quality of ageing kelp (2014) and described kelp detritus as a magnet for animals (2016). Later papers cover algal fatty acids in two urchin species (2018), the food value of urchin feces (2019), red urchins and drift kelp found at 284 m (2020), and how sunflower sea stars eating urchins can help kelp forests recover (2023–2024). Wendel Raymond and Alexander Lowe are linked to him as students in the report's network.

name: Adam M. Reitzel
text:
Adam M. Reitzel is a biologist who studies the evolution and development of marine invertebrates. His ORCID record lists a B.A. in biology from Illinois Wesleyan University (1999), an M.S. in zoology from the University of Florida (2002) and a Ph.D. in biology from Boston University (2008), followed by postdoctoral work at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (2007–2012). Since 2012 he has been on the faculty of the Department of Biological Sciences at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, where he is a professor. His FHL-connected papers in the census run from 2004 to 2020. His early papers on sand dollar hormones were written with Andreas Heyland and with Jason Hodin of FHL. A 2012 paper on sand dollar larvae, which gives an FHL address, grew out of a student project in the FHL summer Larval Biology course.

Most of his FHL-connected work concerns echinoderm larvae. A 2004 paper with Heyland and Hodin showed that thyroid hormone lets sand dollar larvae that normally must feed complete metamorphosis without food, and a 2006 paper found that larvae of a facultatively feeding species make the hormone themselves; both bear on the evolutionary loss of larval feeding. Other 2004 papers compared the growth of Dendraster excentricus larvae on natural and laboratory diets and modelled how spawning date relates to larval development time. The 2012 study tracked the depth of sand dollar larvae relative to haloclines, food and fish cues. From 2018 to 2020, with his student Tyler J. Carrier, who held an FHL Charles Lambert Memorial Endowment fellowship, he studied the bacteria of sea urchin larvae and how they shift with diet, location, development and exposure to Vibrio. Venomix (2018), a pipeline for finding toxin genes, grew out of a computing workshop at FHL.

name: Adam P. Summers
text:
Adam P. Summers is a comparative biomechanist and professor at the University of Washington, appointed in the Department of Biology and the School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences and based at Friday Harbor Laboratories. He earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics and engineering at Swarthmore College, a master's degree in biology at New York University and a PhD at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where he studied tissues of cartilaginous fishes. After a Miller postdoctoral fellowship at the University of California, Berkeley, he joined the faculty of UC Irvine and founded a biomechanics laboratory there in 2001. He moved the lab to FHL in 2009, where he became associate director, and teaches an intensive graduate course there on the biomechanics of fishes. He is a Fellow of the AAAS and held the 2025–26 Rome Prize in Environmental Arts and Humanities. The census lists 116 FHL-connected papers, 2009–2026.

His lab applies engineering and physics to the mechanics, materials and structure of animals, mainly marine fishes, in an evolutionary context. The work relies heavily on museum collections, and the lab's #ScanAllFish project aims to CT-scan all ray-finned fishes. His research has also covered the mechanical properties of cartilage and tendon, shark swimming, and breathing in sharks and rays. Recent FHL-connected papers compare how clingfishes, lumpsuckers and snailfishes stick to rough and soft surfaces (2022), test the armor of poachers and the Pacific spiny lumpsucker and its effect on drag (2023–2026), and analyse jaw mechanics in spotted ratfish (2022), bone density in rattails (2022), tooth indentation in fruit-eating fishes (2025) and the body form of the extinct megatooth shark (2024–2025). He has also co-authored clingfish taxonomy and open-source 3D measurement tools. The report's network links him to more than a dozen students, including Mason Dean and Karly Cohen.

name: Adriana T. Dawes
text:
Adriana T. Dawes is a mathematical biologist who combines modelling with laboratory experiments to study how cells become polarized. Dawes received a Ph.D. in mathematics from the University of British Columbia in 2006. Papers from 2006, 2008 and 2011 list the University of Washington's Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories as an address, and these are Dawes's three census papers. From 2008 to 2011 Dawes was Max Wyman Assistant Professor of Mathematical Biology at the University of Alberta, in its mathematics and statistics department. In 2011 Dawes joined The Ohio State University as an assistant professor in mathematics and molecular genetics, becoming associate professor in 2017 and professor in 2022. Grants listed in Dawes's ORCID record come from NSERC, the National Science Foundation, including a CAREER award, and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

Dawes's work asks how signalling molecules and the cytoskeleton set up and maintain distinct regions within a cell. A 2006 paper with Leah Edelstein-Keshet at UBC built a one-dimensional model of a motile cell in which phosphoinositides and Rho-family proteins regulate actin polymerization to start and sustain directed movement. With the Center for Cell Dynamics as an address, Dawes modelled the dimerization of alpha-catenin at adherens junctions in polarized epithelial cells (2008), and with Edwin Munro proposed that oligomerization of the PAR-3 protein could keep PAR protein domains separate in the early Caenorhabditis elegans embryo without depending on actin (2011). Later grant titles describe projects on intracellular polarization, the organization and dynamics of cortical actin, dynein-mediated positioning of centrosomes in polarized cells, and changing phenotypes by modifying signalling networks; other grants equipped a laboratory for confocal microscopy and C. elegans research.

name: Alberto Stolfi
text:
Alberto Stolfi is a developmental biologist who works on tunicates. He holds a B.S. in plant sciences from Cornell University and a Ph.D. in molecular and cell biology from the University of California, Berkeley, and is an associate professor in the School of Biological Sciences at the Georgia Institute of Technology. In 2014 his address was the Center for Developmental Genetics at New York University; from 2017 his papers give Georgia Tech. He has no FHL address of his own. His seven census papers, from 2014 to 2021, are FHL-connected through co-authors. One is Billie J. Swalla of FHL and the UW Department of Biology. The other is Elijah K. Lowe, who gave FHL and UW addresses in 2017 and a Georgia Tech address, like Stolfi, in 2020.

His lab asks how animal body plans and behaviours arise from the coordinated behaviour of individual cells, using tunicates, the closest invertebrate relatives of vertebrates, with methods such as RNA-seq profiling of progenitor cells and CRISPR/Cas9 gene knockouts. The FHL-connected papers compare the model ascidian Ciona with molgulid ascidians, some of which have lost the swimming tadpole larva. A 2014 paper found that the heart and pharyngeal muscle lineage follows the same cell divisions and fates in Molgula and Ciona, although the regulatory DNA of one does not work in the other. Papers from 2017 to 2021 studied the tailless larvae of Molgula occulta: the loss of melanin pigment through decay of Tyrosinase genes (2017), a regulatory DNA change that reduces expression of the motor neuron gene Ebf (preprint 2019, paper 2020), and a 2021 review of tail loss. He also co-authored tunicate gene-naming guidelines (2014) and the 2017 update of the ANISEED ascidian database.

name: Alexander Fodor
text:
Alexander C. A. Fodor is a biologist who studies the genomics and evolution of ctenophores and tunicates. Fodor's connection to Friday Harbor Laboratories dates to 2012, when Fodor wrote a report on mesoderm- and muscle-specific genes in the ctenophore Pleurobrachia bachei for FHL's Marine Genomics Research Apprenticeship; it is held in FHL's student research papers collection. Fodor is a co-author of the 2014 ctenophore genome paper in Nature, with an address at the University of Florida's Whitney Laboratory for Marine Bioscience. Papers from 2020 to 2023 list the Biology Department of the University of Washington and FHL and are co-authored with Billie J. Swalla, whom the report's mentoring network lists as Fodor's teacher. No faculty page or CV was found, so Fodor's position at UW and FHL is not stated here.

Fodor's research uses genes and genomes to trace the evolution of animal body plans. The 2012 apprenticeship project examined tropomyosin, calponin and beta-catenin in Pleurobrachia and found them expressed in both muscular and epidermal tissues. The 2014 Nature paper reported the genome of Pleurobrachia bachei and proposed that ctenophore neurons and muscles evolved independently of those of other animals. The later FHL papers concern ascidians, tunicates whose tadpole larvae carry a notochord, muscle and dorsal nerve cord in the tail. A 2020 chapter with Swalla and colleagues treats tunicates as transitional chordates. A 2021 paper compares the genomes of the tailed Molgula oculata and the tailless M. occulta, finding much conserved gene order but insertions and deletions that disrupt genes in the tailless species, and a 2023 paper shows that the kinase gene cymric, expressed in gonads, eggs and embryos of M. oculata, is a pseudogene in M. occulta.

name: Alexander T. Lowe
text:
Alexander T. (Alex) Lowe is a marine ecologist whose FHL-connected papers date from 2011 to 2016. After a master's degree in Santa Barbara modelling larval Antarctic krill, he worked at FHL in the NSF-funded Spatial Subsidy Lab led by David Duggins and Megan Dethier, where he led a study of food sources for suspension feeders. He then completed a PhD in Biology at the University of Washington; his dissertation (2018), supervised by Jennifer Ruesink, examined how local ecosystem processes modulate ocean acidification and its effects on benthic foundation species. In 2018 he co-taught FHL's Marine Subtidal Ecology course with Aaron Galloway and dive officer Pema Kitaeff, the first FHL academic course to train a full class as scientific divers. He was later a postdoctoral researcher at the Smithsonian Institution, and his website states that he now works at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration on National Environmental Policy Act issues.

Lowe studies how environmental variability shapes coastal food webs using oceanography, community ecology, physiology and fatty acid and stable isotope biomarkers. His FHL work traced the sources and quality of particulate organic matter and kelp detritus in the San Juan Islands: a 2014 Oikos paper identified phytoplankton as the main source of essential fatty acids for suspension feeders, and a 2016 paper linked pulses of fresher water, with salinity below about 30, to more marine-derived organic matter and higher pH. Other papers dealt with drift seaweeds and their invertebrates (2011), the changing food quality of decaying kelp species (2014), the influence of sedentary urchins on bottom communities below the macroalgal zone (2014), kelp detritus as a magnet for fauna (2016) and the food value of urchin feces (2019). His dissertation also tested eelgrass effects on native and Pacific oysters, and with Galloway he reported red urchins with drift kelp at 284 m (2020).

name: Alison R. Sherwood
text:
Alison R. Sherwood is a phycologist who studies the diversity and classification of algae, especially in the Hawaiian Islands. Her ORCID record lists the School of Life Sciences of the University of Hawaii, and bibliographic records link her to the University of Hawaii from 2002. Her census papers give her address as the Botany Department, University of Hawaii at Manoa (2011, 2015). Wikispecies gives her botanical author abbreviation as A.R.Sherwood. She has no FHL address herself. Her two census papers, from 2011 and 2015, are FHL-connected through co-author Charles J. O'Kelly, who gave an FHL address on both. The first author of the 2011 paper, Amy L. Carlile, is linked to Sherwood as a student in the report's mentoring network.

Her research combines DNA sequences with morphology to classify red and green algae and to document the algal flora of Hawaii, including freshwater red algae; her publications include a 2023 inventory of the seaweeds and seagrasses of the Hawaiian Islands. Wikispecies lists about 60 taxon names she has authored, among them the genera Akalaphycus and Titanophycus and species such as Halymenia hawaiiana (2012). In the 2011 paper, nuclear and chloroplast gene sequences from Hawaiian collections, a culture from Portugal and type specimens placed the green algal genus Cloniophora in the Ulvales rather than the Chaetophorales, and the authors proposed a new family, the Cloniophoraceae. The 2015 paper, led by Heather Spalding, described Ulvales from 64 to 125 m deep at 13 sites across the Hawaiian Archipelago, collected by technical divers, submersibles and remotely operated vehicles. It named three new species in the genera Ulva and Umbraulva.

name: Alli N. Cramer
text:
Alli N. Cramer is a marine and aquatic ecologist. Cramer received a B.A. in biology from the University of Oregon in 2010, a master's degree in applied marine and watershed science from California State University, Monterey Bay in 2015, and a Ph.D. in environmental and natural resource sciences from Washington State University in 2020. Postdoctoral positions followed at NOAA Fisheries' Southwest Fisheries Science Center and the Institute of Marine Sciences at the University of California, Santa Cruz. From December 2021 to March 2024 Cramer was an NSF Ocean Sciences Postdoctoral Fellow in the University of Washington Department of Biology, based at Friday Harbor, and census papers with FHL addresses date from 2022 to 2026. Since August 2024 Cramer has been an assistant professor in the School of Mathematical and Natural Sciences at Arizona State University.

Cramer's work looks for general patterns in how primary production and habitat stability organize ecological communities, and makes wide use of open data. Earlier projects used ROV video to map corals and sponges in the Channel Islands, assessed the effects of bottom trawling on soft-sediment fish habitat off central California, assembled a global dataset of lake area, climate and population, and used acoustic telemetry to tell residency from random movement. The NSF fellowship project concerned substrate mobility as a disturbance in hard-rock marine communities. The FHL-connected papers include an essay arguing that shared observational data can restore the naturalist's tradition of description (2022); a review using dimensionless numbers to compare patchy ecologies, from bacteria to gazelles (2022); a report on the Hacking Limnology data-science workshops for aquatic scientists (2023); and a study, with Emily Carrington and others, of an analog sclerometer for measuring the strength of hard coastal substrates (2026).

name: Amanda L. Rychel
text:
Amanda L. Rychel is a biologist whose papers span molecular phylogenetics, the evolution and development of deuterostomes, and plant cell biology. Her first paper (2004), a molecular phylogeny of baleen whales with Tod W. Reeder and Annalisa Berta, gives the Department of Biology at San Diego State University. From 2005 her papers give the University of Washington, where her ORCID record lists a PhD in Biology without dates. Her papers of 2005 to 2009 were written with Billie J. Swalla and give the UW Biology Department and Center for Developmental Biology; the four from 2007 to 2009 also give Friday Harbor Laboratories, and three of these the Kewalo Marine Laboratory of the University of Hawaii. From 2010 to 2019 her address remained the UW Department of Biology, on papers from Keiko U. Torii's group on stomatal development in plants and on two 2011 protein-structure studies.

Her work with Swalla compared chordates with hemichordates and other deuterostomes to trace the origins of chordate features. A 2005 paper reviewed the development of gill slits and their cartilaginous bars and reported that hemichordate gill bars contain collagen and proteoglycans but no cells. A 2007 study found collagen resembling vertebrate type II collagen in the acellular cartilage of hemichordates and cephalochordates, with SoxE gene expression in nearby endoderm. A 2008 paper followed regeneration of the anterior body in the acorn worm Ptychodera flava, and a 2009 book chapter compared regeneration in hemichordates and echinoderms. She also co-authored a 2009 molecular phylogeny of the Hemichordata that updated the status of deep-sea enteropneusts. Her later papers with the Torii group concern the signals and regulators that pattern stomata on leaves, including a 2010 review of small peptide ligands and a 2019 Nature Plants study of how the SCREAM protein couples MAP kinases to SPEECHLESS.

name: Amy L. Moran
text:
Amy L. Moran is a marine invertebrate biologist; she describes herself as a marine physiological ecologist. Her first papers, from 1997 to 2001, came from the University of Oregon's Oregon Institute of Marine Biology (OIMB), including work with Richard B. Emlet. Papers of 2000 to 2002 give a Friday Harbor Laboratories address; the 2002 paper also lists the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama. Papers of 2003 to 2005 list the University of Southern California and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. She then published from Clemson University's Department of Biological Sciences (from 2007) and from the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa (from about 2013). In 2025 she returned to the University of Oregon, where she is Professor and Director of OIMB. The census counts three FHL-address papers (2000–2002) and five later papers (2007–2020) that are in the FHL bibliography or mention FHL in their text.

Moran's lab studies the ecology, evolution and physiology of marine invertebrates, especially life histories, larval ecology, and responses of larvae and adults to temperature and oxygen, from the tropics to the Antarctic. Her FHL-address papers tested the dye calcein as a marker for newly hatched snails (2000); used field outplants of the snail Nucella ostrina, with Emlet, to show that larger hatchlings grew faster and survived better (2001); and, with Peter B. Marko, linked egg-size divergence to changes in a mitochondrial protein among bivalve sister species separated by the Isthmus of Panama (2002). With H. Arthur Woods she measured and modelled oxygen supply to embryos in gelatinous egg masses (2007, 2008) and compared nudibranch egg masses from Friday Harbor and McMurdo Sound (2010). Papers of 2016 and 2020 with Steven Lane, Caitlin Shishido and Woods examined epibionts and temperature–oxygen limits on body size in two temperate Achelia sea spiders.

name: Amy T. Sewell
text:
Amy T. Sewell is a co-author of ecological and developmental studies carried out at Friday Harbor Laboratories between 1989 and 2020. Four of her five papers in the census, published in 1989, 1990, 1993 and 2020, give her address as Friday Harbor Laboratories, University of Washington; the fifth, a 2020 book chapter, lists no address for her. No faculty page, CV or other biographical source was found, so her position at FHL is not stated here, and what follows is drawn from the papers. Her co-authors in kelp studies of 1989 and 1990 were David O. Duggins of FHL and James E. Eckman of the Skidaway Institute of Oceanography in Georgia. In later work on marine larvae they were Richard R. Strathmann and Megumi F. Strathmann of FHL and Lucienne Fenaux, whose 2020 address is the marine station at Villefranche-sur-Mer.

The first two papers, led by Eckman and Duggins, examined understory kelp environments: the 1989 paper measured how kelps alter water flow and particle transport near the bottom, and the 1990 paper tested how kelps affect the recruitment of benthic invertebrates. Her later papers with the Strathmanns concern how larval development responds to food supply. A 1993 study found that veligers of the Pacific oyster Crassostrea gigas reared at a low food concentration had larger velar lobes and longer prototrochal cilia than well-fed larvae, a response like that known in sea urchin plutei. A 2020 paper described how the posterior coeloms of a brittle star larva first appear, as separate clusters of mesenchyme-like cells near the base of the posterolateral arms, and reported plasticity in larval structures. A 2020 book chapter compared such plasticity in response to food across classes of echinoderm larvae.

name: Andrea B. Kohn
text:
Andrea B. Kohn works in Leonid L. Moroz's group on the genomics and neurobiology of marine invertebrates. Her ORCID record lists the University of Florida, and her papers from 2011 to 2020 give the university's Whitney Laboratory for Marine Bioscience in St. Augustine, Florida, as her address. The sources found for this profile do not give her title or earlier career. Her FHL-connected papers in the census run from 2011 to 2020 and centre on the sea gooseberry Pleurobrachia bachei, a comb jelly (ctenophore) collected from the FHL docks. In spring and summer 2012 she was a co-author, with Moroz and Billie J. Swalla, of student reports from FHL's Marine Genomics Research Apprenticeship and its summer undergraduate internships, and one student thanked her for teaching molecular biology. One of those students, Rebecca Bruders, is linked to her in the report's mentoring network.

Her work addresses how nervous systems evolved, using ctenophores as a test case. A 2011 paper described the small, fast-evolving mitochondrial genome of Pleurobrachia bachei, from animals collected at FHL in 2008–2010. A 2016 review with Moroz argued from genomic and chemical data that neurons and synapses arose more than once in animal evolution. The 2012 student projects at FHL used transcriptome data and in situ hybridization to map where Pleurobrachia expresses developmental and signalling genes, including Wnt pathway genes, LIM homeobox genes, Brachyury, collagens and genes for glutamate signalling. A 2020 preprint used capillary electrophoresis to measure D-glutamate and D-aspartate, amino acids that can act as signalling molecules, in ctenophores, cnidarians, sponges and placozoans, and found D-glutamate dominant only in ctenophores. She was also a co-author of the 2014 paper reporting the Pleurobrachia bachei genome, on which Moroz gave FHL as one of his addresses.

name: Andreas Hejnol
text:
Andreas Hejnol is a zoologist who works in evolutionary developmental biology. He studied biology at the Freie Universität Berlin (diploma 1996) and earned his doctorate at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin in 2002 with a thesis on cell lineage and gene expression in the germ band of two crustaceans. He was a postdoctoral researcher at the Technische Universität Braunschweig (2002–2004) and at the University of Hawaii's Kewalo Marine Laboratory (2004–2009). From 2009 to 2019 he was a principal investigator at the Sars International Centre for Marine Molecular Biology in Bergen, Norway, and from 2019 a professor at the University of Bergen. Since 2021 he has been a professor at Friedrich Schiller University Jena and director of its Phyletic Museum. He received the A. O. Kovalevsky Medal of the St. Petersburg Society of Naturalists in 2018. His FHL-connected papers, from 2011 to 2024, mostly use brachiopods collected near FHL.

His group compares embryos and larvae across animal phyla to ask when developmental mechanisms, organ systems and body openings first appeared, often in less-studied invertebrates such as brachiopods, bryozoans, priapulids and horsehair worms. In his census papers the brachiopod Terebratalia transversa recurs: adults were dredged from rocky seabeds around Friday Harbor, with help from FHL staff and the crew of the R/V Centennial, and kept in FHL seawater tables. Studies from 2011 to 2024 use it to examine larval eyes (2011), the larval anterior nervous system (2012), mesoderm (2015), Hox genes in larvae and juveniles (2017, 2019), a neuropeptide that triggers defensive behaviour in larvae (2017) and Wnt signalling along the head-to-tail axis (2024). Broader comparisons include convergent evolution of nerve cords (2017) and the repeated evolution of protostome and deuterostome development (2017). With his student Ludwik Gąsiorowski he reported evidence for a single origin of ultrafiltration-based excretory organs (2021).

name: Andreas Heyland
text:
Andreas Heyland, a professor in the Department of Integrative Biology at the University of Guelph, studies metamorphosis in marine invertebrates and its hormonal control. He received BSc (1996) and MSc (1999) degrees from the University of Zurich and a PhD from the University of Florida (2004), begun in Larry McEdward's laboratory and later advised by David Julian. In 1999 he took two summer courses at Friday Harbor Laboratories, where Jason Hodin introduced him to the idea that thyroid hormones may act in echinoderm metamorphosis, the subject of his PhD; he spent several summers at FHL during his PhD doing research and teaching. From 2004 to 2007 he was a postdoctoral fellow with Leonid Moroz at the University of Florida's Whitney Laboratory, funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation, studying larval development and metamorphosis in Aplysia californica. His FHL-addressed papers date from 2004 to 2012.

Heyland's work concerns the molecular and physiological mechanisms of life-history transitions and their evolution. His FHL-connected work, much of it with Hodin, centred on thyroid hormones in echinoderm larvae. Papers in 2004 showed that thyroid hormone shifts developmental timing in sand dollar larvae, with implications for how nonfeeding development evolves, and a 2006 study found that larvae of the sand dollar Clypeaster rosaceus, which can develop with or without feeding, make the hormone themselves. He also reviewed hormone signalling in non-model organisms (2004) and co-wrote 2006 symposium papers on what metamorphosis is and how it is signalled and timed. A 2012 paper with Luke Hoekstra (his student in the report's network) described histamine- and FMRFamide-like cells in the sea cucumber Leptosynapta clarki. Later papers cover larval staging, juvenile structures, asymmetry, growth and Vibrio resistance in the purple sea urchin (2014–2020) and thyroid hormone signalling in echinoderm skeleton formation (2024).

name: Andreas Wanninger
text:
Andreas Wanninger is a zoologist who studies how invertebrate body plans develop and evolve. According to his ORCID record, he trained in zoology at Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (diploma 1998, doctorate 2001). He was a postdoctoral research associate at the Zoological State Collection in Munich (2002–2003) and an associate professor of biology at the University of Copenhagen (2004–2011). Since 2011 he has been professor and head of the Department of Integrative Zoology at the University of Vienna. His seven census papers, from 2001 to 2015, are FHL-connected mainly because their animals were collected near FHL and their larvae reared there by his co-workers. One of these was Henrike Semmler, who reared brachiopod larvae during FHL's 2006 Comparative Invertebrate Embryology course and acknowledged an FHL Patricia Dudley Fellowship in a 2010 paper.

His research compares how muscles, nerves and shells form in molluscs, brachiopods, flatworms, sipunculans, entoprocts and related invertebrates, combining microscopic anatomy with studies of developmental gene expression. His 2001 Munich dissertation, on muscle and shell development in molluscs, is in the census because FHL is named in its text. Later FHL-connected papers compare larval muscle development and adult muscle anatomy in the brachiopod Terebratalia transversa and two Argyrotheca species (2009), and describe muscle formation in two polyclad flatworms with a larval stage (2010) and cell and muscle growth in the sipunculan Phascolosoma agassizii (2011). With his student Andreas Altenburger he examined expression of the homeobox genes Not and Cdx in Terebratalia reared at FHL with lab space from Billie Swalla (2011). A 2012 paper followed spiral cleavage in a loxosomatid entoproct collected at FHL. He also co-authored a 2015 survey of opsin genes in echinoderms and hemichordates.

name: Andrew E. Christie
text:
Andrew E. Christie is a neurobiologist who studies peptide hormones and neuromodulators in crustaceans and other arthropods. The addresses on his papers trace his career. In the mid-1990s he was at Brandeis University, co-authoring work with Eve Marder and Katherine Graubard on the crab stomatogastric nervous system, and a 1997 paper gives an address at the University of Pennsylvania. By 2003 he was in the Department of Biology at the University of Washington, where a stomatogastric research directory lists him as an associate of Graubard's laboratory, and his papers from 2004 to 2007 carry a Friday Harbor Laboratories address. By 2010 he was at the Mount Desert Island Biological Laboratory in Maine, and from at least 2015 at the Békésy Laboratory of Neurobiology, Pacific Biosciences Research Center, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa. Yun-Wei A. Hsu is linked to him as a student in the report's network.

Christie identifies the peptide hormones and neuromodulators of decapod crustaceans and studies how they act on small neural circuits, such as those of the stomatogastric and cardiac systems, using anatomical, mass spectrometric, molecular and physiological methods. The FHL-connected papers centre on Cancer crabs, especially the red rock crab Cancer productus. They describe a neurosecretory site within the stomatogastric nervous system (2004); the hormones of the sinus gland and pericardial organ, a tachykinin-containing neuroendocrine organ and members of the crustacean hyperglycemic hormone family (2005–2006); a novel FMRFamide-like peptide (2006); and the cloning of hyperglycemic hormone precursors (2007). Others cover SIFamide in the American lobster (2006) and a peptide whose end resembles vertebrate neuropeptide Y (2007). A 2008 study found that the pyloric circuit of the herbivorous crab Pugettia producta responds weakly to several neuromodulators. His later work mines transcriptomes to predict the neuropeptides of lobsters, crabs, copepods and other arthropods.

name: Antonio C. Marques
text:
Antonio Carlos Marques is a Brazilian marine biologist who specializes in cnidarians. His ORCID record lists a Ph.D. in zoology from the Universidade de São Paulo (1993–1997) and a position in zoology there from 2000, with the title of full professor. His papers give two addresses at the university: the Departamento de Zoologia of the Instituto de Biociências and the Centro de Biologia Marinha in São Sebastião. He has no FHL address of his own. His five census papers, from 2011 to 2017, are FHL-connected mainly through co-author Claudia E. Mills of FHL and the UW Department of Biology, who worked with Marques and his student Lucília S. Miranda on stalked jellyfishes. A 2011 paper is included because it appears in the FHL bibliography.

His research covers the taxonomy, phylogeny and evolution of cnidarians, especially medusozoans such as hydroids, box jellies and stalked jellyfishes. His publications listed on Wikispecies also include work on fossil conulariids, bryozoans and areas of endemism in the Southwestern Atlantic. The FHL-connected papers centre on Staurozoa, the stalked jellyfishes. In 2012, with Miranda and Mills, he recorded Lucernariopsis capensis in Brazil, its first record outside its type locality in South Africa. In 2016 the same group used mitochondrial and nuclear gene sequences to propose the first phylogenetic classification of Staurozoa. It found that the traditional suborders, defined by the presence or absence of a claustrum, are not natural groups, and divided the class into two new groups. Other papers compared staurozoan internal anatomy (2016) and reviewed the group's global diversity and natural history (2017). The 2011 paper named the Bonaire banded box jelly, Tamoya ohboya.

name: Arthur H. Whiteley
text:
Arthur H. Whiteley (1916–2013) was a developmental biologist who studied sea urchin embryos at the University of Washington and Friday Harbor Laboratories. He received a BA in biology from Kalamazoo College (1938), an MS in zoology from the University of Wisconsin (1939) and a PhD in biology from Princeton (1945), where he did war-related research with E. Newton Harvey, and then held posts in Galveston and at Caltech. He began teaching at UW in 1947, the start of a long association with FHL, where he had a laboratory. He headed an NIH-sponsored interdepartmental developmental biology training program for 20 years and retired in 1985 as professor emeritus of zoology. He founded the Helen Riaboff Whiteley Center at FHL. The census lists 33 FHL-connected papers, 1953–2011.

Whiteley's research moved from the metabolism of echinoid embryos to the genetic mechanisms controlling development, mostly in the purple sea urchin Strongylocentrotus purpuratus and the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus. His FHL-connected papers of the 1950s and 1960s dealt with respiration and DNA synthesis, the enzymes urease and malate dehydrogenase, and the uptake and transport of phosphate. From about 1970 he turned to RNA: the conservation of early-development RNA sequences among echinoderms, the expression of maternal and paternal genomes in hybrid embryos, histone gene expression, and comparisons with limpet and oyster embryos. In the 1980s his group isolated and cultured micromeres and primary mesenchyme cells, the cell line that forms the larval skeleton, and followed their protein synthesis and gene expression. Later papers address spawning in a chiton (2003) and the history of embryology at FHL (2011). Students in the report's network include Michael Harkey, John Spieth and Hironobu Ozaki.

name: Aurel Wintner
text:
Aurel Wintner (1903–1958) was a Hungarian-born mathematician who worked in analysis, probability, number theory, differential equations and celestial mechanics. He studied at the University of Budapest and then at the University of Leipzig, where he received his doctorate; Wikipedia gives the year as 1928 and the MacTutor archive as 1929. Wikipedia names Leon Lichtenstein as his doctoral adviser. MacTutor says Lichtenstein encouraged his doctoral work and employed him as an assistant, and Wikidata also lists Julius Bauschinger as an adviser. After stays in Rome and Copenhagen in 1929–30, he joined Johns Hopkins University in 1930, became a full professor in 1946 and stayed until his death. He spent 1937–38 at the Institute for Advanced Study and was associate editor of the American Journal of Mathematics from 1936 and editor from 1944. He has no FHL papers.

Wintner published proofs of basic facts about Hilbert spaces in 1929 and wrote several papers that put George W. Hill's lunar theory on a rigorous footing. Wikipedia counts him among the founders of probabilistic number theory, and the Jessen–Wintner and Wiener–Wintner theorems carry his name. MacTutor credits him with about 437 papers and nine monographs. His books include a work on the spectral theory of infinite matrices (1929), The Analytical Foundations of Celestial Mechanics (1941) and The Fourier Transforms of Probability Distributions (1947). His tie to FHL is a line of doctoral advisers recorded in Wikidata. His student Monroe H. Martin supervised Simon A. Levin, whose FHL-connected papers in the census deal with plankton-feeding fishes (2002) and marine ecosystem-based management (2008). Levin's own student Daniel Grünbaum later taught in FHL's summer Larval Biology course.

name: Billie J. Swalla
text:
Billie J. Swalla is an evolutionary developmental biologist and professor emerita at the University of Washington, based at Friday Harbor Laboratories. She earned her BS, MS and PhD (1988) at the University of Iowa, then studied ascidian eggs as a postdoctoral fellow with William R. Jeffery at the University of Texas at Austin and was an assistant research developmental biologist at the University of California, Davis's Bodega Marine Laboratory (1991–94). She was an assistant professor at Vanderbilt University (1994–97) and Pennsylvania State University (1997–99), joined UW Zoology in 1999, and was professor from 2009 until becoming emerita in 2023. She was FHL's interim director from 2012 and director from 2014 to 2019, the first woman to hold the post, and taught FHL courses on the evolution and development of marine invertebrates. She was president of the Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology (2013–15). The census lists 72 FHL-connected papers, 2001–2024.

Her research uses tunicates, especially ascidians, and hemichordates to study how the chordate body plan evolved, combining embryology, gene expression, phylogenetics and genomics. Long-running themes include the loss of the larval tail in molgulid ascidians such as Molgula occulta, metamorphosis and coloniality in ascidians, regeneration in the acorn worm Ptychodera flava, and the relationships among deuterostome groups. Her FHL-connected papers include a cold-water clade of acorn worms (2013), phylogenomic analyses of hemichordates and echinoderms (2014) and of the major tunicate lineages (2017), a survey of hemichordate diversity (2016), a study of the disrupted Cymric gene in tailless Molgula (2023), and reviews of tunicates and vertebrate origins (2020) and of deuterostome ancestors (2024). She is also a co-author of FHL Ocean Observatory seawater datasets covering 2018 to 2024. Her former PhD students include Brad Davidson, Federico Brown, Amanda Rychel, Max Maliska and Shawn Luttrell.

name: Brad Davidson
text:
Brad Davidson is a developmental biologist and Associate Professor of Biology at Swarthmore College, where he earned a B.S. in biology in 1991. He took a Ph.D. in zoology at the University of Washington (1997–2002), was a postdoctoral fellow in Molecular and Cellular Biology at the University of California, Berkeley (2002–2006), and was an assistant professor of Molecular and Cellular Biology at the University of Arizona (2007–2012) before returning to Swarthmore in 2012. His FHL connection comes from his doctoral-era research on ascidian metamorphosis with Billie J. Swalla; their 2002 paper lists both the UW Zoology Department and Friday Harbor Laboratories. The census counts three FHL-address papers from 2002 to 2007, and the FHL bibliography also lists a 2013 paper on which he is senior author.

Davidson's lab uses the sea squirt Ciona intestinalis, whose simple embryos share many heart genes with vertebrates, to study the first steps of heart formation. It examines how fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling directs early heart cells, and has described an 'invasive signaling' mechanism, involving the neighbouring epidermis, that boosts it and may bear on cancer metastasis. His FHL-connected papers concern the solitary ascidian Boltenia villosa. In 2002 he and Swalla compared larval and juvenile transcripts by PCR subtraction and found that many genes expressed at metamorphosis match innate immune genes, suggesting an immune-like role in remodelling larval tissues. A 2003 paper characterized the morphology and gene expression of B. villosa metamorphosis, and a 2007 paper led by Brock Roberts proposed that a complement response may help trigger it. The 2013 paper showed that adhesion to the extracellular matrix controls where heart progenitors are induced in Ciona.

name: Brian Helmuth
text:
Brian Helmuth is a marine ecologist and Professor in the Department of Marine and Environmental Sciences at Northeastern University, with a joint appointment in the School of Public Policy and Urban Affairs, based at its Marine Science Center in Nahant, Massachusetts. He earned a BS at Cornell University (1989), where C. Drew Harvell supervised his research, an MS at Northeastern (1991) and a PhD in zoology at the University of Washington (1997) with Thomas Daniel, and was a postdoctoral researcher with Mark Denny at Stanford's Hopkins Marine Station (1997–1999). He was on the University of South Carolina faculty from 1999 to 2012 and moved to Northeastern in 2013. His CV lists an FHL seminar in May 2002, and FHL's list of visitors in the Whiteley Center's first two years names him, with Gretchen Hofmann, Ann Kinzig and Bruce Menge, in a group studying how environmental stress shapes rocky intertidal distributions.

Helmuth's research forecasts the ecological effects of climate change on coastal ecosystems, with a focus on the body temperatures of intertidal animals such as mussels. His group builds and deploys mussel-like temperature loggers ('robomussels'), runs physiological experiments and maps species' vulnerability to inform marine spatial planning. His FHL-connected papers run from 1996 to 2016. The first, with Dianna Padilla, Drew Harvell and Jessica Marks, examined inducible aggression and competition for space in the bryozoan Membranipora membranacea. Later papers treat latitudinal patterns of intertidal thermal stress (2002), the value of mechanistic biophysics for climate-change ecology (2005, with Joel Kingsolver and Emily Carrington), wave exposure and mosaic patterns of thermal stress on rocky shores (2006), temperature-dependent photosynthesis in the alga Fucus gardneri (2014, with Carrington and his doctoral student Nicholas Colvard, who held an FHL Alan and Marian Kohn Fellowship), and a long-term record of mussel-bed temperatures from biomimetic sensors (2016).

name: Brian S. Leander
text:
Brian S. Leander is a Professor in the Departments of Zoology and Botany at the University of British Columbia, where he was Assistant Professor from 2003, Associate Professor from 2008 and Professor from 2013. He earned a BSc in engineering science at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo (1993), a BSc and MA in comparative zoology at what is now Cal Poly Humboldt and a PhD in comparative biology at the University of Georgia (2001), and was an NSF postdoctoral fellow in UBC's Program in Microbial Biology (2001–2003). He was a Fellow and Senior Fellow of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (2003–2017) and a Tula Investigator (2007–2017), and has been a Hakai Research Affiliate since 2018. In his 2017–2019 census papers FHL is a collecting site, not an address: his group towed a plankton net off the FHL dock in June 2016, and FHL hosted one of its flatworm sampling campaigns.

Leander's laboratory studies the diversity, ultrastructure and evolution of marine microbial eukaryotes and tiny animals, with a focus on predatory protists. Its questions include how complex organelles such as the eye-like ocelloids and harpoon-like extrusive organelles of dinoflagellates arose, how parasitic gregarine apicomplexans evolved from free-living ancestors, and why unrelated lineages converge on similar traits. The group combines electron microscopy, including FIB-SEM, with transcriptomics, single-cell genomics and molecular phylogenetics, and collects at sites including Calvert Island, Bamfield and Curaçao. Its three FHL-connected papers are a 2017 study, led by his former doctoral student and postdoctoral fellow Gregory Gavelis, showing that the nematocyst-like organelles of dinoflagellates such as Polykrikos and Nematodinium arose independently of those of cnidarians; a 2018 molecular phylogeny of trigonostomine flatworms, with postdoctoral fellow Niels Van Steenkiste, that described four new northeast Pacific species; and a 2019 description of a 'nuclear net' of membranes inside the dinoflagellate nucleus.

name: Brooke L. Weigel
text:
Brooke L. Weigel is a marine ecologist who studies kelp forests and the microbes that live on kelp. She holds a BA in biology and environmental studies from St. Olaf College (2013), an MS in marine biology from the University of North Carolina Wilmington (2016) and a PhD in evolutionary biology from the University of Chicago (2021). Her doctoral research dealt with kelp forest ecology on Tatoosh Island, Washington, and was where she began studying kelp-associated microbes. She was then the Kelp Conservation Postdoctoral Researcher at FHL, studying why kelp are declining in Puget Sound, and a National Science Foundation postdoctoral fellow at Western Washington University. She is now assistant professor of oceans at Stanford University, with her laboratory at Hopkins Marine Station. The census lists eight FHL-connected items by her from 2022 to 2025.

Her research examines the feedbacks between climate change, kelp forests, microbes and ocean carbon cycling, using field and laboratory experiments, algal culturing, genomics, bioinformatics and scientific diving. At FHL she worked on the bull kelp, Nereocystis luetkeana, whose life cycle includes microscopic stages. A 2022 student report she co-authored and a 2023 paper test how temperature and nutrients affect gametophytes and young sporophytes, and another 2023 paper compares the effects of temperature and nitrogen on bull kelp and sugar kelp (Saccharina latissima). This work identified temperature thresholds for growth, survival and reproduction across the bull kelp life cycle. Her microbiome papers describe the diversity and functional capacity of microbes on coastal macrophytes (2022), map the kelp microbiome at micron scales (2022) and show that warm, nutrient-poor seawater changes the microbial community on a canopy kelp (2025). She also co-authored a 2025 population-genomic study of genetic drift in bull and giant kelp, aimed at guiding conservation.

name: Bruce W. Frost
text:
Bruce W. Frost, an oceanographer specializing in marine zooplankton, published his first paper in 1967, on a new harpacticoid copepod from Kodiak Island, Alaska, from the University of California's oceanography department at La Jolla; from 1974 his papers give the University of Washington as his institution. Rosters of the UW–FHL Advisory Board and Advisory Committee archived in 2004 list him, as Director of the UW School of Oceanography, among the members of both. His FHL-connected papers in the census date from 1990 to 2000. Most are studies of copepod behaviour written with Stephen M. Bollens, and FHL's 2000 list of publications resulting from research at the laboratories includes the series. The last is a 2000 progress report, with Christopher D. Jones of UW's Applied Physics Laboratory, on a portable acoustic laboratory first tested from the FHL pier.

Frost's papers range over copepod taxonomy, including the 1974 description of Calanus marshallae, copepod feeding and subarctic Pacific plankton ecology. His FHL-connected work centres on diel vertical migration in copepods and what drives it. With Bollens he examined how ultraviolet light affects the vertical distribution of Acartia hudsonica (1990) and, in 1991, reported enclosure experiments in which A. hudsonica quickly changed its depth and migration behaviour when threespine sticklebacks were present, which they read as behavioural flexibility of individuals rather than genetic change caused by selective predation. Further papers gave field evidence for the predator-avoidance hypothesis (1992), compared the vertical distributions and vulnerability to vertebrate predators of Metridia lucens and Calanus pacificus (1993), and tested chemical, mechanical and visual cues for migration (1994). The 2000 report, which names Frost as principal investigator of the project's UW part, concerns how organisms and biogenic structures affect sound propagation in seabed sediments.

name: Bruno Pernet
text:
Bruno Pernet is a professor of biological sciences at California State University, Long Beach, who studies the development, functional morphology and evolution of the larvae of marine invertebrates. He received a BA in biology from the University of California, Santa Cruz, and a PhD in zoology from the University of Washington; his papers from the late 1990s give addresses in UW's Department of Zoology and at Friday Harbor Laboratories. After postdoctoral research at the Smithsonian Marine Station at Fort Pierce, Florida, he spent several years teaching and doing research at the Oregon Institute of Marine Biology and at Friday Harbor Laboratories before moving to Long Beach. His FHL-addressed papers date from 1996 to 2004, and several later papers also draw on work at the laboratories. At Long Beach he led an NSF-funded project comparing how larvae with different ciliary feeding mechanisms capture food particles of different sizes.

Pernet's work centres on larval form and feeding, especially in annelids. His FHL-connected papers describe the capture of large particles by scaleworm larvae (1996), egg masses and development of the syllid Amblyosyllis speciosa (1998), opposed ciliary bands and large mouths in opheliid and echiurid larvae (1999), gamete interactions and genetic differentiation among three co-occurring polychaetes (1999), a scaleworm's setal "snorkel" and the reproduction of symbiotic scaleworms (2000), and ancestral feeding structures that persist in nonfeeding annelid larvae (2003). In 2004 he described the cryptic filtering house of an invertebrate larva and showed that dichromate oxidation underestimates the energy content of annelid eggs. Later work examined feeding by larvae of two developmental modes in Streblospio benedicti (2006), the risks of moving ghost shrimp as live bait (2008), larval feeding in a capitellid (2015), surveys for the annelid Ficopomatus enigmaticus (2017) and methods for rearing echinoderm larvae through metamorphosis (2018).

name: C. C. Ashley
text:
Christopher C. Ashley, a muscle physiologist at the University Laboratory of Physiology, Oxford, is named in FHL's account of discoveries made at the laboratories as one of the two scientists, with Ellis Ridgway, who first used aequorin as an intracellular calcium indicator. Aequorin, a calcium-sensitive light-emitting protein, had been isolated from luminescent jellyfish by Frank Johnson and Osamu Shimomura. Ashley and Ridgway injected it into single giant barnacle muscle fibres at Friday Harbor and recorded a calcium-driven light signal that preceded contraction; FHL's account notes that all the aequorin they used came from the laboratories. His FHL-connected papers in the census span 1970 to 2001, and FHL is among the author addresses on barnacle muscle papers of 1991 and 1993. With A. K. Campbell he edited the 1979 volume Detection and Measurement of Free Calcium in Cells.

Ashley's research concerns how calcium controls the activation, mechanics and relaxation of muscle, using the giant fibres of the barnacle Balanus nubilus alongside frog skeletal muscle. His 1970 paper with Ridgway in the Journal of Physiology related membrane potential, the calcium transient and tension in single barnacle fibres. Later FHL-connected work turned to the calcium-binding protein troponin C: a 1991 functional characterization of the two troponin C isoforms of Balanus nubilus, and studies from 1994 to 2000, with J. D. Potter, L. D. Allhouse and others, of genetically engineered barnacle troponin C, including mutants lacking particular calcium-binding sites, in skinned myofibrillar bundles. Other papers studied relaxation with the compound diazo-2 (1994, 1999), reviewed barnacle muscle calcium, activation and mechanics (1993), and used time-resolved X-ray diffraction to follow skinned skeletal muscle fibres during activation and shortening (2001).

name: C. Drew Harvell
text:
C. Drew Harvell (Catherine Drew Harvell) is a marine ecologist and Professor Emerita of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at Cornell University, which she joined in 1986. She earned BSc (1978) and MSc (1981) degrees in zoology at the University of Alberta, the latter with Fu-Shiang Chia, and a PhD in zoology at the University of Washington (1985) with a thesis on partial predation and inducible defences in the bryozoan Membranipora membranacea. She is affiliate faculty in UW's School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences and has taught Cornell's invertebrate biology course at Friday Harbor Laboratories, where her current research is based. She has led an NSF research coordination network on marine disease and curated Cornell's Blaschka glass invertebrate collection. Her honours include fellowship of the Ecological Society of America and the Society of American Naturalists' Jasper Loftus-Hills Award. Her books include A Sea of Glass (2016) and Ocean Outbreak (2019).

Harvell's FHL-connected papers run from 1984 to 2026. Her early work concerned inducible defences in bryozoans: a 1984 Science paper reported a predator-induced defence in a marine bryozoan, and papers through 1998 examined the cues, costs, genetic variation and evolution of inducible spines and polymorphism in Membranipora and other colonial animals. She later turned to disease in a warming ocean. Since 2015 her group's FHL-connected work has covered the sea star wasting epizootic, including ochre star mortality and the stars' immune responses; 2025 papers identified Vibrio pectenicida as a cause of the disease in the sunflower sea star. A parallel series on eelgrass wasting disease in the San Juan Islands finds that deeper, cooler meadows act as refuges, that grazers influence the disease and that altering the eelgrass microbiome can reduce its severity. Students linked to her in the report's network include Erika Iyengar, Maya Groner and Olivia Graham.

name: Carolyn C. deRoos
text:
Carolyn C. deRoos published research on the endocrinology of sharks and their relatives from 1962 to 1992. A 2015 notice in the Journal of the San Juans says she studied at the University of California, Berkeley, and describes her as the research partner of the comparative endocrinologist Roger McLean deRoos (1930–2015). He earned a PhD in zoology at Berkeley under Howard Bern and joined the University of Missouri faculty in 1961. According to the notice, the two spent most summers at FHL, where they studied glucose regulation in the spiny dogfish. The sources found do not give her own degrees or positions, so this profile rests mainly on her published record. The census lists eight FHL-connected papers by her. The three from 1962 to 1973 list FHL as an address, and the later five appear in FHL's research bibliography.

Her papers trace how the pituitary and the interrenal glands, which make corticosteroid hormones, work in cartilaginous fishes. The 1962 paper, with Bern and E. G. Biglieri, identified aldosterone and other corticosteroids from chondrichthyan interrenal glands, and a 1967 paper reported corticotropin (ACTH) activity in their pituitary glands. From 1973, working with Roger deRoos, she published a series of studies on blood glucose in the spiny dogfish, Squalus acanthias. These showed that mammalian ACTH (1973) and catecholamines (1978) raise plasma glucose, described severe hypoglycaemia caused by insulin (1979), and found that glucose rises after partial removal of the pituitary or after sham surgery (1980). Later papers measured glucose, alanine, lactate and beta-hydroxybutyrate in unfed dogfish after surgery and insulin infusion (1985), and the effects of ACTH on fuels and gluconeogenic substrates in the blood (1992). All eight papers appeared in General and Comparative Endocrinology.

name: Charles Bradley Shuster
text:
Charles Bradley (Brad) Shuster is a cell biologist at New Mexico State University (NMSU). The faculty directory lists him as professor and head of the Department of Biology, with research on the regulation of the actin and microtubule cytoskeletons. A 2015 NMSU announcement, when he was an associate professor, described two grants worth more than $1.2 million together. One, from the National Science Foundation, was on G-protein regulation of the actin cytoskeleton in the cleavage-stage embryo, and the other, from the National Institutes of Health, was on spindle orientation in echinoderm embryos. A 2017 seminar listing named him director of NMSU's Molecular Biology graduate program. His laboratory and John Henson's at Dickinson College share an NSF-supported study of cytokinesis, and the two groups work together in summers at FHL, using its sea urchins. The census lists eight FHL-connected papers by him, from 2008 to 2024.

Shuster studies how dividing embryonic cells build and position the cleavage furrow, using live imaging of sea urchin, sea star and sand dollar eggs injected with fluorescent fusion proteins. A 2012 paper with Victoria Foe and others tracked the centralspindlin and chromosomal passenger complexes in echinoderm embryos, in both normal and so-called Rappaport furrows. Papers with Henson's group describe the arrangement of actin and myosin II filaments in the contractile ring (2017), the ring's start as clusters of myosin II, anillin and septin (2021), and its later maturation, including the recruitment of alpha-actinin (2024). Other papers cover the role of Cdc42 in shaping sea urchin primary mesenchyme cells (2018), polar lobe formation in scallop embryos (2019) and the Wnt-pathway protein Dishevelled in the vegetal cortex of the egg (2021). His census list also includes a 2008 biochemistry paper on the signalling protein Grb7, which is listed in FHL's research bibliography.

name: Charles C. Lambert
text:
Charles C. Lambert (died 2011) was a developmental and reproductive biologist who worked mainly on ascidians (sea squirts). An FHL centennial timeline records that his association with the laboratories began in summer 1964, when as a graduate student he took the Invertebrate Zoology course; Gretchen Lambert, his research partner and co-author on many papers, began hers the same summer. He taught in the Department of Biological Science at California State University, Fullerton, for 28 years and was its campus Outstanding Professor for 1986. After retiring in 1998 he moved to Seattle to continue research in association with the University of Washington. He co-taught FHL's summer Comparative Invertebrate Embryology course in 1999 with Steve Stricker and in another year with Mark Martindale, and co-edited the 2001 volume The Biology of Ascidians. The census credits him with 23 FHL-connected papers, 1971-2014.

Lambert's research centered on fertilization and early development in ascidians. Early papers dealt with gene transcription during development and metamorphosis of Ascidia callosa (1971) and with light-triggered larval release in compound ascidians (1973); a 1978 Science paper with Gretchen Lambert showed that tunicate eggs use ammonium ions for flotation. Much of his later work examined gamete interactions: the ascidian sperm reaction and sperm mitochondrial movement (1982, 1984), a glycosidase released by eggs that helps block polyspermy (1989-1994), sperm-surface proteases (1994, 2001), and the block to hybridization and self-fertilization between two Ciona species (2000). He also studied sperm formation in the ratfish Hydrolagus colliei (1985, 1990), signaling pathways in oocyte maturation and the roles of follicle cells (2005-2011), and took part in rapid-assessment surveys of non-native species in harbors of California and southern England (2002-2006). His 2011 oocyte-maturation paper came from a symposium held at FHL in 2010.

name: Charles H. Greene
text:
Charles H. Greene is a biological oceanographer. He received a B.A. in biological oceanography from the University of Colorado in 1978 and a Ph.D. from the University of Washington in 1985, then spent a year as a postdoctoral fellow at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. He joined Cornell University in 1986 as a visiting assistant professor in the Division of Biological Sciences and became a professor in the Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences. He directed Cornell's Biological Resources Program and its Ocean Resources and Ecosystems Program, and his Cornell page now lists him as professor emeritus. His graduate-era papers on plankton predators (1985–1986) are in the FHL bibliography, and many later papers mention FHL or its Whiteley Center in their text. Since 2022 he has published with a Friday Harbor Laboratories affiliation, and the census counts three FHL-address papers (2022–2025).

Greene's early work asked how zooplankton predators choose prey. Papers of 1985 and 1986, two with Michael R. Landry, studied prey selection by the copepod Euchaeta elongata and the ctenophore Pleurobrachia bachei and grouped planktivores by how they encounter and capture prey. He then turned to bioacoustics, using high-frequency sound to measure zooplankton size distributions (1989) and studying sound scattering by gelatinous animals such as Aequorea victoria (1998). From 1993 he organized field courses in marine bioacoustics. In 2000 he organized the MERCINA working group on North Atlantic ecosystems and climate. Papers from 2003 to 2021 trace how climate shifts and Arctic change have affected Northwest Atlantic shelf ecosystems and the endangered North Atlantic right whale. Erin Meyer-Gutbrod, his student in the network, led a 2022 paper on shifting right whale habitat use. Since 2022 his papers have also proposed marine algae as a basis for sustainable aquaculture.

name: Charles J. O’Kelly
text:
Charles J. O'Kelly is a phycologist and protistologist who studies the diversity and evolution of algae and protists. His earliest papers, around 1980, came from the University of Washington's botany department and dealt with marine Chaetophoraceae, small green algae. From 1982 to 1985 his address was the botany department at Ohio State University, and his later papers list Massey University in New Zealand, the Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences in Maine and the University of Hawaii. At Bigelow he and Robert Andersen led an NSF-funded project (2000–2004) toward a monograph of the Ulvellaceae, and he took part in 2003 NASA Astrobiology Institute projects on eukaryotic origins. His papers from 2011 to 2022 give Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address; a 2022 review also lists him as Director of Applied Research at Cyanotech Corporation in Hawaii. The census counts 11 FHL-address papers by him, from 2011 to 2022.

O'Kelly uses cultures, microscopy and gene sequences to define species and lineages of small algae and protists. In the 1980s he studied the flagellar apparatus of algal motile cells as evidence on green algal phylogeny. He co-described the flagellate Malawimonas jakobiformis (1999) and co-authored the 2011 description of Subulatomonas tetraspora, a member of a previously unrecognized major clade of eukaryotes, and a 2017 study of Paramoeba amoebae and their endosymbionts. His FHL-period papers treat algal systematics: red algal orders around the genus Rhodella (2011), a new family for the green alga Cloniophora (2011), the Aegagropila clade of Cladophorales (2012), Ulva of Narragansett Bay (2013), a revision of Ulvella from cultured strains and tufA gene sequences (2013), new Ulvaceae from mesophotic Hawaiian habitats (2015), the genus Wittrockiella (2017) and Ostreobium, a green alga that lives inside rock (2022). Two 2012 papers concern amoebae and other contaminants of microalgal production cultures.

name: Christiane H. Biermann
text:
Christiane H. Biermann is an evolutionary biologist whose research concerns how marine invertebrates, especially sea urchins, become reproductively isolated. Bibliographic records link her papers from 1996 to 1999 to Stony Brook University. From about 1999 she was a postdoctoral researcher at FHL, studying the evolution of reproductive barriers and the population genetics of gamete-recognition proteins; FHL's 2002 program review lists 2001 funding to her and Jeb Byers through the UC Davis Marine Ecosystem Health Project. In 2004 UW described her as a research associate at FHL and adjunct biology faculty at Portland State University, and later FHL researcher listings give her affiliation as Portland State. Her FHL-connected papers date from 1999 to 2008. The census also holds a 1992 FHL paper by C. H. Biermann, with G. O. Schinner and Richard Strathmann, on how sunlight, algal fouling and currents affect egg-laying sites and embryo survival in a dorid nudibranch.

Most of her work concerns strongylocentrotid sea urchins and the molecules by which sperm and eggs recognise their own species. A 1998 single-author paper traced the molecular evolution of the sperm protein bindin in six species. Later papers described geographic divergence of gamete recognition in two Strongylocentrotus species (1999), showed with Paulo Mourão's group in Rio de Janeiro that sulfated fucans in the egg jelly of S. droebachiensis and S. pallidus ensure species-specific fertilization (2002), and, using green sea urchins from the San Juan Islands, proposed carbohydrate-based recognition as another route to speciation (2004). With Jessica Marks and colleagues she compared sperm polymorphism in Pacific and Atlantic populations of S. droebachiensis (2008). With Stephen Palumbi she studied the phylogeny of strongylocentrotid urchins as model species (2003), and with Erik Sotka and Jennifer Hempelmann she found genetic evidence of postglacial population expansion in the Puget Sound rockfish Sebastes emphaeus (2005).

name: Christopher W. Petersen
text:
Christopher W. Petersen is a biologist who studies the reproductive behaviour and ecology of marine fishes. He completed a doctoral dissertation at the University of Arizona in 1985 on the mating systems of tropical reef fishes in the Gulf of California, with case studies of simultaneous hermaphroditism and paternal care. His papers of 1986 to 1989 list the University of Arizona or the Department of Psychology at the University of Washington, and those of 1989 to 1991 list the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama and Friday Harbor Laboratories. Since 1992 his papers have come from the College of the Atlantic in Bar Harbor, Maine, most recently in 2025 and 2026. The census counts three FHL-address papers, from 1989 to 1991. A 2013 paper on plainfin midshipman fish in his census list is by a namesake, Christopher L. Petersen of Brooklyn College.

Petersen's research asks how mating systems, sex allocation and parental care evolve in reef fishes. His FHL-era papers include a 1989 study, with Karen Marchetti, of filial cannibalism (parents eating their own eggs) in the Cortez damselfish Stegastes rectifraenum and a 1989 paper showing that female carmine triplefins prefer males that are already mating. Two 1990 papers related population density, body size and mating tactics to reproductive success and gonad allocation in the hermaphroditic sea bass Serranus fasciatus. A 1990 paper with D. Ross Robertson and Jeffrey Brawn examined lunar spawning cycles in bottom-brooding reef fishes, and a 1991 study with Helen Hess examined spawning synchrony in a Caribbean damselfish. Later papers concern fertilization in the bluehead wrasse (1992), sex allocation in the chalk bass (1996), osmoregulation (2006) and spawning (2010) in the mummichog, shellfish and river herring co-management in Maine (2025) and intertidal hydroids of Mount Desert Rock (2026).

name: Clara F. Asnes
text:
Clara F. Asnes is a cell biologist who worked on microtubules and their protein, tubulin. Her earliest papers, from 1976 to 1981, were written with Leslie Wilson, and a 1979 paper gives her address as the Department of Biological Sciences at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Her papers from 1979 to 1983 carry a Friday Harbor Laboratories address, and the five FHL-connected papers in the census fall in those years. From 1984 to 1986 she published from the Department of Biology at the University of Rochester, including work with Joanna Olmsted on the microtubule-associated protein MAP 4. From 1999 to 2015 her name appears on papers from the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biophysics at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, with Elliot Elson and others, on cell contractility, growth cone motility and engineered heart tissue. No biographical source was found, so her positions are not known.

At Friday Harbor she worked with sea urchin eggs and sperm flagella. With Thomas E. Schroeder she examined the fine structure of cleaving eggs and reported evidence against the idea that aster microtubules stimulate the cleavage furrow at the cell's equator (1979). With Wilson she analysed inhibitors of microtubule assembly in sea urchin egg extracts and found evidence that a protease was responsible (1981). This followed a 1976 study that measured the tubulin content of unfertilized eggs of the sea urchin Strongylocentrotus purpuratus by colchicine binding. With Melvyn Little, Richard Ludueña and colleagues she compared how alpha- and beta-tubulins from distantly related species are cut by proteases (1981), and they proposed two major types of alpha-tubulin (1982). A 1983 paper with Jerome Parness and Susan Band Horwitz reported that the drug taxol binds differently to sperm-tail outer-doublet microtubules than to microtubules reassembled from their tubulin.

name: Claudia E. Mills
text:
Claudia E. Mills is a marine biologist who studies gelatinous zooplankton, especially medusae and ctenophores. She earned a B.A. in biology at Colorado College (1972), an M.S. in zoology at Florida State University (1976) with Richard N. Mariscal, and a Ph.D. in biology at the University of Victoria in Canada (1982) with George O. Mackie. She took summer courses at Friday Harbor Laboratories in 1974 and 1976, has been based at FHL since 1978 and works there year-round. She is an affiliate professor in the University of Washington Department of Biology and describes herself as an independent research scientist. She has held visiting postdoctoral or research posts of several months in New Zealand, at the marine stations of Villefranche-sur-Mer and Roscoff in France, and at Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution in Florida. The census counts 31 FHL-address papers by her from 1981 to 2023.

Mills's work ranges from individual behaviour to the structure of midwater communities. Early FHL papers dealt with swimming behaviour and feeding in hydromedusae (1981) and with how medusae and ctenophores change density and ion balance with salinity (1984). Dives in manned submersibles in the Ligurian Sea and the western Atlantic (1989, 1991) gave in situ observations of foraging and of the small-scale distribution of macroplankton, and papers on nematocysts and kleptocnidism related stinging-cell types to diet. She described a new medusa (1985) and a new colonial hydroid (1993) from the waters of British Columbia and Washington, documented two Black Sea hydromedusae introduced to San Francisco Bay (1995), and asked whether jellyfish blooms are increasing worldwide (2001, 2012). Recent work covers the anatomy and systematics of stalked jellyfishes (Staurozoa), including Haliclystus sanjuanensis (2023), and contributions to the 2014 ctenophore genome paper and to studies of trachymedusan swimming and ctenophore speciation.

name: Clyde Manwell
text:
Clyde Manwell was a zoologist and comparative biochemist who studied respiratory pigments and, later, protein variation in animals. His FHL-connected papers, from 1957 to 1960, give his address as the Department of Biological Sciences at Stanford University together with the University of Washington's marine laboratories at Friday Harbor. A 1963 paper lists the University of Illinois at Urbana, a 1969 paper the Marine Biological Association laboratory at Plymouth, England, and by the early 1970s he was a professor in the Department of Zoology at the University of Adelaide. With C. M. Ann Baker he wrote Molecular Biology and the Origin of Species: Heterosis, Protein Polymorphism and Animal Breeding (1970). In the early 1970s he publicly criticized aspects of the South Australian government's fruit-fly spraying; a complaint by his head of department led to an attempt to dismiss him, which failed after about four years. He took early retirement in 1986.

Manwell's FHL-period papers used oxygen-equilibrium and alkaline-denaturation measurements to compare hemoglobins and related pigments across animal groups. He described changes in hemoglobin during development in the cabezon, Scorpaenichthys marmoratus (1957), and the skate Raja binoculata (1958), and compared the hemoglobins of two diving birds (1958). He measured the hemocyanin and myoglobin of the gumboot chiton Cryptochiton stelleri (1958), annelid hemoglobins (1959), the hemoglobin of the sea cucumber Cucumaria miniata, which lacks a Bohr effect (1959), and heme–heme interactions in invertebrate myoglobins (1960). A 1960 paper compared body-cavity and muscle hemoglobins in the polychaete Travisia pupa and the echiuran Arhynchite pugettensis. From the 1960s, often with Baker, he used starch-gel electrophoresis to study protein polymorphism, hybrid vigor and species differences in animals from sea cucumbers to birds, sheep and cattle.
