name: Colette J. Feehan
text:
Colette J. Feehan is a marine ecologist and Associate Professor of Biology at Montclair State University in New Jersey. She completed a doctoral thesis at Dalhousie University in Halifax, Nova Scotia, in 2015 on the regulation of sea urchin populations in Nova Scotian kelp beds. Her papers of 2010 to 2015 come from Dalhousie's Department of Biology, many written with Robert E. Scheibling. She then published from the Department of Marine and Coastal Sciences at Rutgers University and, from 2017, from Montclair State. Her papers of 2017 and 2018 also list Friday Harbor Laboratories and report sea urchin studies with FHL-based co-authors, among them Richard R. Strathmann, Megan N. Dethier and David O. Duggins. The census counts three FHL-address papers from 2017 to 2018.

Montclair State lists her research interests as marine ecosystems, host–pathogen and predator–prey interactions, disease ecology and climate-change ecology. In Nova Scotia she studied outbreaks of an amoebic disease that kill sea urchins and help kelp beds persist; a 2016 paper linked these outbreaks to storms, and a 2015 paper with Karen Filbee-Dexter and Scheibling documented large-scale degradation of kelp beds in an ocean-warming hotspot. Her FHL papers concern Northeast Pacific sea urchins. With Dara Yiu she showed in 2017 that articulated coralline algae shelter juvenile urchins from predatory crabs. Another 2017 paper found that detritus from the kelp Nereocystis luetkeana is high-quality food for urchin larvae. A 2018 study, prompted by the 2013–2016 warm 'Blob', found that warm water combined with scarce phytoplankton or a kelp-detritus diet slowed development and raised mortality in larvae of Strongylocentrotus droebachiensis. Later papers address kelp forests, Caribbean Diadema urchins and tropical cyclones.

name: D. A. Dorsett
text:
D. A. Dorsett is a neurobiologist who studied the nervous systems and behaviour of marine invertebrates, especially opisthobranch molluscs. His publications, from 1961 to 1991, give the Department of Zoology at Queen Mary College, London (1961), University College Ibadan in Nigeria (1962) and, from 1962, the Marine Science Laboratories at Menai Bridge, Anglesey, of the University College of North Wales; papers of 1989 to 1991 give its biology schools at Bangor. A 1980 paper describes him as Reader in Marine Biology at the University College of North Wales. His work on Tritonia with A. O. D. Willows and Graham Hoyle began with a 1969 paper whose addresses include the University of Oregon. Three 1973 papers with Willows and Hoyle give Dorsett's address as Friday Harbor Laboratories, and a 1975 paper with Willows gives both FHL and Menai Bridge. No biographical source was found, so his role at FHL is not stated.

Dorsett's early papers concerned tube-building and reproduction in the polychaete Polydora ciliata, flight preparation in hawk-moths, and the innervation, sense organs and glands of the ragworm Nereis. From 1967 he worked on giant neurons in the brain of the nudibranch Tritonia. The FHL-connected series with Willows and Hoyle mapped the functional organization of the central nervous system of Tritonia diomedea, proposed a standard system of abbreviations and cell numbers for its ganglia, nerve trunks and giant cells, and showed that the motor pattern of escape swimming, a fixed action pattern, originates centrally and can be produced by the isolated brain. Papers in 1974 and 1975 compared the neurons controlling branchial tuft withdrawal in T. hombergi and T. diomedea and related the evolution of swimming to its neural correlates. His later work examined feeding circuits of T. hombergi, barnacle proprioceptors, and the buccal neurons and muscles of Philine aperta.

name: DO Duggins
text:
David O. Duggins is a marine ecologist who worked at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 1979 as research vessel master and research biologist. He received a BA in zoology (1974) and a PhD in wildlife biology (1980) from the University of Washington; his dissertation was an experimental study of sea urchins, their predators and their algal food in kelp-dominated communities. His 2002 CV lists him as Marine Technologist and Research Vessel Master at FHL from 1979 and Senior Research Biologist from 1985, and lists teaching at the Bamfield Marine Station in British Columbia and in Carleton College and Northeastern University programs. In 1999 he began working with local schoolteachers on K-12 marine science. In early 2016 FHL reported that he had retired as its Marine Operations Manager more than a year earlier; its people page still lists him among resident scientists. His census papers run from 1980 to 2013.

Duggins studies kelp forests and other nearshore communities through field experiments and measurements of water flow. Early work included rocky shore surveys for the National Park Service's Dixon Harbor Biological Survey (1975, 1976). He took an experimental approach to kelp beds and sea otters (1980) and showed how starfish predation creates mosaic patterns in a kelp-dominated community (1983). With Megan Dethier he described an indirect commensalism between marine herbivores (1984) and compared strong interactions on Washington and Alaska shores (1988); with James Estes he reviewed sea otters and kelp forests in Alaska (1995). With James Eckman, from 1989, he studied how understory kelps alter water flow and how flow speed affects the growth of suspension feeders (1993) and larval settlement (1998). Later papers dealt with chemical defences in Washington kelps (1998), currents, waves and kelp biomechanics (2003), bull kelp bed size (2008) and seaweed isotope and fatty-acid variation that can confound food-web studies (2013).

name: Daniel Grünbaum
text:
Daniel Grünbaum is an oceanographer who applies mathematical models and fluid mechanics to biological questions. He received his PhD from Cornell University in 1992 under Simon A. Levin, with a dissertation modelling bryozoan feeding currents and density-dependent aggregation in Antarctic krill. His papers of the late 1990s give Cornell, the mathematics departments of the University of Utah and the University of British Columbia, and the UW Department of Zoology; from 2008 they give the UW School of Oceanography, where a 2014 BioScience paper lists him as an associate professor. His bryozoan papers of 1995 to 1998 mention FHL or appear in its bibliographies, and the census counts FHL-connected papers from 2010 to 2020. Kit Yu Karen Chan, listed in Wikidata as his doctoral student, and Sasha K. Seroy were his co-authors on this larval and ocean-acidification work. He is also an author of 2018–2020 datasets from the sensor array of the Friday Harbor Laboratories Ocean Observatory.

His work asks how small organisms feed, swim and aggregate. Papers of 1995 to 1998 modelled feeding currents in encrusting bryozoans, showing interference between zooids within a colony, analysed the hydromechanics of colony organization and the cost of defence in Membranipora membranacea, and examined the geometry of ciliated tentacle arrays in suspension feeders. A 2008 paper tested whether advection–diffusion equations describe swarming and schooling groups. From 2010 his FHL-connected work centred on ciliated larvae: with Tansy W. Clay he examined how swimming performance constrains the form of echinoid plutei and how morphology and flow lead to stage-selective vertical transport of sand dollar larvae in shear, and with Chan he studied how temperature, diet and acidification-induced changes in shape alter larval swimming and feeding. Later papers addressed ocean acidification and the interaction between Membranipora and the nudibranch Corambe steinbergae near FHL (2018, with Seroy) and the vertical distribution of echinoid larvae in pH-stratified water (2020).

name: Dara S. Yiu
text:
Dara S. Yiu is a marine ecologist whose published work deals with nearshore communities in Washington State and, more recently, kelp forests and turf reefs in the Gulf of Maine. No biographical profile was found, so this summary relies on the affiliations printed in Yiu's papers. All three census papers, from 2017, 2019 and 2024, give Friday Harbor Laboratories as an address, and the 2019 paper also lists the University of Washington's School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences. A 2022 paper lists Montclair State University in New Jersey together with that UW school, and papers from 2025 and 2026 list the Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences in East Boothbay and the University of Maine. Co-authors on the FHL papers are Colette Feehan, Megan Dethier, Julia Kobelt, Lindsay Wentzel and Jennifer Ruesink.

Yiu's research concerns how habitat structure, predators and physical conditions shape the survival of young invertebrates, and how kelp loss changes reef ecosystems. The FHL-connected papers show that articulated coralline algae give juvenile sea urchins a refuge from predatory crabs (2017, with Colette Feehan), examine how the influence of abiotic and biotic factors on the performance of juvenile clams depends on context (2019), and describe how clam recruitment varies among beaches and years in Washington State (2024). A 2022 multi-author study found that warming speeds kelp decomposition and lowers the carbon sink potential of kelp forests. Papers from 2025 and 2026 examine how the replacement of kelp forests by turf algae changes reef chemistry, the reef microbiome, energy flow to predators and functional diversity, and a 2025 University of Maine thesis listed under Yiu's name compares reef fish communities on kelp- and turf-dominated reefs in the Gulf of Maine.

name: David H. Gire
text:
David H. Gire is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Washington, in its Neural Systems and Behavior area, and was promoted with tenure in 2022; a 2022 paper also lists him in the UW Astrobiology Program. He trained at the University of Colorado at Denver School of Medicine (2009). His FHL-connected papers date from 2021 to 2025 and come from octopus research done at the laboratories. A 2021 paper notes that Gire and Dominic Sivitilli, whose UW PhD (2023) Gire advised, received funding and research support from FHL. Gire was also the UW faculty mentor and a close collaborator for Willem Weertman's master's research at Alaska Pacific University, whose experiments took place at FHL.

Gire's laboratory studies how neural circuits process sensory signals during active sensing to guide behaviours such as finding food, with a focus on mammalian olfaction and comparisons across species; its methods include electrophysiology, calcium imaging, optogenetics and automated analysis of behaviour. At FHL the group has turned these questions to octopuses. Papers with Sivitilli argue that the octopus's distributed nervous system offers lessons for soft robotics (2022, with Joshua Smith) and show that arm search without visual feedback relies on contact and local coordination among suckers (2023); Sivitilli's dissertation identified sucker recruitment as a key search mechanism. Gire was also a coauthor of a 2021 paper presenting the lesser Pacific striped octopus, Octopus chierchiae, as a laboratory model. Work with Weertman, David Scheel and Venkatesh Gopal, reported from 2021 and published in PLOS ONE in 2025, showed in a flume at FHL that Octopus rubescens tracks odour plumes to find food.

name: David O. Duggins
text:
David O. Duggins is a marine ecologist who worked as a research scientist at Friday Harbor Laboratories for 40 years before retiring in 2016. He earned a bachelor's degree in zoology and a Ph.D. in wildlife biology at the University of Washington. His academic expertise is the effect of disturbance on ecological communities, studied mainly in marine systems. At FHL he founded and directed the Marine Science Outreach Program, a partnership among the university, public and private schools and government agencies for K-12 science education and stewardship. He was also among the FHL supervisors of graduate student Aaron Galloway (2007-2013), with whom he published fatty acid studies of nearshore food webs. The census counts 27 FHL-address papers from 1981 to 2026; his co-authored papers continue after his retirement.

Duggins's research concerns kelp forests and the food webs they support. Early papers examined growth and longevity in a crustose red alga (1979), facilitation among benthic grazers and sea urchin responses to short-term diet changes (1981), and herbivory and algal competition in a low intertidal habitat (1985). A 1989 Science paper with Charles Simenstad and James Estes used a natural experiment to show that benthic suspension feeders grew much faster where kelp detritus was present and that kelp-derived carbon is found throughout the nearshore food web. Related studies covered how understory kelps affect water flow, invertebrate recruitment and suspension-feeder growth (1989-1994), chemical defences in kelps and rockweeds, and kelp gametophytes living inside red algae (1999). Later FHL work used fatty acid and stable isotope biomarkers to trace kelp detritus through benthic food webs, and examined drift kelp as habitat for invertebrates and as food for sea urchins and their larvae (2011-2019).

name: Dawn Vaughn
text:
Dawn Vaughn is a marine biologist who has studied the defences of planktonic invertebrate larvae and the effects of warming on intertidal snails. Her FHL-connected papers, from 2007 to 2011, give her address as the University of Washington Department of Biology and Friday Harbor Laboratories, and in 2008 news coverage described her as a biology doctoral student at FHL. She then worked at FHL as a postdoctoral researcher in Emily Carrington's laboratory. FHL's autumn 2012 newsletter reported that she had left for a faculty position at California State University, Northridge, and FHL's December 2013 Tide Bites newsletter described her postdoctoral research on snails.

Most of her FHL work asks how planktonic larvae respond to predators. In a 2007 paper, larvae of the snail Littorina scutulata reared with crab larvae developed rounder shells with smaller openings and survived predation better. In 2008 Vaughn and Richard Strathmann reported in Science that larvae of the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus clone in response to predator cues: exposed to fish mucus, they produced clones within a day, and the clones were smaller, which may help against fish that hunt by sight. Later papers asked whether mothers influence this response (2009), showed with Kathryn McDonald that an abrupt increase in food can also trigger cloning (2010), and presented cloning and smaller size as an inducible defence (2010). As a postdoctoral researcher she used heat lamps over outdoor tanks at FHL to test how warmer low-tide air affects foraging and growth of male and female snails, including Nucella ostrina in a 2011 student project.

name: Deborah A. Giles
text:
Deborah A. Giles is a marine mammal biologist who studies the endangered Southern Resident killer whales (Orcinus orca) of the Salish Sea. She received her PhD from the University of California, Davis, in 2014, with a dissertation on the Southern Residents. From 2009 to 2021 she worked as a vessel captain for the University of Washington, using a scat-detection dog to find floating killer whale feces so that the whales' physiological health could be monitored. That program is now run by the nonprofit Wild Orca, where she is science and research director. She is a resident scientist and lecturer at FHL, where she teaches Marine Mammals of the Salish Sea and Marine Biology. The census lists twelve FHL-connected items by her from 2018 to 2026, both journal papers and conference abstracts.

Her work combines non-invasive sampling with behavioural and acoustic study of free-ranging whales. A 2018 paper profiled contaminants in Southern Resident fecal samples as a baseline before any oil spill and found signs of possible exposure to vessel exhaust. Most of her other FHL-connected papers come from a collaborative study, with Marla Holt, Jennifer Tennessen and others, in which archival tags recorded the movements and sounds of individual fish-eating killer whales. Two 2019 papers used hidden Markov models to describe daily patterns of behaviour, and identified the movement signatures of prey capture, finding differences between males and females. Papers in 2021 and 2024 report that vessels and their noise reduce prey-capture effort and success, in part through auditory masking. A 2023 paper compares foraging strategies between killer whale populations that share the same waters, and a 2026 paper describes daily cycles of echolocation-based foraging.

name: Dianna K. Padilla
text:
Dianna K. Padilla is Professor in the Department of Ecology and Evolution at Stony Brook University, where she joined the faculty in 1998 and became Professor in 2006, with an affiliated appointment in the School of Marine and Atmospheric Sciences. She earned BAs in zoology and biological oceanography at the University of Washington (1978), an MS at Oregon State University (1982) and a PhD in zoology at the University of Alberta (1987), was a postdoc at Cornell (1987–1989) and was on the zoology faculty at the University of Wisconsin–Madison (1989–1998). She was an NSF program director in Integrative Organismal Systems (2006–2007) and president of the American Malacological Society (2004–2005). Her FHL ties include doctoral fieldwork partly done at FHL, seminars there in 1990–1992, a 1994 honours thesis she supervised at FHL, the FHL Academic Advisory Board from 2002, research at FHL in 2012–2016 and co-teaching Advanced Invertebrate Biology there in 2014.

Padilla studies phenotypic plasticity, especially inducible offences and defences in marine invertebrates, and the ecology of introduced species. Her doctoral work related seaweed calcification and form to how herbivores feed, and a 1993 paper described 'rip stop' features that limit herbivore damage in algae. FHL-based papers examined inducible aggression and competition for space in the bryozoan Membranipora membranacea (1996, with Drew Harvell, Jessica Marks and Brian Helmuth) and radula production and diet-induced radula change in Lacuna snails (1996, 1998); her later FHL research turned to the snails' crab and sea-star predators. Other FHL-connected papers treat the Pacific oyster Crassostrea gigas as a non-native ecosystem engineer (2010) and its larval food selection (2020), and predator-induced phenotypes in a marine snail (2019); several acknowledge the Whiteley Center. Many census entries concern the spread and impacts of zebra and quagga mussels, much of it with collaborator Alexander Karatayev.

name: Dina F. Mandoli
text:
Dina F. Mandoli is a plant developmental biologist. Her early papers (1981–1985) came from the Carnegie Institution of Washington's Department of Plant Biology at Stanford and concerned phytochrome and light-piping in plant tissues such as etiolated oat seedlings. From 1990 her papers give the University of Washington's Department of Botany as her address, and her 2006 paper the UW Department of Biology and Center for Developmental Biology. Her FHL-connected papers, from 1999 to 2006, come from her laboratory's work on the green alga Acetabularia acetabulum. FHL course lists name her, alongside G. M. Odell, as an instructor of research apprenticeships on development and morphogenesis in Acetabularia (2000) and on the cell biology of morphogenesis and development (2002), and a 2004 paper acknowledges an FHL apprenticeship course among its sources of support. She also edited a 2000 collection on emerging models in plant biology for the Journal of Plant Growth Regulation.

Mandoli's research uses Acetabularia, a giant single-celled green alga of the Dasycladales, as a model for subcellular localization and morphogenesis during development. Her FHL-listed papers address the roles of light and the nucleus in timing reproductive onset (1999, with René Kratz), physiological factors that help zygotes and juveniles differentiate (1999), and the developmentally regulated subcellular localization of Aaknox1, a knotted1-like homeobox gene (1999, with Kyle Serikawa). Others found subcellular domains of calcification and of proton and oxygen flux along the cell (2000), related growth, shape and wall stress in the stalk (2001, with Michelangelo von Dassow and G. M. Odell), compared expressed sequence tags from juvenile and adult phases (2004), and showed with spectroscopy and biochemistry that walls of the diploid phase are mainly a para-crystalline mannan, while the haploid gametangia have cellulose-based walls (2006).

name: Dorothy Hinshaw Patent
text:
Dorothy Hinshaw Patent is a zoologist and an author of nonfiction books for young readers. She earned a B.A. from Stanford University in 1962, and an M.A. (1965) and Ph.D. (1968) in zoology from the University of California, Berkeley, and studied at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 1965 to 1967. She was a postdoctoral fellow at Sinai Hospital in Detroit (1968–1969) and a postdoctoral researcher at the Stazione Zoologica in Naples (1970–1971). She later held faculty affiliate appointments at the University of Montana in zoology (1975–1990, including a term as acting assistant professor in 1977) and in environmental studies (from 1995). Rather than become a professor or researcher, she chose to focus mainly on writing for young readers. The census counts three FHL-address papers, from 1969 and 1970, which give both the Berkeley zoology department and FHL as her address.

Her FHL papers deal with basket stars of the genus Gorgonocephalus, brittle stars with branching arms. A 1969 paper followed the reproductive cycle of G. caryi through monthly gonad samples, finding an annual cycle with spawning spread over six months, and a 1970 paper described its early embryology. A second 1970 paper described the life history of G. eucnemis in the San Juan Islands and reported very small young living inside polyps of the soft coral Gersemia, where it suggested the embryos develop. She has since written more than 100 nonfiction books for children, including The Lives of Spiders (Golden Kite Award, 1980). With Vicki Cobb she co-founded iNK Think Tank, a group of nonfiction writers for young readers. She received the American Nature Study Society's Eva L. Gordon Award (1987) and the Washington Post/Children's Book Guild Nonfiction Award (2004).

name: Douglas J. Eernisse
text:
Douglas J. Eernisse is a marine biologist and Professor in the Department of Biological Science at California State University, Fullerton, where he has worked since 1994. He received a BS in zoology from the University of Washington and a PhD from the University of California, Santa Cruz. His 1986 monograph on the chiton genus Lepidochitona, part of his doctoral work, gives his former address as UC Santa Cruz's Institute of Marine Sciences and his present address as FHL, and says its final revisions were made while he held an FHL postdoctoral fellowship. A 1988 paper with Diarmaid Ó Foighil also gives FHL as the authors' address. FHL's list of visitors in the Whiteley Center's first two years records him co-writing a book synthesizing animal relationships, and his 2010 description of a new sea star was supported by FHL and an NSF grant held with Richard Strathmann, with drafts prepared during Whiteley Center visits.

Eernisse's papers concern the systematics, reproduction and evolution of marine invertebrates, especially chitons (Polyplacophora), and his FHL-connected papers span 1986 to 2010. His 1986 revision of Lepidochitona in the Oregonian and Californian provinces described three new species, among them L. fernaldi, a brooding hermaphroditic chiton named for Robert L. Fernald, whom the monograph calls a teacher of invertebrate reproduction at FHL; a 1993 paper with John Buckland-Nicks described its sperm and egg ultrastructure and mechanism of fertilization. He also reported tissue hemoglobins in the red foot of a lepidopleurid chiton (1988, with Nora and Robert Terwilliger) and, with Ó Foighil, used enzyme variation to identify widespread, non-hybridizing sympatric strains of the brooding clam Lasaea (1988). With Richard Strathmann he reviewed what molecular phylogenies show about the evolution of larval forms (1994), and with Megumi and Richard Strathmann he described the brooding sea star Henricia pumila (2010).

name: E B Ridgway
text:
Ellis B. Ridgway, a physiologist, studied calcium signals in muscle, nerve cells and eggs using aequorin, a calcium-sensitive photoprotein from jellyfish. His papers of 1988 and 1993 give the Department of Physiology at the Medical College of Virginia in Richmond as his address. Wikipedia's article on aequorin cites his 1967 paper with C. C. Ashley on calcium transients in single muscle fibres for the first experiments in which injected aequorin was used to visualise the release of calcium, in barnacle muscle fibres. In 1970 he and Ashley related membrane potential, calcium transient and tension in barnacle fibres, and in 1971 he published with P. F. Baker and A. L. Hodgkin on calcium entry in squid giant axons. His papers with a Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) address or acknowledgement run from 1976 to 1999, and several thank the FHL director and staff for their hospitality.

At FHL, Ridgway worked mainly with the giant barnacle Balanus nubilus, whose large muscle fibres he injected with aequorin; the barnacles were dredged from Lopez Pass and kept in the laboratory's running seawater. With Albert M. Gordon of the University of Washington he showed that calcium release depends on fibre length (1976), then studied how shortening and stretch after stimulation change calcium binding to the activating sites and how this relates to cross-bridge attachment and force (1984–1993); they also measured resting free calcium with modified aequorins (1993, 1995). In 1977 he co-authored a study of calcium entry in aequorin-injected mollusc neurons with Roger Eckert and D. L. Tillotson. From 1987 to 1999 he worked with Gary Freeman of the University of Texas on hydrozoans such as Phialidium, studying oocyte maturation and using the animals' own photoproteins to follow calcium during fertilization, cleavage and larval metamorphosis, and calcium fluxes tied to exocytosis and endocytosis.

name: E. J. Lund
text:
Elmer Julius Lund (1884–1969) was an American physiologist who studied bioelectricity and growth. He received a bachelor's degree from Hamline University in 1910 and a PhD from Johns Hopkins University in 1914. In 1926 he joined the Department of Zoology at the University of Texas, where he was a professor until 1949. After investigating a large fish kill at Port Aransas in 1935, later attributed to a red tide, he persuaded the university to build a marine laboratory on the Texas coast. The Institute of Marine Science was formally founded there in 1941, with Lund as its first director until 1949. The census counts nine FHL-address papers from 1921 to 1931, when the station was the Puget Sound Biological Station. Four of them appeared in the station's own Publications series in 1929 and 1930.

Lund asked whether steady electrical potentials in living tissue are tied to cell oxidation and help set the polarity of growth. A five-part series in the Journal of Experimental Zoology (1921–1925) used regenerating stem segments of the hydroid Obelia to show the colony's normal electrical polarity, and measured how applied currents of different density and orientation delay or inhibit polyp formation. Later papers showed that cyanide, ether and chloroform reversibly suppress the electrical polarity of Obelia and frog skin (1926), and related bioelectric potential quantitatively to cell oxidation (1928). From 1929 to 1931 he mapped electric polarity in the Douglas fir, including the electrical dominance of growing tips and the potentials between living cells of cortex and wood. He summarized this program in the book Bioelectric Fields and Growth (1947). At Port Aransas he and his student Gordon Gunter studied Texas marine fishes and fouling on ships' bottoms.

name: E. Sanford Branscomb
text:
E. Sanford Branscomb's published work, from 1976 to 2014, concerns the larvae of barnacles and crabs. The two 1976 papers come from the University of Maryland's Chesapeake Biological Laboratory at Solomons. One, with S. D. Sulkin and Robert E. Miller, concerns inducing winter spawning and rearing larvae of the blue crab. The other, a single-author study, examines causes of death limiting the distribution and abundance of the barnacle Balanus improvisus in Chesapeake Bay. The 1981 paper lists the University of Washington Zoology Department at Friday Harbor Laboratories, and the 1982 paper lists FHL. Papers of 1984 and 1985, with Dan Rittschof and John D. Costlow, list the Duke University Marine Laboratory in Beaufort, North Carolina. A 2014 paper again lists FHL and the UW Department of Biology. The census counts three FHL-address papers (1981, 1982 and 2014). No public biography was found, so no positions are given.

Branscomb's FHL work, with Karen Vedder and Richard R. Strathmann, concerns how barnacle larvae develop, settle and hatch. The 1981 paper treated settlement where young barnacles die as a cost of larval dispersal and examined how intertidal plants and algae affect settlement. The 1982 paper described the naupliar stages of three Puget Sound barnacles, Balanus glandula, B. cariosus and B. crenatus; the larvae of the first two had not been described before. The 2014 paper found that B. glandula broods reaching hatching stages at different times over winter all hatched within about two weeks in spring. Crabs breaking a brooding barnacle's shell set off hatching, while whelks, which leave the shell plates in place, posed a greater risk to the brooded larvae. At Duke the work concerned settlement in relation to water flow and surfaces, low-frequency sound as a deterrent, and settlement inhibitors from the whip coral Leptogorgia virgulata.

name: E. W. Misty Paig‐Tran
text:
E. W. Misty Paig-Tran is a functional morphologist and biomechanist who works mainly on fishes, especially cartilaginous filter feeders. She received a B.S. in marine biology from California State University, Long Beach (2006) and a Ph.D. in biology from the University of Washington (2012). Her supervisory committee was chaired by Adam P. Summers, then associate director of FHL. Since 2014 she has been in the Department of Biological Sciences at California State University, Fullerton, where her ORCID record lists her as professor. Her 2011 paper gives FHL as her address, and her doctoral papers through 2014 list FHL among the authors' addresses. A Strathmann Fellowship paid for her housing at FHL, and excised gill arches were shipped to FHL for examination for her thesis. Later papers, through 2025, have FHL-based co-authors, and some used micro-CT scanning at FHL's Karel F. Liem imaging center.

Her research asks how the shape and material of biological structures determine how they perform. Her dissertation examined filtration in the devil rays (Mobulidae) using dissection, scanning electron microscopy, histology, modelling and measurements of live feeding. It described rigid, chevron-shaped cartilaginous filter pads and a flow path that turns abruptly through the filter pores. Related papers used physical models of ram-feeding fishes to predict how swimming speed and gill-slit design affect size selectivity and filtering efficiency (2011), described variation in devil ray filter pads (2013) and compared the branchial filters of suspension-feeding sharks and rays (2014). Later FHL-linked papers covered jaw protrusion in the king-of-the-salmon (2019), the scales of a small armored catfish (2020) and baleen structure in rorqual whales (2023). A 2025 group of papers concerns biological armor, armadillo-inspired tiles, mobulid filters and bioinspiration. Her ORCID record also lists work on whale sharks, manta rays and megamouth sharks.

name: Edsel A. Caine
text:
Edsel A. Caine is a marine invertebrate zoologist whose papers, from 1974 to 1998, deal mainly with caprellid amphipods (skeleton shrimps). His earliest papers, of 1974 and 1975, several giving Florida State University, covered feeding morphology in caprellids of the northwestern Florida Gulf coast, feeding in crabs and anomurans, and the zoogeography of Florida's cave crayfishes. The census counts four FHL-address papers from 1976 to 1980; the first gives both the Department of Biology at the University of Tampa and Friday Harbor Laboratories, and a 1978 paper gives the Department of Zoology at Mississippi State University. From 1980 his papers give the Department of Marine Science at the University of South Carolina at Beaufort, often with the Belle W. Baruch Institute for Marine Biology and Coastal Research, and in 1998 the Department of Biology at USC Beaufort. No biographical source was found, so his positions and role at FHL are not stated.

Caine studied how caprellids feed, groom, swim and use their habitats. His FHL papers concern caprellids of Puget Sound and the Washington shore: a 1976 paper compared cleansing (grooming) mechanisms of North American caprellids, a 1977 paper related feeding mechanisms to possible resource partitioning among Puget Sound species, and papers in 1979 and 1980 described the population structure of two species and the ecology of two littoral species in Washington. Related papers of the same years examined habitat adaptations of North American caprellids (1978) and the function of their swimming setae (1979). In South Carolina he went on to study community interactions of Caprella penantis on sea whips, epibionts on the carapaces of nesting loggerhead turtles, floating-dock fouling communities, wave exposure and caprellid robustness, caprellid behaviour under fish predation, reproductive behaviour and sexual dimorphism, and a caprellid–hydrozoan mutualism (1998).

name: Edward J. DeVillez
text:
Edward J. DeVillez is a comparative physiologist and biochemist whose published research, from 1964 to 1986, concerns the digestive enzymes of invertebrates. No biographical notice was found, so this profile rests on the addresses given in his papers. A 1965 paper gives the Department of Physiology and Biophysics at the University of Illinois, Urbana. From 1967 to 1985 his papers give the Department of Zoology and Physiology, later the Department of Zoology, at Miami University in Oxford, Ohio. Three papers, from 1964, 1967 and 1975, give Friday Harbor Laboratories as an address. The 1964 note lists FHL alone, and the 1967 and 1975 papers list it alongside Miami University. No source was found that describes his role at the station.

His papers deal with proteolytic enzymes, especially trypsin-like enzymes, that invertebrates use in digestion. Early papers isolated and characterized proteinases from the gastric juice of the crayfish Orconectes virilis. From Miami University he published on the molecular weight of crustacean trypsin, the digestive proteinases of the earthworm Lumbricus terrestris and where its trypsin is produced and secreted, polychaete trypsin, and trypsin secretion in the oesophagus of the polychaete Nereis virens. Later papers described a chymotrypsin-like enzyme from the sipunculan Phascolopsis gouldii (1982) and hepatopancreatic cell types in the crayfish Orconectes rusticus (1986). His FHL-connected papers belong to the same line of work: a 1964 note on preparative acrylamide electrophoresis using a conventional vertical starch-gel apparatus, a 1967 survey with Karen Buschlen of a tryptic digestive enzyme across crustacean species, and a 1975 study of proteolytic enzymes in the digestive fluid of the barnacle Balanus nubilus.

name: Edwin Munro
text:
Edwin Munro is a cell and developmental biologist who studies how cells and embryos generate polarity, force and shape. He studied at Hampshire College and earned a PhD in cell and developmental biology at the University of Washington, where around 2000 he co-authored, with George von Dassow, Eli Meir and Garrett Odell, a model of the Drosophila segment polarity network. An FHL centennial timeline lists him as one of the postdoctoral scholars, resident at FHL from about 2000, on the team awarded a 2002 National Institute of General Medical Sciences grant that set up the Center for Cell Dynamics at FHL. He was also a postdoctoral fellow at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center; his papers of 2004-2011 give the Center for Cell Dynamics as his address. He is now Professor of Molecular Genetics and Cell Biology at the University of Chicago. The census lists 18 FHL-connected papers, 2002-2015.

Munro combines live imaging, quantitative image analysis and computer modeling. His FHL-connected papers fall into three groups. Work on ascidian embryos showed that notochord patterning is regulative and robust and that polarized basolateral cell motility drives notochord invagination and convergent extension (2002), and went on to the role of the polarity gene prickle (2005), FGF3 signaling from the floor plate in Ciona (2008) and the sequential apical and basolateral contractions that drive endoderm invagination (2010). Work on the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans showed that cortical flows powered by asymmetric contraction carry PAR proteins to set up anterior-posterior polarity in the early embryo (2004), with later papers on symmetry breaking (2009) and PAR-3 oligomerization (2011). Modeling and biophysical papers covered gene networks (2002), clustering of self-aggregating particles (2012, 2014) and force generation by myosin II filament isoforms (2015).

name: Eliza C. Heery
text:
Eliza C. Heery is a marine ecologist who studies how coastal urbanization affects seafloor (benthic) ecosystems. She received a BS from Emory University, an MS from Virginia Tech and, in 2017, a PhD from the University of Washington Department of Biology, advised by Kenneth P. Sebens of Friday Harbor Laboratories. As a doctoral candidate she was also a graduate fellow in UW's IGERT Program on Ocean Change. She was then a postdoctoral researcher at the National University of Singapore before moving to the Smithsonian's MarineGEO program; some of her 2020 and 2021 papers give her address as MarineGEO at Friday Harbor Laboratories. In December 2022 she joined the University of Washington Tacoma as an Assistant Professor in Ecology. Her census papers run from 2018 to 2026, and FHL's 2026 people page lists her on its Research Advisory Committee.

Her research asks how marine life responds to the artificial structures and armoured shorelines of coastal cities. For her doctoral work she dived at natural rocky outcrops and at breakwaters, fishing reefs and riprap-covered pipelines in Puget Sound, from north of Everett to south of Tacoma, photographing standard areas of seafloor to compare communities along an urbanization gradient. Papers from this work show that artificial structures can raise detrital loads in nearby sediments (2018) and describe how giant Pacific octopuses use urban habitats (2018). With colleagues in Singapore she tested ways of making seawalls and shorelines better habitat, among them added microhabitats for fishes, seaweed farming and lower-pH concrete, which gave little biodiversity gain (all 2020). She also co-authored a global estimate of the extent of marine built structures (2020). A 2026 paper presents a tool that measures urbanization across seascapes and predicts where habitat-forming seaweeds occur in the Salish Sea.

name: Elizabeth G. Boulding
text:
Elizabeth G. Boulding is an evolutionary biologist and Professor in the Department of Integrative Biology at the University of Guelph, where she is also affiliated with the One Health Institute. She earned a BSc at the University of British Columbia (1980), an MSc at the University of Alberta (1983) and a PhD at the University of Washington (1990). Her FHL-connected papers run from 1983 to 2010. Her Alberta master's thesis on crab predation on buried bivalves thanks the director and staff of Friday Harbor Laboratories and Bamfield Marine Station for the use of their facilities. A 1993 paper from her doctoral years gives a University of Washington, Friday Harbor Laboratories address, and later papers from her Guelph group are listed in the FHL research bibliography. In the report's network she is linked to Hyuk Je Lee, whose Guelph doctoral thesis examined population genetic structure in five northeastern Pacific Littorina species.

Boulding's lab asks whether a population can adapt to a change in its biological environment without going extinct, using field experiments, quantitative genetics and genomics. Her early FHL-connected papers concern shell-breaking crabs and their prey. A 1986 study with Michael LaBarbera showed that repeated loading lets crabs open larger bivalves, and papers with Sylvia Behrens Yamada (1996, 1998) looked at how mobile crab predators shape the zonation of intertidal snails and how claw form relates to prey size selection. In 1993 she examined the quantitative genetics of shell form in an intertidal snail and the survival and growth of two Littorina species on wave-exposed and protected shores. Later papers concern male mate choice in Littorina subrotundata (2008), hatchery pedigrees of northern abalone and the population structure of salmon lice (2009), and, with Lee, larval development and genetic structure in littorinid snails (2009) and body size clines in Littorina keenae (2010).

name: Elizabeth L. Brainerd
text:
Elizabeth L. Brainerd is a vertebrate functional morphologist and biomechanist. She received an A.B. (1985) and a Ph.D. (1991) from Harvard University and was a Junior Fellow of the Harvard Society of Fellows from 1990 to 1993. She was on the faculty of the University of Massachusetts Amherst from 1994 to 2005, then moved to Brown University, where she has been Robert P. Brown Professor of Biology and Professor of Medical Science since 2020. She was president of the International Society of Vertebrate Morphology (2016-2019) and the Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology (2019-2021), and received the Joseph S. Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award in Ichthyology (2021) and the Society for Experimental Biology's Bidder Prize Lecture (2023). The census lists ten FHL-connected items by her from 1993 to 2020, including two 2015 reports from FHL's Blinks-NSF REU-BEACON internship program; her own 2018 and 2020 papers list an FHL address.

Brainerd's research combines anatomy of the musculoskeletal system with methods from engineering to study how vertebrates breathe, feed and move, including the evolution of lung ventilation, prey capture in fishes and fish escape responses. She is one of the developers of XROMM (X-ray Reconstruction of Moving Morphology), which combines CT scans with biplanar X-ray video to show skeletal motion in three dimensions, and has directed Brown's Keck XROMM Core Facility since 2008. Her FHL-connected papers deal with Northeast Pacific fishes: lift and ground effect during pectoral-fin swimming in the northern spearnose poacher (2009), the move from water into sand in sand lances (2011), pectoral-fin movements during turns in the Pacific spiny dogfish (2018), and neurocranial motion and the sternohyoideus muscle in suction feeding (2018, 2020). Nicholas Gidmark and Yordano Jimenez, listed in the report's network as her students, are first authors of the 2011 sand lance and 2018 neurocranial papers.

name: Emily A. Roberts
text:
Emily A. Roberts is a marine biologist who studies the energetics of marine invertebrates and their responses to temperature, food and seawater chemistry. After a professional master's degree in marine biology at Northeastern University (2011), she completed a PhD in Biology at the University of Washington (2014–2019), advised by Emily Carrington. Her papers from these years give the UW Department of Biology and Friday Harbor Laboratories, and a 2015 paper gives FHL alone. Her FHL-connected papers and datasets in the census run from 2015 to 2025. She was then a postdoctoral fellow in the Keck Science Department of Claremont McKenna College (2019–2021), a National Academies postdoctoral researcher at the NOAA Fisheries laboratory in Milford, Connecticut (2021–2023), a quantitative research ecologist there (2023–2024), and from 2024 a postdoctoral associate in Stony Brook University's School of Marine and Atmospheric Sciences.

Her doctoral research measured the energetic cost of byssal attachment in mussels. With Mytilus trossulus and M. galloprovincialis, she combined laboratory temperature and food experiments and field studies with scope-for-growth energy budgets. A 2021 Functional Ecology paper showed that cutting threads to induce extra thread production reduced shell and tissue growth in M. trossulus, at an estimated cost of about 1 joule per thread, and a 2023 paper found that energetic scope limited growth but not thread production in two mytilid species. Earlier she co-authored FHL seawater studies: a 2015 analysis of a 2011–2013 time series from the FHL dock pump house, describing an inland sea with high nitrate, low chlorophyll and naturally high pCO2, and a 2016 paper relating freshwater influence to particulate organic matter and pH in the San Juan Archipelago. With Carrington she released FHL's Cantilever Point weather station records for 2006–2021 (2022). Later work models ocean and air warming effects on the barnacle Balanus glandula (2025).

name: Emily Carrington
text:
Emily Carrington is a marine biomechanist and professor of biology at the University of Washington, working on the Seattle campus and at Friday Harbor Laboratories. She received a BA from Cornell University (1985) and a PhD from Stanford University (1992), advised by Mark Denny, then was a Killam Postdoctoral Fellow with John Gosline at the University of British Columbia and a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford's Hopkins Marine Station. She was on the faculty of the University of Rhode Island from 1996 to 2005, then joined UW Biology and FHL as associate professor in 2005, becoming professor in 2010. At FHL she directed the Ocean Acidification Environmental Laboratory (2012–14) and was named a Turn Point Faculty Fellow in 2020. From 2016 to 2019 she was a program director at the National Science Foundation, and she was named an AAAS Fellow in 2021. The census lists 50 FHL-connected items, 2007–2026.

Her work combines materials science, fluid mechanics, organismal biology and environmental science to understand how organisms of wave-swept shores stay attached and how they will fare in changing oceans. Mussel byssal threads are a central system: her group has measured how attachment varies with season, wave action, temperature, low oxygen and ocean acidification, and how thread production trades off against growth. She has also studied drag on seaweeds, feeding in barnacles and the thermal behavior of intertidal snails. Recent FHL-connected papers cover the energetic cost of byssus production (2021, 2023), microplastics and mussel biodeposits (2021), kelp physiology under different temperatures and nitrogen levels (2023) and seasonal thermal sensitivity (2025). Many census entries are datasets: her lab launched an FHL weather station in 2005, and she is a co-author of FHL Ocean Observatory seawater records. Her PhD students include Michael Nishizaki, Laura Newcomb, Hilary Hayford and Matthew George.

name: Emília P. Martins
text:
Emília P. Martins is an evolutionary biologist and professor in the School of Life Sciences at Arizona State University, where she leads the Martins Lab. Her lab page describes her main interest as the evolution of complex and multimodal communication. Her connection to FHL comes through its imaging facility. The census holds two of her papers, from 2024 and 2026, that name FHL in the text but not in the author addresses. For the 2024 study, lizard specimens were micro-CT scanned at the Karel F. Liem Bio-Imaging Center at Friday Harbor Laboratories, and the authors thanked Adam Summers, Mackenzie Gerringer and FHL staff for help with collecting and analysing the CT data. The 2026 paper's acknowledgments also name FHL and the Liem center. The report's network links her to Julio A. Rivera, a postdoctoral researcher in her lab from 2017 to 2021 and first author of the 2024 paper.

Martins's lab studies body form and communication in Sceloporus lizards and sensory biology in fishes. One current project asks whether closely related Sceloporus species living in the same areas differ in body form and ecology. It works in Mexico and the southwestern United States, using CT scans of museum specimens, field surveys and phylogenetic analyses. Another project, with the Arizona Game and Fish Department as a partner, tests how temperature, acidity, water flow and light affect the senses of zebrafish and of native and non-native desert minnows. Both FHL-connected papers apply phylogenetic comparative methods to CT data. The 2024 paper, on male skulls of 57 Sceloporus species, found that evolutionary shifts to larger body size went with more compact skulls. The 2026 paper found that in two of three live-bearing lineages, larger body size evolved with flatter, wider female pelvises, which the authors related to habitat rather than to reproduction.

name: Eric D. Tytell
text:
Eric D. Tytell is a biologist at Tufts University, where his faculty page lists him as Associate Professor of Biology and where he leads the Tytell Laboratory. He received a BA in biology and physics from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (1998), an MPhil in zoology from the University of Cambridge (1999) and a PhD in biology from Harvard University (2005). His FHL connection comes through collaboration. The census holds three papers from 2017 to 2022 written with colleagues affiliated with Friday Harbor Laboratories, Adam P. Summers and Karly E. Cohen. Cassandra M. Donatelli, who completed her PhD with Tytell at Tufts between 2014 and 2019, is a co-author on all three, and the report's network links her to him. On these papers Tytell's own address is Tufts; FHL appears through his co-authors' affiliations and the specimens used.

Tytell studies the biomechanics and neural control of locomotion, mainly in fishes. His work asks how fishes produce the forces that move them forward and let them manoeuvre, and how they keep their swimming stable in changing environments. His lab also asks how sensory systems detect such changes and how neural circuits control movement, combining experimental measurements, physical models and computational simulations. The FHL-connected papers deal with the fish body axis. The 2017 study measured long-axis twisting, or 'wobble', during swimming in six elongate fishes from intertidal, nearshore and subtidal habitats and found that species from the same habitat moved alike. A 2021 paper tested whether vertebral shape predicts the behaviour and ecology of fishes. A 2022 study used micro-CT scans of 79 species, with specimens donated from the FHL ichthyology collection, and found vertebral features that point to more flexible spines in bottom-dwelling fishes than in open-water swimmers.

name: Erika V. Iyengar
text:
Erika V. Iyengar is an invertebrate ecologist and Professor of Biology at Muhlenberg College in Allentown, Pennsylvania. She holds a BS with honors from Stanford University and a PhD from Cornell University. Her FHL-connected papers run from 2001 to 2024. The earliest, written with C. Drew Harvell in 2001 and 2002, deal with defenses in marine invertebrates. Most of the later papers come from summer research at Friday Harbor Laboratories. Her college profile says her summer research often takes place there and that many Muhlenberg students have come with her. Several held NSF Research Experiences for Undergraduates positions at FHL, among them Kerry L. McGowan, co-author of the epibiont studies. The report's network links her to McGowan and to Brooke Z. Torjman, whose hermit crab studies with her (2021, 2024) were supported by FHL's Blinks-NSF REU-BEACON program.

Iyengar studies interactions between species, especially feeding and defense, and uses present-day ecology to address evolutionary questions. A central subject is the snail Trichotropis cancellata, which steals food from the tube worm Serpula columbiana. Her papers describe this kleptoparasitism (2002), the snail's performance on different hosts (2004), its seasonal changes in feeding mode (2005) and the function of the flexible hairs on its shell (2008). A 2008 review compared kleptoparasitism across the animal kingdom. With Harvell she studied predator deterrence in the early stages of sea stars and sea cucumbers with yolk-feeding larvae (2001) and the cues that trigger defensive spines in the bryozoan Membranipora membranacea (2002). Later work with students covers host specificity in Crepidula adunca (2011), epibionts on intertidal snail shells (2014, 2017), feeding by the native slug Ariolimax columbianus and the invasive Arion rufus (2014–2015), and the cost to hermit crabs of carrying heavy shells (2024).

name: Esther M. Leise
text:
Esther M. Leise is a neurobiologist and invertebrate zoologist who studies the development of molluscan nervous systems and metamorphosis. She received a B.S. in zoology from the University of Maryland University College (1975) and a Ph.D. in zoology from the University of Washington (1983), where she was also a teaching assistant. She was a postdoctoral fellow at the University of California, Davis (1983–1988) and a postdoctoral researcher at Georgia State University (1988–1990), then an assistant researcher at the University of Hawaii's Kewalo Marine Laboratory (1990–1991). In 1991 she joined the Department of Biology at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro as assistant professor. She became associate professor in 1998 and professor in 2008. Her FHL-connected papers, from 1979 to 1986, come from her graduate work, and a 2009 study used a diatom culture isolated at FHL.

As a graduate student she studied molluscan larvae and juveniles. A 1979 paper with Richard R. Strathmann, for which FHL provided space, filmed the beating of cilia and the paths of food particles to study feeding mechanisms and clearance rates in molluscan veligers. Her papers of 1984 and 1986 followed the integument of the chiton Mopalia muscosa through metamorphosis and the development of its sensory organs in juveniles. A 1988 paper described sensory organs in the hairy girdles of mopaliid chitons. As a postdoctoral researcher she worked on crayfish neurophysiology, including sensory afferents, motor neurons and the lateral giant escape neuron. At Greensboro she has studied metamorphosis in the mud snail Ilyanassa obsoleta. This work tests how serotonin, nitric oxide, GABA, programmed cell death in the larval apical ganglion and cues from benthic diatoms regulate the change from larva to juvenile.

name: Eugene N. Kozloff
text:
Eugene N. Kozloff (1920–2017) was a marine biologist and botanist known especially for his field guides to the plants and animals of the Pacific Northwest. He earned master's and doctoral degrees at the University of California, Berkeley, and taught biology and invertebrate zoology at Lewis & Clark College in Portland, Oregon, before joining the University of Washington's Friday Harbor Laboratories in 1966. He later became emeritus professor at FHL. With Richard Norris he started a course that combines marine zoology and botany, and he took his turn teaching on the Seattle campus. He also worked at marine laboratories in Roscoff, France, and in Tunisia. From 2007 he continued his research for several years at Western Washington University's Shannon Point Marine Center. The census counts 15 FHL-address papers by him, from 1965 to 2008.

Much of Kozloff's research concerned small parasites and symbionts of marine invertebrates. He described a new orthonectid from a tube-building polychaete (1965) and later the plasmodium of the orthonectid Rhopalura ophiocomae (1994). Other papers described new acoel flatworms (1965), a ciliate without cilia that parasitizes a sabellid worm (1966, 1967), reproduction in the acoel Otocelis luteola (1999–2000) and umagillid flatworms from echinoderm intestines, among them a new species from the sea cucumber Stichopus californicus (1987). From 2001 to 2008 he published on the ciliate Orchitophrya stellarum as a parasite of Leptasterias and other sea stars. His books include Seashore Life of Puget Sound, the Strait of Georgia, and the San Juan Archipelago (1973), a key to the region's marine invertebrates (1974), Seashore Life of the Northern Pacific Coast (1983), Marine Invertebrates of the Pacific Northwest (1987) and the textbook Invertebrates (1990). Two genera and nine species are named after him.

name: Federico D. Brown
text:
Federico D. Brown is an evolutionary developmental biologist at the University of São Paulo (USP), where he has been Professor Doutor in the Institute of Biosciences since 2013 and also works at USP's Centro de Biologia Marinha (CEBIMar). He studied biology at the Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador (Licenciado, 2001), working in Eugenia del Pino's laboratory. With a Fulbright, he did his PhD (2002-2008) in Billie Swalla's laboratory at the University of Washington and Friday Harbor Laboratories, with visits to Anthony De Tomaso's laboratory at Hopkins Marine Station, and took FHL's Comparative Embryology course taught by Swalla and George von Dassow. He was a postdoctoral researcher in Ralf Sommer's laboratory at the Max Planck Institute for Developmental Biology and an assistant professor at the Universidad de los Andes in Bogotá (2010-2013). He is an elected member of the Ecuadorean Academy of Sciences. His FHL-connected papers date from 2007 to 2012.

Brown studies how colonial animals are built, focusing on germ cells, budding and regeneration in colonial ascidians (sea squirts); as a student he also studied developmental modes of Neotropical frogs. His FHL-connected papers on the colonial ascidian Botrylloides violaceus describe expression of the germline gene vasa (2007, with Swalla) and whole-body regeneration (2009). With De Tomaso and Stefano Tiozzo he traced the early specification of long-lived germline precursors in Botryllus schlosseri (2009), evidence that a clonal animal sets aside its germline early, and reviewed regeneration and stem cells in ascidians (2008). A 2008 review with Andrew Prendergast and Swalla examined chordate origins, and a 2012 paper with Swalla used ascidian coloniality as a case study in the evolution of budding by stem cells. At CEBIMar he has coordinated graduate courses on the comparative embryology of marine invertebrates and on coloniality and modularity.

name: Fernanda X. Oyarzún
text:
Fernanda X. Oyarzún is a marine biologist and visual artist who studies the reproduction and development of marine invertebrates. She holds a bachelor's degree in biology from the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile and a PhD in Biology from the University of Washington (2010), with a thesis on brooding, sibling rivalry and population structure in the polychaete Boccardia proboscidea. As a UW graduate student she took FHL's Comparative Embryology course in 2004, taught by Richard Strathmann and George von Dassow, which led her to change her thesis. She later held a Fondecyt postdoctoral project and worked at the Universidad Católica de la Santísima Concepción in Chile; in 2024 FHL described her as an associate researcher at the Coastal Social-Ecological Millennium Institute (SECOS), directing its art and science research. A Fulbright scholar, she was an FHL artist in residence in autumn 2023. Her FHL-connected papers date from 2006 to 2019.

Her research centres on poecilogony, the production of more than one type of larva within a single species, in spionid polychaete worms of the genus Boccardia. With Billie Swalla and colleagues she described the population structure of B. proboscidea along the US Pacific coast and found that worms of different reproductive types can share the same mitochondrial haplotype (2011). Experiments on egg capsules from San Juan Island worms indicated that larval type is fixed early in development, while nurse-egg supply and cannibalism by sibling larvae affect hatching size and survival (2014). A 2009 study found genetic similarity between North American B. proboscidea and worms on cultured abalone in South Africa. With Strathmann she reviewed plasticity in hatching and in the length of planktonic development (2011), and with Stephanie Kamel and Richard Grosberg she discussed family conflict and offspring size (2010). Other papers concern clam digging (2006) and larval feeding while swimming (2019).

name: Frank H. Johnson
text:
Frank Harris Johnson (1908–1990) was a professor of biology at Princeton University who studied bioluminescence. His papers carry a Princeton address from 1931 to 1980. In 1960 he brought Osamu Shimomura from Japan to his laboratory and asked him to purify the light-emitting substance from jellyfish light organs. In the summer of 1961 Johnson, Shimomura and a small team collected the jellyfish Aequorea at Friday Harbor, cutting strips from the luminous rings and taking extracts from about 10,000 animals back to Princeton. Johnson's five FHL-connected papers date from 1962 and 1963 and list the Friday Harbor Laboratories alongside Princeton's Department of Biology or Moffett Biological Laboratory. Shimomura and Johnson collected at Friday Harbor over many summers. When Shimomura resumed the work in Johnson's laboratory in 1967, Johnson built a machine that sped up cutting the rings.

Johnson's papers from the 1930s dealt with respiration and light production in luminous bacteria, and he applied reaction-rate theory to biological processes. His books include The Kinetic Basis of Molecular Biology (1954) and The Theory of Rate Processes in Biology and Medicine (1974), written with Henry Eyring and Betsy Jones Stover. Four of his FHL-connected papers, with Shimomura and Yo Saiga, report the discovery and early study of aequorin: its extraction and purification (1962), further data on its properties (1963), a similar protein, halistaurin, from the hydromedusa Halistaura (1963), and the use of its light to measure small amounts of calcium (Science, 1963). A footnote in the 1962 paper mentioned the green protein later known as green fluorescent protein, for which Shimomura shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The fifth, a 1962 Science note with Dixy Lee Ray, gave a simple method of collecting the isopod Limnoria.

name: Frederick D. Dooley
text:
Frederick D. Dooley is a biologist who has worked on the physiology of seagrasses and on the biology of the cephalopod Nautilus. He earned a BS in biology and a BA in anthropology at the University of Washington in 2009 and a PhD in Biology there in 2015, with a dissertation on the tolerance of seagrasses to hydrogen sulfide advised by Peter D. Ward. The vita in his dissertation records that he took part in the ZooBot class of 2008 at Friday Harbor Laboratories, with Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria as his advisor there, and was a research technician in the seagrass laboratory at Friday Harbor in 2009–2010. Wyllie-Echeverria was a co-author on his seagrass papers, which give UW Biology and FHL as addresses, and his experiments used containers with flowing seawater at FHL. The census counts four FHL-connected papers from 2012 to 2016. Papers of 2026 give the School of Biology, Everett Community College, Washington.

His dissertation starts from the loss of eelgrass, Zostera marina, from Westcott Bay on San Juan Island in the late 1990s and early 2000s. His FHL-connected papers showed that eelgrass seedlings are sensitive to hydrogen sulfide (2012), that seedlings of the surfgrass Phyllospadix scouleri tolerate even less sulfide (2015), and that stored eelgrass seed loses viability over time (2013). Sampling at eight embayments in the San Juan Archipelago and nearby Salish Sea in 2014 linked sediment sulfide levels to the presence or absence of eelgrass, and he suggested sediment capping as a restoration option for high-sulfide sites. With Ward he also reported increased growth and germination in plants given hydrogen sulfide (2013). His Nautilus work with Ward, Gregory J. Barord, Lauren E. Vandepas and Billie J. Swalla includes baited underwater video surveys in the Philippines, Australia, Fiji and American Samoa (2014), a 2016 phylogeography of Nautilus pompilius, and 2026 studies using acoustic telemetry and stable isotopes.

name: Fu-Shiang Chia
text:
Fu-Shiang Chia (1931–2011) was a marine invertebrate zoologist. After a BS in biology from Taiwan Normal University, he earned an MS (1962) and a PhD in zoology (1964) at the University of Washington, doing his graduate research at Friday Harbor Laboratories. He taught for 24 years at the University of Alberta, including five years as chair of zoology and ten as dean of the Faculty of Graduate Studies and Research. He then moved to the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, retired from there in 1997, and directed Taipei Sea World for three years. His obituary credits him with more than 200 research papers and more than 40 graduate degrees supervised. His FHL-connected papers span 1966 to 1995. He was a frequent researcher at the laboratories and served on the FHL Advancement Board.

Chia's research dealt with the reproduction, development and larval biology of marine invertebrates. His early FHL papers described the development of the cushion star Pteraster tesselatus (1966, based on work in the summers of 1960 and 1963), changes in the pyloric caeca of the brooding sea star Leptasterias hexactis (1969), and settlement and delayed metamorphosis in the sea star Mediaster aequalis (1971, with Charles Birkeland and Richard Strathmann). Later work with Alberta students and colleagues covered sea anemones, including a revision of the genus Epiactis (1986), predation on planktonic larvae, a test of Garstang's hypothesis on gastropod torsion (1985), larval settlement cues and sperm formation in chitons. The report's network records him as supervisor of two Alberta doctoral students: J. Timothy Pennington (PhD 1986), on the meroplankton of San Juan Channel and predation on larvae, and Glenys D. Gibson (PhD 1993), on development in the sea slug Haminaea callidegenita.

name: Gareth J. Fraser
text:
Gareth J. Fraser is an evolutionary developmental biologist and Associate Professor in the Department of Biology at the University of Florida, where he is listed as Term Professor for 2024–2027. He received his PhD from King's College London, in the Department of Craniofacial Development and Stem Cell Biology at the Dental Institute. His 2019 paper on pufferfish lists him at both the University of Sheffield (Department of Animal and Plant Sciences and Bateson Centre) and the University of Florida. His FHL-connected papers run from 2019 to 2025. An FHL New Faculty Fellowship supported his ratfish collections. The report's network links him to Karly E. Cohen, a postdoctoral researcher in his group who has also held an FHL affiliation. In 2022 Fraser and Cohen mentored an NSF REU student at FHL.

Fraser's lab studies how evolution, development and regeneration are linked in vertebrate teeth, skin appendages and sensory structures. It works mainly with sharks, pufferfishes and cichlids. Recent work covers stem cell niches in the continuously replaced teeth of sharks, the tooth-to-beak transition in pufferfish and a Turing-like patterning mechanism for shark skin denticles. Among the FHL-connected papers, a 2019 study showed that pufferfish skin spines develop through EDA signalling, a pathway shared with other vertebrate skin appendages, and thanked FHL colleagues for pufferfish CT scans. A 2022 REU project described the denticles of the Pacific spiny dogfish. In 2025, with Cohen and Michael Coates, he reported in PNAS that the head clasper of male spotted ratfish carries true teeth grown from a dental lamina. Another 2025 paper described a possible ratfish nursery site in San Juan Channel.

name: Garrett M. Odell
text:
Garrett M. (Garry) Odell was a mathematical and computational biologist at the University of Washington, in the Department of Zoology and later Biology, where he was Professor of Biology. Bibliographic records place his earlier papers at Johns Hopkins University and then Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (1975-1988). FHL describes him as a long-time researcher at the laboratories. He directed the NIH Center for Cell Dynamics, located at FHL from 2002 to 2010, which modelled cell and developmental processes; FHL traces this $14 million centre, funded by NIH and UW, to one of its early research apprenticeship teams in cell biology. In 2002 he and Victoria Foe were working at FHL's Whiteley Center on the dynamics of actin and microtubules in cell shape change and division in early embryos of marine invertebrates. His FHL-connected papers in the census date from 1989 to 2012. He died in May 2018.

Odell built mathematical and computer models to ask how gene networks, proteins and mechanical forces produce pattern and shape in embryos and cells. With Victoria Foe he studied mitotic domains in fly embryos (1989) and, with Christine Field, the distribution of actin and myosin in the early Drosophila embryo (2000). With George von Dassow, Eli Meir and Edwin Munro he modelled the Drosophila segment polarity gene network, reporting in Nature (2000) that it behaves as a robust developmental module, and followed with the Ingeneue modelling software and a study of lateral inhibition in the neurogenic network (2002). With Munro he showed that ascidian notochord formation is regulative and driven by polarized cell movements (2002). Later work modelled actin-based propulsion of the bacterium Listeria with Jonathan Alberts (2004, 2009), modelled how microtubules position the cleavage furrow (2008, with Foe), and explored parameters of fisheries food-web models with Sarah Gaichas and colleagues (2012).

name: Gary Freeman
text:
Gary Freeman is an experimental embryologist whose papers give addresses at the University of Texas at Austin, first in the Department of Zoology's Center for Developmental Biology and later in the Section of Integrative Biology. He has used embryos from many animal groups, including ctenophores, hydrozoans, phoronids, brachiopods and molluscs, to compare how embryonic axes and regional fates are established, working at marine stations that include FHL, the Marine Biological Laboratory at Woods Hole, the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute's Naos Marine Laboratory in Panama and the Kristineberg Marine Research Station in Sweden. Many of his papers from 1981 to 2009 list Friday Harbor Laboratories as an address, some jointly with Texas, and the census credits him with 16 FHL-connected papers from 1976 to 2009.

Freeman's experiments manipulate eggs and early embryos to find when and how axes and cell fates are specified. In ctenophores he altered cleavage planes to study the localization of developmental potential (1976) and traced the establishment of the oral-aboral axis (1977). In hydrozoans he showed that the site where cleavage begins establishes the posterior pole of the embryo (1981) and that eggs can be fertilized only at the site of polar body formation (1982), and he studied direct-developing trachyline and siphonophore embryos (1983), calcium signaling at fertilization and metamorphosis (1987-1993, with Ellis B. Ridgway) and how larval age affects the polyp prepattern of the planula (2005, 2009). Work on lophophorates traced regional specification in Phoronis larvae (1991) and in brachiopod embryos, including Terebratalia (1993, 2003), and, with Mark Q. Martindale, the origin of mesoderm in phoronids (2002); a 2006 paper related egg organization in the limpet Lottia to axial specification.

name: George von Dassow
text:
George von Dassow is a cell and developmental biologist who studies cell behavior in embryos and larvae of marine invertebrates. At the University of Washington he worked with Eli Meir, Edwin Munro and Garrett Odell on a computer model showing that the Drosophila segment polarity gene network is a robust developmental module (2000). An FHL centennial timeline names him, with Victoria Foe and Odell, as a recipient of a 2000 Seaver Institute grant for a second confocal microscope at FHL, and as one of the postdoctoral scholars, resident at FHL from about 2000, on the team awarded a 2002 federal grant that set up the Center for Cell Dynamics there. He co-taught an undergraduate research apprenticeship and became a regular instructor in FHL's summer Comparative Embryology course. By 2009 he had moved to the University of Oregon's Oregon Institute of Marine Biology, where he is Associate Professor.

His FHL-connected papers, dated 2002 to 2011 in the census, span genetic network modeling and the cell biology of division. Papers from 2002-2003 introduced Ingeneue, a software tool for reconstituting genetic networks, and explored robustness in the segment polarity and neurogenic networks and in evolution. He then worked mainly on cytokinesis in echinoderm embryos and other cells: light microscopy methods for echinoderm embryos (2004), a microtubule-dependent zone of active RhoA that marks the cleavage plane (2005), fluorescent actin probes based on the actin-binding domain of utrophin (2007), how stable and dynamic microtubules shape the zone of myosin activation (2008), and how asters sharpen a furrow-positioning signal from the spindle (2009). He also contributed to studies of the microtubule regulators MCAK (2005, 2007) and Kif18A (2008) and to larval biology, including the mitraria larva of the polychaete Owenia collaris (2009). At Oregon he has studied nemertean pilidium larvae.

name: Gerald J. Audesirk
text:
Gerald J. Audesirk is a neurobiologist and textbook author who taught at the University of Colorado Denver. He earned a doctorate in neurobiology at the California Institute of Technology. His 1975 thesis there dealt with the organisation of the eye of the sea hare Aplysia californica and the relationship between two neuronal circadian oscillators in that animal. He and Teresa Audesirk then worked as postdoctoral researchers at the University of Washington's marine laboratories, and his papers from 1978 to 1980 give Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address. From 1982 to 2006 the two taught introductory biology and neurobiology at the University of Colorado Denver, where both are now emeritus professors of biology. With Bruce Byers they are authors of the introductory textbook Biology: Life on Earth, which had reached an eleventh edition by 2016.

At Friday Harbor, Audesirk studied the neural basis of behaviour in the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea, a sea slug much used in neuroethology, the study of how nervous systems control behaviour. His six FHL-connected papers (1978 to 1980) follow one line of work. A 1978 Nature report and a companion paper describe central motor neurons that drive the cilia the animal uses to crawl. A 1979 study with Richard McCaman and A. O. Dennis Willows examined the role of serotonin when identified neurons control ciliary activity on the foot. Papers in 1979 and 1980 with Teresa Audesirk describe mechanoreceptors of the mouth and other complex mechanoreceptors. At Colorado Denver, with funding mainly from the National Institutes of Health, the Audesirks' laboratory studied how low levels of environmental pollutants harm neurons and how estrogen protects them.

name: Graham Hoyle
text:
Graham Hoyle was an English neurophysiologist who studied neuromuscular transmission in a wide range of invertebrates. His 1960 paper on the swimming sea anemone Stomphia coccinea gives his address as the Department of Zoology, University of Glasgow, together with the marine biological laboratories at Puget Sound. A 2021 column by Dennis Willows says Hoyle had recently moved to the University of Oregon from University College London when he was among the visiting scientists at Friday Harbor Laboratories in the summer of 1963. His FHL-connected papers run from 1960 to 1973. Willows, who later directed FHL, was Hoyle's graduate student, and a 2025 review of Tritonia research places him in the FHL marine invertebrate zoology course in the summer of 1964. The report's network links the two as advisor and student.

In 1963, with Thomas Smyth, Hoyle described the neuromuscular physiology of the giant muscle fibres of the barnacle Balanus nubilus. Willows's column recounts how Hoyle used a glass electrode to show that each fibre is a single cell, the largest muscle cell found in any animal. A 1965 paper with H. L. Atwood and Smyth dealt with single crab muscle fibres. With Willows and D. A. Dorsett he then turned to the nudibranch Tritonia. Papers in 1969 and a four-part series in the Journal of Neurobiology in 1973 described the organisation of its central nervous system, how nerve impulse patterns relate to muscle contraction, and the neuronal mechanism of a fixed action pattern, shown to originate centrally in the isolated brain. He also studied horseshoe crabs, sea squirts and locusts, and in 1984 published an essay in Behavioral and Brain Sciences on the scope of neuroethology.

name: Gregory A. Wray
text:
Gregory A. Wray is an evolutionary biologist at Duke University. His ORCID record dates his biology professorship there from 1999, and Scholars@Duke also lists professorships in Evolutionary Anthropology (from 2008) and Cell Biology (from 2022). He received a BS from the College of William and Mary in 1981 and a PhD from Duke in 1987. Several papers of 1989 to 1991 give Indiana University, all of them with Rudolf A. Raff. Papers of 1991 and 1992, two of them with Raff, give his address as Friday Harbor Laboratories and the UW Department of Zoology. From 1993 to 1999 he was assistant and then associate professor of ecology and evolution at Stony Brook University. FHL's research bibliographies also list several of his papers from 1996 to 2000, and a 1997 Nature paper with Christopher J. Lowe mentions FHL in its text.

Wray studies how genes and genomes evolve, focusing on changes in gene expression; his main study systems are sea urchins and primates, including humans. His current projects examine how variants in regulatory DNA affect gene function and fitness and how natural selection acts on regulatory elements. His FHL-period papers dealt with the evolution of development in marine invertebrates: the wrinkled blastula of the sea urchin Heliocidaris erythrogramma (1991), a review with Raff of how developmental strategies evolve in marine invertebrates (1991), rates of evolution in developmental processes (1992), and changes in larval form during the post-Paleozoic radiation of echinoids (1992). Later FHL-listed work used molecular data to argue for deep Precambrian divergences among animal phyla (1996), traced changes in the roles of homeobox and other regulatory genes during echinoderm evolution (1997, 2000), studied gene expression during echinoderm metamorphosis (2000), and addressed the systematics of sea stars (2000).
