name: Gretchen Lambert
text:
Gretchen Lambert is an ascidian biologist and taxonomist. An FHL centennial timeline records that her association with the laboratories began in summer 1964, when as a graduate student she took the Marine Algology course; Charles Lambert, her long-time research partner, began his the same summer. Until 1998 the Lamberts were based in the Department of Biological Science at California State University, Fullerton. That year they moved to Seattle to do research in association with the University of Washington, and in 2016 an FHL newsletter described her as a long-time FHL researcher and Whiteley Scholar. She has compiled the twice-yearly bulletin Ascidian News since 1975 (with Charles Lambert until 2011), had organized and taught at least 25 ascidian taxonomy workshops by 2023, and in 2016 was one of eight Ascidiacea editors of the World Register of Marine Species. The census lists 23 FHL-connected papers, 1978-2023.

Her research spans the ecology, physiology and especially the systematics of ascidians. A 1968 paper described the ecology and growth of the solitary ascidian Corella willmeriana, and papers with Charles Lambert reported ammonium-based flotation of tunicate eggs (1978) and uric acid accumulation in Corella inflata (1998); she has also studied spicule formation in ascidians. Since 2000 most of her FHL-connected papers have documented non-native ascidians: a global overview of introductions (2001), rapid-assessment surveys of harbors and marinas in southern California, San Francisco Bay, the northeastern United States and southern England (2002-2006), the identity of the invasive colonial ascidian Didemnum vexillum (2009), and records from the Panama Canal (2011), the Galapagos (2019), Puerto Rico (2021) and southern California (through 2023). She described Distaplia alaskensis as a new species (2001) and has reported ascidian faunas from Singapore, Madeira and British Columbia.

name: H. A. Lessios
text:
H. A. (Harilaos A.) Lessios is a marine evolutionary biologist who studies sea urchins and sand dollars. His papers with FHL-connected co-authors give his address as the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) in Balboa, Panama. He has no FHL address of his own; his tie to the laboratory runs through Kirk S. Zigler. Zigler gave both STRI and Friday Harbor Laboratories as affiliations on a 2005 paper with Lessios, and the report's network records Lessios as his probable postdoctoral supervisor at STRI around 2002–2005. Their joint papers in the census run from 2003 to 2013. Some list FHL in an author affiliation or appear in the FHL research bibliography. The acknowledgments of the 2008 and 2013 papers credit fellowships to Zigler from FHL and the Smithsonian Institution.

Lessios's research concerns speciation and the evolution of reproductive isolation in echinoids. It combines phylogeography, molecular evolution and fertilization data. With Zigler he traced the evolution of the sperm protein bindin. A 2003 paper reviewed 250 million years of bindin evolution. Another 2003 paper linked adaptive bindin evolution in Heliocidaris to the shift to direct development. A 2004 study followed speciation and bindin evolution in Lytechinus along New World coasts. A 2005 analysis of five sea urchin genera found that amino-acid divergence in bindin predicts whether gametes of different species can fertilize each other, with as few as ten changes giving complete incompatibility. A 2013 study of 185 Mellita sand dollars from 31 localities recognized eleven species, six of them cryptic. Only one split was clearly caused by the closing of the Isthmus of Panama, about 3 million years ago.

name: H. Gary Greene
text:
H. Gary Greene is a marine geologist. Moss Landing Marine Laboratories (San José State University) lists him among its emeritus faculty as Professor of Geological Oceanography, with a Ph.D. from Stanford University (1977). Bibliographic records place him at the U.S. Geological Survey from about 1969 into the early 1990s and at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute from about 1996 to 2008, alongside a long association with Moss Landing. Since the mid-2010s his papers have given addresses at the Tombolo Mapping Lab on Orcas Island, the SeaDoc Society, Moss Landing's Center for Habitat Studies and Friday Harbor Laboratories. The census counts four papers with an FHL address between 2016 and 2023, among ten FHL-connected items from 2016 to 2025, and lists him as still connected with FHL.

His listed research interests are marine geology, benthic habitats, submarine canyons and landslides, tsunamis and coastal processes. His FHL-connected work maps the seafloor habitat of the Pacific sand lance (Ammodytes personatus), a forage fish that burrows into sandy bottoms in the San Juan Archipelago. A 2016 study with Joseph Bizzarro, Adam Summers and others described the fish's burrowing behaviour and functional morphology, using fish held at FHL. A 2017 paper combined sediment sampling, acoustic Doppler current profiling and multibeam bathymetry and found that a large subtidal sand-wave field kept its shape over the years studied. With Matthew Baker of FHL and others he surveyed sand lance habitat from a crewed submersible with a stereo-camera array (2021), assessed hazards to the sand-wave field (2021) and compiled an atlas of sand lance habitat (2024). He also produced oil-spill assessment maps of central Salish Sea seafloor and coastal habitats (2023).

name: Hans Jorgen Fyhn
text:
Hans Jørgen Fyhn is a Norwegian zoophysiologist who spent most of his career at the University of Bergen. At the University of Oslo he received the cand.real. degree in 1970 and the dr.philos. in 1976, and he held posts there from 1965 to 1980, the last as associate professor (førsteamanuensis) at the Institute of Physiology. He became professor at the University of Bergen in 1981, and Norwegian Wikipedia lists his employment there until 2007. His research stays abroad included Cambridge, the University of Washington, Duke University and Aarhus University. He was a subject adviser to the European Union's CODEST programme and sat on the board of the European Society for Comparative Physiology and Biochemistry. His FHL-connected work is three papers from 1972 to 1974, written with J. A. Petersen and Kjell Johansen, that give a Friday Harbor Laboratories address. The 1974 paper also gives the Department of Zoophysiology at Aarhus.

Fyhn's research concerns how animals adapt their physiology to their environment. It covers intertidal invertebrates, environmental toxicology and the physiology of fish larvae. His 1976 Oslo work dealt with physiological adaptations to intertidal life, and a 1986 Bergen work with fish larval physiology and anatomy. He also studied molluscs at the Australian Institute of Marine Science and land crabs in Panama and Venezuela. His FHL papers concern the gooseneck barnacle Pollicipes polymerus. The 1972 paper combined field and laboratory work on body temperature, water loss from the stalk and the regulation of body fluids during air exposure and in diluted seawater. A 1973 report in Science described rhythmic, temperature-dependent haemolymph pressures that are unusually high for an invertebrate and attributed them to a functional heart. A 1974 paper compared gas exchange in water and air over the tidal cycle.

name: Harold A. Scheraga
text:
Harold A. Scheraga (1921–2020) was an American biophysicist who worked on the physical chemistry of proteins. He received a B.S. from the City College of New York in 1941 and a Ph.D. from Duke University in 1946, with a thesis on the kinetics of a chlorination reaction, and first worked on proteins during a postdoctoral year with John Edsall at Harvard Medical School. He joined Cornell University as an instructor in 1947, became full professor in 1958 and George W. and Grace L. Todd Professor of Chemistry in 1965, chaired the chemistry department from 1960 to 1967, and became emeritus in 1992. His honours included a Guggenheim Fellowship (1956), the Eli Lilly Award in Biological Chemistry (1957), election to the National Academy of Sciences (1966) and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (1967), and the William H. Nichols Medal (1974). He has no FHL-connected papers in the census.

Scheraga's research concerned how proteins interact with water, the part the hydrophobic effect plays in protein folding, and how polypeptide chains fold into their native structures. He developed statistical-mechanical models of the hydrophobic effect, contributed to early molecular-mechanics models and force fields for simulating proteins and peptides, and in later work compared molecular dynamics simulations of folding with NMR measurements. His place in the report's network comes through one student. Lynn Riddiford earned her Ph.D. in zoology at Cornell in 1961, advised by Marcus Singer and Scheraga, and went on to faculty positions at Harvard and the University of Washington. Wikipedia lists Riddiford as the doctoral advisor of James W. Truman, and in 2016 the two set up their laboratory at Friday Harbor Laboratories. This places Scheraga two academic generations before FHL's recent work on insect development and metamorphosis.

name: Helen R. Whiteley
text:
Helen Riaboff Whiteley (1921–1990) was a microbiologist at the University of Washington (UW). She received a B.S. in microbiology from the University of California, Berkeley (1941), a master's degree from the University of Texas in Galveston and a Ph.D. from UW (1951). She then returned to California and worked for two years for the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission, rejoining UW in 1953; she became a full professor in 1965. She chaired the physiology division and the publications board of the American Society for Microbiology and served as its president in 1976. Her census papers with a Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) address run from 1960 to 1988; most were written with the UW zoologist Arthur H. Whiteley, who later founded the Helen Riaboff Whiteley Center at FHL in her memory, a working retreat for scientists, scholars and artists.

Her research centred on bacterial physiology. With Ernest Schnepf she studied the insecticidal crystal (Cry) proteins of Bacillus thuringiensis, work her Wikipedia entry credits with laying the foundation for genetically modified organisms that express them. Her first FHL-address paper (1960) surveyed the formate-activating enzyme and related tetrahydrofolate enzymes across animal tissues; her later FHL papers concern echinoderm development. With Arthur Whiteley, Brian McCarthy and others she compared base sequences of the RNA used in early development across echinoderms (1970), and followed the replication and expression of maternal and paternal genomes in a blocked echinoid hybrid (1972) and histone gene expression in interspecies hybrid embryos (1974). With Shigeki Mizuno she traced egg-type RNA among the blastomeres of cleaving embryos of the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus (1973–1975). A 1988 paper with Michael Harkey described five transcripts that accumulate together in primary mesenchyme cells during skeleton formation in sea urchin embryos.

name: Hilary A. Hayford
text:
Hilary A. Hayford is a marine ecologist and Habitat Research Director at the Puget Sound Restoration Fund (PSRF). She joined PSRF in 2020 to develop and carry out science-based plans for restoring Olympia oyster and bull kelp habitat. She received a Ph.D. in biology from the University of Washington in 2016, and her PSRF biography notes earlier work with Friday Harbor Laboratories and the Partnership for Interdisciplinary Studies of Coastal Oceans (PISCO). Her dissertation examined how tidal migration patterns moderate thermal risk in the intertidal snail Nucella ostrina, with experiments run at FHL in 2014; the report's network lists Emily Carrington as her thesis teacher. The census counts four FHL-address papers from 2014 to 2017, and her 2017 paper acknowledges Ragen, Strathmann and Behavior & Neurobiology fellowships from FHL.

Hayford's FHL work asked how intertidal animals avoid heat stress. In field experiments on San Juan Island with Sarah Gilman and Carrington, she showed that Nucella ostrina forages on the coolest available rock faces and at the coolest points in the tidal cycle, which limits its exposure to heat (2014). They also measured body temperatures of a barnacle and two whelk predators in relation to shore height, solar aspect and microhabitat (2015). Other papers examined seasonal changes in gastropod tolerance of heat and desiccation (with William Stickle, 2016), used radio tracking to detect behavioural thermoregulation in snails (2017) and showed how tidal cues reduce the thermal risk of climate change for a foraging snail (2021). At PSRF she has co-authored studies of an unprecedented heatwave's effects on Salish Sea intertidal shellfish (2022, 2024) and a 2026 metric for rating stressors on kelp.

name: Hironobu Ozaki
text:
Hironobu Ozaki is a developmental biochemist who worked on the eggs and embryos of sea urchins and sand dollars from the mid-1960s to the mid-1980s. Sea urchin papers under the name H. Ozaki begin in 1965–1967 with A. Tyler and colleagues on protein and RNA synthesis in eggs, oocytes and early embryos, work that the census record associates with the California Institute of Technology. With Arthur H. Whiteley he studied malate dehydrogenase in the purple sea urchin, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus (1967, 1970), in papers with an FHL address. A 1974 paper on acetylcholinesterase gives Kitasato University School of Medicine in Japan as his address, and a 1976 paper on the same enzyme lists Michigan State University's Department of Zoology together with FHL. His census papers with an FHL address run from 1967 to 1986. No biographical notice was located, so this outline rests on publication records.

Ozaki's research followed how enzymes, nucleic acids and proteins change as sea urchin embryos develop. With Whiteley he characterised L-malate dehydrogenase and its changes during development of S. purpuratus. Other papers examined chromatin from embryos and sperm (1967, 1971), histones of unfertilized eggs and their changes at fertilization (1973, 1979), and RNA and protein synthesis in normal and animalized embryos with W. R. Eckberg (1972–1975). His acetylcholinesterase studies described the enzyme's multiple molecular forms and its localization and differentiation in embryos (1974, 1976). In the 1980s he turned to yolk and egg formation. A 1980 paper characterised yolk proteins of the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus. Two 1986 papers showed that the major yolk glycoprotein precursor is secreted by coelomocytes into the coelomic plasma and described a glycoprotein in the accessory cells of the echinoid ovary and its role in vitellogenesis.

name: Hugh P. Stanley
text:
Hugh P. Stanley, a cell biologist and electron microscopist, studied how sperm cells form in fishes, amphibians and insects. OpenAlex lists two Oregon State theses by him, on the reproductive tracts of the nutria (1957) and on reproduction in the ratfish Hydrolagus colliei (1961), and his papers of 1958 to 1963 give the Department of Zoology at Oregon State as his address. Papers from 1965 to 1971 also list the University of Washington School of Medicine, the Zoological Station of Naples and the University of Minnesota. From 1966 to 1990 his papers list Utah State University in Logan, first its Department of Zoology and later its Department of Biology. All five of his FHL-connected papers, from 1983 to 1990, give both Utah State and Friday Harbor Laboratories. No biographical source was found, so his positions and his role at FHL are not confirmed.

His papers describe, at the level of fine structure, how sperm cells develop and are released. In the 1960s and early 1970s he studied the testis or sperm formation of a goby (1965), the catshark Scyliorhinus and the ray Torpedo (1966), a lamprey (1967), the tidepool sculpin Oligocottus maculosus (1969), the dogfish Squalus suckleyi (1971) and the clawed toad Xenopus laevis (1972). With James T. Bowman and colleagues at Utah State he used male-sterile mutants of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster to study genetic control of sperm development (1972 to 1977). His FHL papers return to the ratfish. He described its sperm (1983) and, with Harold Kasinsky and Niels Bols, reported chromatin diminution during meiosis (1984). With Charles Lambert he examined how an actin-myosin system in Sertoli cells forms sperm bundles (1985) and the fate of mitochondria in maturing sperm (1990); a further 1990 paper described sperm release (spermiation).

name: Hwan Su Yoon
text:
Hwan Su Yoon is a South Korean phycologist who leads the SKKU Evolutionary Genomics Laboratory in the Department of Biological Sciences at Sungkyunkwan University in Suwon. He earned his B.S., M.S. and Ph.D. (1999) in biology at Chungnam National University, with a doctoral thesis on the molecular phylogeny of the kelp families Alariaceae and Laminariaceae. He was a postdoctoral fellow and then senior scientist at the University of Iowa (2000–2007) and a principal investigator at the Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences (2007–2011), then joined Sungkyunkwan University in 2011 and became professor in 2014. He was vice president of the International Society of Protistologists (2012–2013) and an associate editor of Phycologia (2012–2014). The FHL affiliation on his 19 census papers (2011–2026) comes from co-authors: FHL's Robert A. Andersen is a co-author on all but one, and Charles J. O'Kelly on the 2011 Rhodella paper.

Yoon's laboratory studies the diversity and genome evolution of algae, especially red algae and the groups whose plastids descend from them, such as cryptophytes, haptophytes, stramenopiles and dinoflagellates. It combines field collection with genome sequencing, including sequencing from single protist cells. Current projects address early plastid evolution in Paulinella, sex in the yellow-green alga Vaucheria, heat and acid tolerance in Cyanidiophyceae, and multicellularity in brown algae. His FHL-connected papers are of two kinds. Taxonomic papers re-examine algal genera using material from their type localities, among them Chrysotila (2014), Ochromonas (2017) and Sarcinochrysis (2018), and describe new species, new genera and a new class, Phaeosacciophyceae (2020). Genomic papers use single-cell genome data to link phagotrophy with the origin of plastids (2012), compare the plastid genomes of dictyochophytes (2019) and cyanidiophytes (2023), and date the origin of brown algae to the Ordovician (2024).

name: Iván Quesada
text:
Iván Quesada is a biologist at the Universidad Miguel Hernández (UMH) in Elche, Spain. His ORCID record lists him as Professor of Nutrition at UMH since 2018. His recent papers also give addresses at UMH's Instituto de Investigación, Desarrollo e Innovación en Biotecnología Sanitaria de Elche (IDiBE) and at CIBERDEM, the Spanish biomedical research network for diabetes and associated metabolic diseases. Bibliographic records show papers with UMH addresses from 1999 onward. From 2003 to 2006 his papers gave addresses in the Department of Bioengineering and at Friday Harbor Laboratories of the University of Washington, where he worked with Pedro Verdugo, who is listed as his teacher in the report's network. The census counts four FHL-address papers from 2003 to 2006, and the FHL research bibliography lists his papers from 2003 to 2007.

His ORCID keywords describe his current research: pancreatic beta and alpha cells, insulin, glucagon, diabetes and obesity. His FHL-connected papers concern calcium signalling and regulated secretion. With Wei-Chun Chin and Verdugo he reported ATP-independent oscillations and release of calcium and hydrogen ions from mast-cell secretory granules (2003). With Verdugo he described InsP3-driven, pulse-modulated calcium signals in the nucleus of ciliated airway epithelial cells (2005). Two papers extended the work to marine phytoplankton: they demonstrated regulated exocytosis in the single-celled alga Phaeocystis globosa (2004) and analysed the signal transduction behind its light-stimulated secretion (2006). Later conference abstracts, listed by FHL or giving a Friday Harbor address, dealt with modelling calcium and proton oscillations in secretory granules (2007), airway defence (2010) and the storage and release of brevetoxin in the dinoflagellate Karenia brevis (2012).

name: J. A. Petersen
text:
Jorge A. Petersen, who usually published as J. A. Petersen, worked on the zoology and comparative physiology of marine invertebrates. His papers, from the 1960s to 1986, came mainly from the Universidade de São Paulo, including its Department of General and Animal Physiology and Institute of Marine Biology. In the late 1960s he worked with Kjell Johansen on oxygen uptake in a tube-dwelling polychaete worm, and with Johansen, Claude Lenfant and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen on breathing in the electric eel (1968) and a freshwater turtle (1970); those papers list São Paulo, Duke University and the University of Washington. His five FHL-connected papers, from 1971 to 1974, give Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address, two of them with the UW Department of Zoology. A 1986 paper again lists São Paulo. No biographical source was found, so his positions and his role at FHL are not known.

In Brazil he studied acorn worms (enteropneusts), with a 1964 note in Nature, with C. Burdon-Jones, on a giant enteropneust and a 1971 report of asexual reproduction in Glossobalanus crozieri. He also wrote a long series of biochemical studies of worms, snails and other invertebrates with F. B. De Jorge. At Friday Harbor he turned to the breathing and circulation of local marine invertebrates. With Johansen he measured gas exchange and active ventilation in the starfish Pteraster tesselatus (1971) and gas exchange in the giant chiton Cryptochiton stelleri (1973). With Hans J. Fyhn and Johansen he studied the ecophysiology of the intertidal barnacle Pollicipes polymerus (1972) and its breathing in water and in air (1974), and the three reported heart activity and high-pressure circulation in barnacles in Science (1973). A 1986 paper with John P. Sutherland and S. Ortega examined the patch dynamics of mussel beds near São Sebastião, Brazil.

name: James A. Murray
text:
James A. Murray is a neuroethologist who studies how nervous systems control orientation and navigation, mainly in sea slugs. He received a B.S. in neurobiology and behavior from Cornell University (1988) and a Ph.D. in zoology from the University of Washington (1994). His ORCID record lists a National Institute of Mental Health fellowship, from 1995, for research on social communication and reproduction in electric fish. He was associate professor of biology at the University of Central Arkansas (1999–2007), and since 2008 has been associate professor of biological sciences at California State University, East Bay. His FHL-connected work began with papers of 1992 and 1996 co-authored with A. O. Dennis Willows, who gave an FHL address on the 1992 paper. It continued through a 2011 field study that relied on FHL staff for slug collection and dive equipment, and through FHL student research reports he co-authored from 2013 to 2015.

Murray's research uses the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea (now T. tetraquetra) to link identified neurons to behaviour. His early papers showed that pedal neurons sensitive to water flow help the slug orient to currents (1992) and identified the nerves that carry out this orientation (1996). Later papers showed that a single identified cell, pedal neuron 3, helps the slug turn while crawling (2005), and reviewed work on the neural basis of orientation and navigation (2006). A 2011 study tracked slugs in the wild day by day to measure how water flow affects their orientation, crawling and drag. He also contributed to a 2000 confocal-montaging method for imaging neural networks and a 2015 study of nudibranch mitochondrial genomes. FHL student reports he co-authored tested for magnetic sensitivity in Tritonia (2013) and in the nudibranch Armina californica (2015), and he co-authored a 2014 paper giving evidence of magnetic sensitivity in chitons.

name: James B. McClintock
text:
James B. McClintock is a marine biologist at the University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB), which he joined in 1987 and where he holds the title Endowed University Professor of Polar and Marine Biology. He received a B.S. from the University of California, Santa Cruz in 1978 and a Ph.D. from the University of South Florida in 1984, followed by a National Science Foundation postdoctoral fellowship at Santa Cruz. Since 1989 he has led or co-directed fourteen U.S. Antarctic Program expeditions, working from McMurdo and Palmer Stations. McClintock Point in McMurdo Sound was named for him in 1998, and he was elected a Fellow of the AAAS in 1999. His eight census papers (1993–2017) are linked to FHL mainly through the laboratories' research bibliography and through work there by his doctoral student Minako Vickery.

McClintock's research centres on the chemical ecology of Antarctic marine organisms, the effects of warming and ocean acidification on calcified marine organisms, and the possible impact of king crabs entering Antarctic shelf waters on seafloor communities. His FHL-linked papers include work on the energy content and chemical defences of an Antarctic brachiopod (1993), a 2014 research framework for ocean acidification, and a 2017 study of the diets of seaweed-associated amphipods on the western Antarctic Peninsula, whose fatty-acid extractions were done at FHL. The largest group comes from work with Vickery, who conducted most of her research at FHL: a 1998 Nature note on regeneration in larvae, a 2000 comparison of sea star tube feet, two 2001 papers on larval regeneration and on genes expressed early in sea star larval regeneration, and a 2002 study of regrowth in sea star larvae and in larvae of the echinoid Dendraster excentricus cultured at FHL.

name: James E. Byers
text:
James E. (Jeb) Byers is a marine ecologist at the University of Georgia's Odum School of Ecology, where his ORCID record lists him from 2008, now as Professor and Associate Dean. He received his PhD in ecology, evolution and marine biology from the University of California, Santa Barbara, in 1999. FHL's fall 1999 newsletter announced that he would start a two-year FHL postdoctoral fellowship on 1 January 2000, to study how non-native species affect resident invertebrates and whether those effects are greater in marine reserves than in harvested areas. From 2001 to 2008 he was on the zoology faculty of the University of New Hampshire, starting as assistant professor. He has been a visiting fellow at the University of Wollongong and the University of Technology Sydney (2007 to 2008) and a Fulbright fellow at the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile (2017). His FHL-connected papers run from 2000 to 2006.

Byers measures the impacts of non-indigenous species on native species, and also studies parasites, ecosystem engineers and marine reserves, mostly working with molluscs and crustaceans. His first papers with a Friday Harbor address (2000, 2001) came from a northern California salt marsh, where the introduced mudsnail Batillaria attramentaria is displacing the native Cerithidea californica. They showed that the invader converts food into growth more efficiently and better survives low oxygen, and, in a model built with Lloyd Goldwasser, that its lower mortality alone could drive the native snail extinct. In the San Juan Islands he showed that crab predation and sediment type confine the introduced clam Nuttallia obscurata to sandy upper-shore sediments (2002), and that marine reserves raised the abundance, but not the competitive impact, of the harvested non-native clam Venerupis philippinarum (2005). With John J. Meyer he found that cropping of clam siphons, as fishes do, nearly doubled the predation mortality of Venerupis (2005).

name: James M. Newcomb
text:
James M. Newcomb is a neurobiologist who studies the nervous system and behaviour of nudibranch sea slugs. His early papers, from 2001 to 2004, were written with Winsor H. Watson III, and those on the nudibranch Melibe leonina give addresses at the Zoology Department and Center for Marine Biology of the University of New Hampshire and at Friday Harbor Laboratories. He then worked with Paul S. Katz at the Neuroscience Institute of Georgia State University, and his later papers give the Department of Biology and Health Science at New England College in Henniker, New Hampshire, as his address. The census counts five papers with an FHL address (2001 to 2004) and ten FHL-connected papers in all, running to 2021; the later ones describe animals collected at FHL and experiments done there, and several thank the laboratories' staff.

All of Newcomb's FHL-connected papers concern Melibe leonina. The early ones mapped neurons in its central nervous system that appear to produce nitric oxide (2001), showed that nitric oxide modulates swimming (2002), described neural activity correlated with swimming (2002) and tested how light affects locomotion (2004). With Katz he compared Melibe with Tritonia diomedea, which swims differently, and showed that homologous serotonergic interneurons and serotonin play different roles in the two species' swimming, so that the evolution of the behaviour involved changes in the functions of the same identified neurons (2009). Later papers with Watson examined daily rhythms of crawling and swimming (2014), putative circadian clock transcripts in the brain (2018), a small cardioactive peptide that may promote nighttime arousal, feeding and swimming (2020), and whether the digestive diverticula harbour photosynthetic symbionts, which they do not (2021).

name: James S. Albert
text:
James S. Albert is an ichthyologist and professor of biology at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. He earned a B.S. in zoology at the University of California, Berkeley in 1987 and an M.S. and Ph.D. in zoology at the University of Michigan. He has written more than 100 papers on the evolution and diversity of fishes, and he and colleagues have described 50 new species. He co-edited Historical Biogeography of Neotropical Freshwater Fishes (2011, with Roberto E. Reis), which explores how the Amazon and other Neotropical fish faunas formed, and the Field Guide to the Fishes of the Amazon, Orinoco, and Guianas (2017, with Peter van der Sleen). His eight census papers (2018–2026) come from work with Kassandra Ford and Kory Evans, whom the report's network links to him as students, and with FHL's Adam Summers. Several rely on CT scans of fish specimens made at FHL.

Albert's research centres on the systematics and biodiversity of Neotropical electric fishes (order Gymnotiformes). His FHL-connected papers concern the shape of the electric-fish head and skull. Two from 2018 examine sexually dimorphic head shapes in Neotropical electric fishes, treated as weapons, including how they scale with body size and their performance trade-offs. A 2020 paper redescribes a deep-channel ghost knifefish and assigns it to a new genus. In 2022 Ford, Albert and colleagues compared skull shape in 391 specimens of 78 species of South American Apteronotidae and African Mormyridae, CT-scanned at FHL, and found the convergence between the two families incomplete, or 'only skin deep'. Other 2022 papers trace mosaic craniofacial evolution in ghost knifefishes and relate functional diversity to abiotic gradients. A 2023 review surveys methods for comparative anatomical studies, and a 2026 paper treats craniofacial evolution in mormyrids.

name: James W. Truman
text:
James W. Truman is an American biologist who studies the hormonal control of insect development and the development and evolution of insect nervous systems. He completed a Ph.D. at Harvard in 1970 on the control of ecdysis in silkmoths; Wikipedia lists Lynn Riddiford as his doctoral advisor. After a junior fellowship in the Harvard Society of Fellows, he set up his laboratory at the University of Washington in 1973, retiring as professor emeritus in 2007. He was a group leader at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Janelia Research Campus from 2007 to 2016, then returned to the University of Washington, where he and Riddiford set up their laboratory at Friday Harbor Laboratories. All 31 of his census papers, from 2017 to 2026, carry an FHL affiliation. His honours include the Newcomb Cleveland Prize (1970) and election to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2009) and the National Academy of Sciences (2022).

Truman's earlier work identified eclosion hormone, the neurohormone that triggers ecdysis behaviour in moths. Using brain transplants in silkmoths, he showed that the clock timing adult emergence lies in the brain, and he documented the reorganization of the central nervous system during metamorphosis in Manduca sexta. Many of his FHL-affiliated papers concern the Drosophila ventral nerve cord: the developmental organization of its neurons and the lineage-restricted origin of neurotransmitter identity (2019), a shared naming system (2020) and a library of lineage-specific genetic driver lines (2025). Others trace larval circuits for locomotion, chemotaxis, wind-guided navigation and reward learning (2018–2019) and the remodelling of memory circuits at metamorphosis (2023). A second strand, mostly with Riddiford, concerns juvenile hormone and the evolution of metamorphosis, including reviews (2019, 2026), the larval role of the gene chinmo (2022) and the hormone's embryonic role in the firebrat Thermobia domestica (2023).

name: James William Truman
text:
James W. Truman is an insect neurobiologist and endocrinologist. After undergraduate work at the University of Notre Dame in the mosquito laboratory of George B. Craig, he earned a Ph.D. at Harvard University in 1970 under Lynn Riddiford and was a junior fellow of the Harvard Society of Fellows until 1973. He joined the University of Washington zoology faculty in 1973 and stayed for 34 years; in 2007 he became a group leader at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Janelia Research Campus. After nine years there he retired and returned to the University of Washington as professor emeritus of biology, continuing his research at Friday Harbor Laboratories. His honours include the Newcomb Cleveland Prize (1970), a Guggenheim Fellowship (1986) and election to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2009) and the National Academy of Sciences (2022). The census counts 26 FHL-address papers from 2017 to 2026.

Truman's research concerns how hormones direct the development and function of the insect nervous system, especially its remaking at molting and metamorphosis. His thesis work on adult emergence in giant silkmoths led to the isolation of eclosion hormone, and later work in moths, including the hornworm Manduca sexta, examined how ecdysone and juvenile hormone govern neurogenesis, neuronal death and remodelling. He later turned to Drosophila, mapping neuronal lineages and circuits. His FHL-connected papers include a systematic nomenclature for the Drosophila ventral nerve cord (2020), studies of larval circuits for navigation, chemotaxis and forward and backward crawling (2018-2019), and a 2023 account of how memory circuits are rebuilt at metamorphosis. A parallel line on juvenile hormone, including its embryonic role in the firebrat Thermobia domestica (2023) and reviews of the evolution of insect metamorphosis (2019, 2026), asks how complete metamorphosis arose.

name: James Winton
text:
James R. Winton is a fish-disease researcher whose address on his 2004 FHL-connected paper was the Western Fisheries Research Center in Seattle. No faculty page, staff profile or curriculum vitae could be retrieved for this profile, so it is limited to what the census papers show. His two census papers, from 2002 and 2004, came from work on diseases of Puget Sound fishes with Paul Hershberger and Richard Kocan of the University of Washington School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences. Their FHL connection is through co-authors: on the 2004 paper the first author, Christina Mork, gave Friday Harbor Laboratories as her address, and several co-authors of the 2002 paper had FHL addresses. FHL's research bibliography also lists papers by the same group with J. R. Winton as co-author, on viral hemorrhagic septicemia in Pacific herring and on Ichthyophonus infections (1999–2004).

The two papers concern pathogens of wild marine fishes in Puget Sound. The 2002 study surveyed the incidence of the pathogen Ichthyophonus hoferi in Puget Sound fishes and found that infection in Pacific herring increases with age. The 2004 study describes a rhabdovirus isolated from a single starry flounder that showed no signs of disease, collected during a virus survey of marine fishes in northern Puget Sound. The bullet-shaped, enveloped virus grew best at 15 °C in cultured fish cells. Protein analysis and PCR tests ruled out several known fish rhabdoviruses, and a partial sequence of its polymerase gene set it apart from other sequenced rhabdoviruses. The authors tentatively named it starry flounder rhabdovirus and noted how little is known about the viruses that infect marine fishes in the North Pacific.

name: Janet L. Leonard
text:
Janet L. Leonard is a biologist who studies invertebrate behaviour, especially in cnidarians and gastropod molluscs, and the evolution of hermaphrodite mating systems. Her five FHL papers, published from 1980 to 1983, give addresses at the Department of Zoology of the University of Wisconsin–Madison and at Friday Harbor Laboratories. The 1982 Journal of Experimental Biology paper reports observations made at FHL in 1976 and 1977, thanks the laboratories' staff, and gives her current address as the Division of Medical Physiology at the University of Calgary. Her later papers give addresses at Calgary, the University of California, San Diego, and the University of Oklahoma in the 1980s and early 1990s, then at Oregon State University's Hatfield Marine Science Center and, from 1999, the Joseph M. Long Marine Laboratory of the University of California, Santa Cruz. The sources read do not describe a formal role at FHL.

Leonard's FHL papers analyse how a simple animal organises its behaviour. Working with the hydromedusa Sarsia tubulosa, she described the temporal organisation of its swimming (1980) and its density regulation (1980), used maximum entropy spectral analysis to find transient rhythms in swimming (1982), made an experimental test of the 'Jennings hypothesis' of behavioural organisation (1982) and tested the effect of environmental factors on swimming (1983). She proposed that switching among several short-lived rhythms, which may arise in the marginal pacemaker system, accounts for much of the variability in Sarsia's swimming. Her later work turned to gastropods: ethograms of the sea slugs Navanax inermis (1984) and Aplysia californica (1986), studies of the Aplysia gill-withdrawal reflex, and a long series on mating in simultaneous hermaphrodites, from sperm trading in Navanax (1984) to theory on sexual selection and sexual systems and the reproductive biology of Ariolimax slugs.

name: Jaquan M. Horton
text:
Jaquan M. Horton is a comparative biomechanist who has studied the mechanical properties of fish tissues and the locomotion of fishes and amphibians. No faculty page or CV was found, so this profile rests on his papers and thesis record. His first paper (2004) gives Organismic and Evolutionary Biology at the University of Massachusetts Amherst as his address. A 2009 paper gives the Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at the University of California, Irvine, together with Friday Harbor Laboratories, and his locomotion papers of 2009 and 2011 give FHL alone. He completed a Ph.D. in biology at the University of Washington in 2020. A 2022 paper from that thesis was supported in part by an FHL fellowship awarded to him and Emily Carrington. His FHL-connected work runs from 2009 to 2022. His current position is not known.

His FHL-connected papers apply materials testing and motion analysis to fishes. With Adam P. Summers he used bending tests on the ribs of the great sculpin, Myoxocephalus polyacanthocephalus, to measure the stiffness of acellular bone (2009). Two studies with Summers and Elizabeth L. Brainerd, led by Bryan Nowroozi and Nicholas J. Gidmark, measured lift and ground effect in the northern spearnose poacher Agonopsis vulsa swimming with its pectoral fins (2009) and how sand lances change their undulating movements as they pass from water into sand (2011). For his thesis he built a pressure-inflation method to measure the passive mechanics of the intestine in two stomachless surfperches, Cymatogaster aggregata and Embiotoca lateralis. The front part of the intestine was stronger, more extensible and tougher than the rear, which suggests it works like a stomach. He reported the C. aggregata results with John M. Gosline and Carrington in 2022.

name: Jason Hodin
text:
Jason Hodin is a developmental and evolutionary biologist who studies the larvae of marine invertebrates. He received a BA in biology from Wesleyan University (1991) and a PhD in zoology from the University of Washington (1999), with a dissertation supervised by Lynn Riddiford on the evolution of reproductive strategies in dipteran insects. Between 1999 and 2004 he taught at several colleges in Seattle and California, and from 2005 he worked with David Epel at Stanford University's Hopkins Marine Station as co-principal investigator and staff scientist on the high-school education projects Virtual Urchin and I2SEA. Since October 2015 he has been a Senior Research Scientist at FHL, where he taught Research in Marine Biology (FHL 470) in 2019 and has led the University of Washington's captive rearing of the sunflower sea star, Pycnopodia helianthoides, in a partnership with The Nature Conservancy. The census lists 19 FHL-connected papers, 2004-2026.

Hodin's research asks how hormones and environmental cues shape larval development and the timing of metamorphosis and settlement. Papers in 2004 showed that thyroid hormone shifts developmental timing in sand dollar larvae and can determine their developmental mode, followed by reviews on hormone signaling and metamorphosis (2004-2006). A later series examined how turbulence affects larvae: turbulent shear spurs settlement in sea urchin larvae (2013), late-stage sand dollar larvae respond more readily to it, and brief intense turbulence produces a lasting life-history shift (2015-2019). He has also published a staging scheme for late larval development in the purple sea urchin (2014) and methods for rearing echinoderm larvae (2018). His papers since 2021 center on the sunflower star: life-cycle culture (2021), its predation on urchins and kelp forest recovery (2023), larval tolerance of warming (2025), and sea star wasting disease, including the 2025 identification of Vibrio pectenicida as a causative agent.

name: Jennifer R. Hoffman
text:
Jennifer R. Hoffman is a marine ecologist who later turned to climate-change adaptation. The census papers appear to belong to Jennifer Hoffman, an affiliate of EcoAdapt. Its listing says she has an undergraduate degree in geology from Brown University and a Ph.D. in marine ecology from the University of Washington, began studying the effects of global change as a toxicologist in 1992, co-founded EcoAdapt, and now works independently through Adaptation Insight. She co-wrote Climate Savvy: Adapting Conservation and Resource Management to a Changing World with Lara Hansen, who also co-authored her 2003 FHL paper. Bibliographic records give her addresses at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (1995), at FHL (2000 to 2004) and at the National Wildlife Federation (2012). The report's network lists Terrie Klinger, her co-author, as a teacher.

Her FHL work examined how ultraviolet radiation, alone and with temperature, affects the early life stages of marine organisms. With Benjamin Miner and Steven Morgan she tested whether chromatophores in decapod crustacean postlarvae collected from the FHL docks are an adaptation to UV radiation (2000). With Hansen and Klinger she exposed early stages of the brown algae Alaria marginata and Fucus gardneri to combinations of UV and temperature. Each factor changed the effect of the other, which limits what single-factor experiments can show (2003). With Miles Lamare she studied natural variation of carotenoids in the eggs and gonads of Strongylocentrotus sea urchins and its bearing on UV protection (2004). She also co-authored papers on risk and the evolution of embryonic cell-cycle durations (with Richard Strathmann, 2002) and on thyroxine and non-feeding development in echinoids (2001). Her 2007 popular book Ocean Science thanks the 2005 FHL Invertebrate Zoology students.

name: Joann J. Otto
text:
Joann J. Otto is a cell and developmental biologist whose papers deal with the cytoskeleton of eggs and oocytes. Her earliest FHL-connected paper, a 1976 chapter in Coelenterate Ecology and Behavior, gives addresses in developmental and cell biology at the University of California, Irvine, and at Friday Harbor Laboratories. From the early 1980s into the early 2000s her papers list the Department of Biological Sciences at Purdue University; her 1984 papers give both Purdue and FHL addresses. The census counts four FHL-address papers between 1976 and 1984, written alone or with Thomas E. Schroeder of FHL, and the FHL research bibliography lists further papers of hers through 1996. In the report's network, Richard A. Heil-Chapdelaine, her co-author at Purdue, is listed as her student. No biographical source was found, so her rank and years at Purdue are not given here.

Otto's papers concern how actin filaments and microtubules are organized and remodelled during oocyte maturation and early cleavage. The 1976 chapter described early development and planula movement in the stalked jellyfish Haliclystus. Three 1984 papers with Schroeder analysed actin bundles and actin-associated proteins in the isolated cortex of starfish oocytes, the cyclic assembly and disassembly of cortical microtubules during maturation and early development, and microtubule arrays near the germinal vesicle. Later papers with Schroeder examined actin and myosin in the contractile ring of dividing sea urchin eggs (1990) and described 'snoods', a periodic network containing cytokeratin in the starfish oocyte cortex (1991). She also worked on the actin-bundling protein fascin, reviewing actin-bundling proteins (1994) and helping to clone a mouse fascin (1995). With Heil-Chapdelaine she measured changes in F-actin during starfish oocyte maturation and during the first cell cycle of the sea urchin egg (1996).

name: Johanna Taylor Cannon
text:
Johanna Taylor Cannon is an evolutionary biologist who uses molecular phylogenetics and phylogenomics to work out relationships among animal groups, especially hemichordates. Her ORCID record lists a B.A. in biology from Bryn Mawr College (2004) and work as a neuroscience laboratory technician at the University of Virginia (2004–2006). It also lists a Ph.D. in biological sciences from Auburn University (2013) and, from 2014, a postdoctoral post in the Department of Zoology at the Swedish Museum of Natural History (Naturhistoriska riksmuseet) in Stockholm. Her papers from 2018 to 2024 give an address in the Department of Ecology, Evolution and Marine Biology at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Her FHL link came through her doctoral research on hemichordates. She held an FHL Patricia L. Dudley Fellowship, and several papers from 2009 to 2016 with Billie J. Swalla list the laboratories among the authors' addresses.

Her doctoral research, co-authored with Kenneth M. Halanych at Auburn and with Swalla, built molecular phylogenies of the Hemichordata, the acorn worms and their relatives. A 2009 paper updated the status of deep-sea acorn worms (enteropneusts). A 2013 study, supported by her FHL fellowship, identified a cold-water clade of harrimaniid acorn worms, and a 2013 paper reported that modern Antarctic acorn worms build tubes. In 2014 she led a phylogenomic analysis that resolved the hemichordate and echinoderm clade. She also contributed to studies of opsin evolution in that group (2015), global hemichordate diversity (2016) and lophotrochozoan phylogenomics (2016). In Stockholm she worked on the place of the Xenacoelomorpha in the animal tree (2016) and contributed to a 2017 study of nerve-cord evolution that used brachiopods collected near FHL. Her later papers deal with eye and opsin evolution in cnidarians, hemichordate mitochondrial genomes and the Mesozoa.

name: John H. Henson
text:
John H. Henson is a cell biologist and the Charles A. Dana Professor of Biology at Dickinson College in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, where he has been on the faculty since 1989. He received a B.A. from the University of Virginia (1979), an M.S. from Florida State University (1983) and a Ph.D. from Harvard University (1989). His research uses marine organisms as experimental systems to study how cells move, change shape and divide. His papers from 2017 to 2024 list Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) as an affiliation alongside Dickinson and describe work carried out during summer residence at FHL, with sea urchins kept in the laboratory's seawater systems and in subtidal cages. Much of this work is a collaboration with Charles B. Shuster of New Mexico State University, supported by collaborative research grants from the National Science Foundation.

Henson's FHL-connected papers centre on cytokinesis, the final step of cell division, in sea urchin eggs and embryos. Using platinum-replica electron microscopy, a 2017 paper described the arrangement of actin and myosin II filaments in the contractile ring and offered new support for a long-standing model of cytokinesis. Papers in 2021 and 2024, which also used super-resolution light microscopy, traced how the ring is assembled: from early clusters of myosin II, anillin and septin, through a septin filament network, to the recruitment of α-actinin, and how inhibiting myosin II alters the process. Related work examined the control of primary mesenchyme cell shape by the GTPase Cdc42 (2018), polar lobe formation in embryos of molluscs collected around San Juan Island (2019), the nanoscale arrangement of the Wnt signalling protein Dishevelled in the egg's vegetal cortex (2021), and methods for high-resolution imaging of the isolated cortex (2019).

name: John P. Geyman
text:
John P. Geyman is a family physician and professor emeritus of family medicine at the University of Washington School of Medicine. He earned an A.B. in geology at Princeton (1952) and an M.D. at the University of California, San Francisco (1960), and practised in rural northern California. He was among the first family practice residency directors, beginning at Santa Rosa, California, in 1969. After working in the University of Utah's Division of Family Practice (1971–72), he developed a network of residency programs in northern California at the University of California, Davis. He chaired the University of Washington's Department of Family Medicine from 1976 to 1990. He was the founding editor of The Journal of Family Practice and edited the Journal of the American Board of Family Practice from 1990 to 2003. He was elected to the Institute of Medicine, now the National Academy of Medicine.

Geyman's work concerns primary care and how health care in the United States is organized and paid for. By 2007 he had published more than 160 journal articles and 10 books; his ORCID record lists 18 books. He served as president of Physicians for a National Health Program in the mid-2000s. His four census papers, from 2011 to 2022, are of this kind. They are a 2011 festschrift for G. Gayle Stephens, two 2021 articles in the International Journal of Health Services on investor-owned health care and on privatized Medicare Advantage, and a 2022 article on private equity ownership in U.S. health care. These papers were matched to FHL through their author affiliation lines. None reports research at the laboratories, and none of the sources describes any work by him at FHL, so they should be read as false matches rather than FHL research.

name: John R. Blinks
text:
John R. Blinks was a physician-trained pharmacologist and muscle physiologist. His curriculum vitae in FHL's 2002 program review records a B.A. from Stanford University (1951) and an M.D. from Harvard Medical School (1955). He taught pharmacology at Harvard Medical School (1958-1968), including a year at University College London with A. F. Huxley and D. R. Wilkie, then chaired the Department of Pharmacology at the Mayo Foundation (1968-1988) and was professor of pharmacology at Mayo Medical School (1973-1990). In 1990 he became Professor of Physiology and Biophysics at the University of Washington. His honours include the 1987 Otto Krayer Award of the American Society for Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics. FHL describes him as spending summers and his retirement years at the laboratories. In 1996 he co-founded the Anne Hof Blinks Fellowship Endowment, which supports FHL's Blinks program for students from diverse backgrounds, and he served on the FHL Advisory Board.

Blinks's research concerned how calcium ions control muscle contraction, especially in heart muscle. To measure free calcium inside living cells he used aequorin, the calcium-sensitive light-emitting protein of the local hydromedusa Aequorea victoria, which he purified from very large numbers of jellyfish. Census papers from 1974, 1980 and 1991 that mention FHL in their text used aequorin to follow calcium in invertebrate photoreceptors, amoeboid cells and muscle. His FHL-address papers (1993-2003) include the cloning of mitrocomin (1993), a method for correcting imbalance in calcium-EGTA buffer solutions (1996) and, with Eugene Vysotski, Boris Illarionov, John Lee and colleagues, studies of obelin from the hydroid Obelia geniculata, covering its cloning, the roles of its calcium-binding sites and how its light emission is triggered (2001-2003). FHL's 2002 review describes his search for photoproteins better suited than aequorin as intracellular calcium indicators. FHL's autumn 2012 newsletter carried a memorial tribute to him by Dennis Willows.

name: John W. Brookbank
text:
John W. Brookbank worked on the biochemistry and development of sea urchin eggs and embryos. His career is traced here through the addresses on his papers. His 1954 paper, written with Arthur H. Whiteley, gives the Department of Zoology and the Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) of the University of Washington. His two 1959 papers give the Department of Biology at the University of Florida in Gainesville together with FHL, and his 1984 paper gives the Department of Microbiology and Cell Science in the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, again with FHL. His 1970, 1972 and 1980 papers give FHL alone. All seven of his census papers, from 1954 to 1984, name FHL, and the 1984 paper thanks the laboratories for research space in the summer of 1982 and used adult sea urchins from the FHL live tanks.

Brookbank's papers use the purple sea urchin, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus, and a sand dollar to study the biochemistry of eggs and the replication and packaging of DNA in early development. The 1954 study with Whiteley measured urease in sea urchin eggs and embryos. Two 1959 papers used antisera against fertilizin to detect fertilizin haptens inside unfertilized eggs and to test how the antisera affect egg respiration. In 1970 and 1972 he followed DNA synthesis and development in reciprocal hybrids between a sea urchin and a sand dollar, measuring the DNA of individual nuclei by microspectrophotometry (the 1972 paper with Joseph E. Cummins). His later papers turned to H1 histones: how the drug cordycepin and the dissociation of embryos into single cells affect H1 synthesis (1980), and the H1 histones of adult sea urchin tissues, with embryos for comparison (1984).

name: Jon L. Norenburg
text:
Jon L. Norenburg is an invertebrate zoologist and curator at the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C., whose work centres on nemerteans, or ribbon worms. He received a B.A. and an M.S. from Acadia University and a Ph.D. from Northeastern University, and he was elected a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 2002. His fields of work include invertebrate zoology, meiofauna and biogeography, and he has authored names of new taxa. His four census papers (2001–2008) are listed in FHL's research bibliography. Svetlana Maslakova, whom the report's network links to him as a student, was first author of his 2004 developmental study and a co-author of the 2007 Nemertea chapter.

Norenburg's publications deal with the taxonomy, phylogeny, biology and development of nemerteans, and also with meiofauna, proseriate flatworms and nemertean toxins. His FHL-connected papers reflect several of these interests. A 2001 comparative study with Stephen Stricker and colleagues examined oogenesis across nemertean worms. A 2004 study with Maslakova and Mark Martindale examined the development of the palaeonemertean Carinoma tremaphoros and showed that this early-branching nemertean displays fundamental properties of the spiralian developmental program. With Pamela Roe and Maslakova he wrote the Nemertea chapter of the fourth edition of The Light and Smith Manual (2007). He was also a co-author of a 2008 phylogenetic study of trachyline hydrozoans led by Allen Collins, which offered new views on the evolution of several problematic groups of these cnidarians.

name: Jonathan B. Alberts
text:
Jonathan B. Alberts is a computational biologist who builds simulations of the cell's cytoskeleton. His FHL-connected papers, from 2004 to 2014, came out of the Center for Cell Dynamics, a National Institutes of Health center that Garrett Odell directed at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 2002 to 2010 and that worked on modelling cell and developmental processes. His 2004 paper with Odell lists both authors at the Center in Friday Harbor. It credits an Alfred P. Sloan Foundation postdoctoral fellowship in computational biology, held by Alberts, for the start of the work, with further support from an NIH grant to the two authors. His papers of 2009 and 2011 also list the Center, and those of 2012 and 2014 give the University of Washington at Friday Harbor. No biographical source was found, so his positions after 2014 are not known.

Alberts writes agent-based simulations, in which individual filaments and proteins are tracked and interact through explicit biochemical and mechanical rules. His 2004 PLoS Biology paper with Odell simulated the actin-based propulsion of the bacterium Listeria monocytogenes. The simulated bacterium moved with realistic speed and tail shape, in nanometre-scale runs and pauses ("nano-saltation") that arose as links between actin filaments and the bacterial surface protein ActA formed and broke together. A 2009 study with Susanne Rafelski and Odell combined experiments and models and found that speed rose with the amount and polarity of ActA. A 2009 PLoS ONE paper set out a method for modelling filament bending in such simulations. Later papers analysed the motion of centrin foci in living cells (2011, with Rafelski, Lani Keller and Wallace Marshall) and how flexibly bonded, low-valence particles form finite clusters (2012 and 2014, with Olga Markova, Edwin Munro and Pierre-François Lenne).

name: Joseph K. Gaydos
text:
Joseph K. Gaydos is a wildlife veterinarian and research scientist and the Science Director of the SeaDoc Society, a marine conservation program of the UC Davis Karen C. Drayer Wildlife Health Center, based in Eastsound, Washington. He has worked on wildlife and ecosystem conservation in the Pacific Northwest for about two decades, has advised policymakers from Washington State to Washington, D.C., and has published more than 75 peer-reviewed papers. He co-wrote the books The Salish Sea: Jewel of the Pacific Northwest and Explore the Salish Sea, and he hosts the video series Salish Sea Wild. His six census papers (2014–2022) are connected to FHL through co-authors with FHL addresses, an FHL course, an FHL student intern, FHL dive support and advice from an FHL scientist.

Gaydos studies diseases that affect both wildlife and human health, and works on seabirds, harbor seals, river otters, porpoises and killer whales. A 2014 paper from FHL's Ecology of Marine Infectious Disease course found that older eelgrass leaves and shallower beds in the San Juan Archipelago are more prone to wasting disease, and a 2016 paper examines Labyrinthula, the agents of seagrass wasting disease. Volunteer and scientific dive surveys showed that sea star wasting disease severely depleted sunflower sea stars in the Salish Sea (2016). With Elizabeth Ashley of SeaDoc he analysed 882 harbor seal strandings in San Juan County from 2002 to 2018, finding that most pup deaths had nutritional causes (2020), and about 13,000 volunteer diver surveys that recorded 138 of the 261 fish species known from the Salish Sea (2022). A 2020 review of 30 river otter carcasses found trauma the main cause of death.

name: Julia N. Kobelt
text:
Julia N. Kobelt is a marine ecologist whose papers deal with nearshore food webs, clams and shoreline habitats in Washington State. Her FHL-connected papers date from 2017 to 2025, and all but one were written with Megan N. Dethier of the Friday Harbor Laboratories. Papers from 2017 and 2018 list her at FHL. Papers from 2018 and 2019 give her address as the Department of Biology at Montclair State University in New Jersey, and Aaron W. E. Galloway's CV marks her as a student co-author on two of them. Her 2023 and 2025 shoreline papers list her at the University of Washington's School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences, and her first-authored 2024 paper on clam recruitment lists her at FHL. An FHL newsletter column from January 2026 thanks her among the laboratories' staff and researchers. The sources do not give her job title.

Kobelt's work combines feeding experiments, biochemical tracers and field surveys. A 2017 paper examined how the kelp crab Pugettia chooses between two kelps. A 2018 study followed how two sea urchin species digest, excrete and build tissue from the fatty acids of brown, red and green seaweeds, and a 2019 paper measured the nutritional value of urchin feces for other bottom-dwelling animals. With Dethier and Jennifer Ruesink she studied juvenile clams: the physical and biological factors affecting their performance (2019), and recruitment of Manila and soft-shell clams to collectors at eight Washington beaches in 2016 and 2017 (2024). With Galloway and others she measured how many purple urchins sunflower sea stars eat and modelled whether their recovery could help kelp forests return (2023). Her shoreline papers compare beaches where armor was removed with natural reference beaches (2023) and armored with unarmored beaches below eroding feeder bluffs (2025).

name: Julius Bauschinger
text:
Julius Bauschinger (1860–1934) was a German astronomer who specialised in orbit determination, including the orbits of comets and minor planets. He studied at Munich and Berlin and took his doctorate at Munich in 1884 under Hugo von Seeliger, with a dissertation on the motion of Mercury. In 1882 he joined the German expedition to Hartford, Connecticut, that observed the transit of Venus. From 1883 he was assistant and observer at the Munich observatory. From 1896 to 1909 he directed the Astronomisches Rechen-Institut in Berlin and was professor of theoretical astronomy. He then directed the Strasbourg observatory (1909–1918) and the Leipzig observatory (1920–1930). He was a member of the Bavarian, Saxon and Prussian academies of sciences. He has no papers in the census; he appears in the report at the root of a mentoring line that reaches FHL.

Much of Bauschinger's work was computational. His Bahnbestimmung der Himmelskörper (1906; second edition 1928) treated the determination of orbits. He published Tafeln zur theoretischen Astronomie (1901) and, with Jean Peters, eight-place logarithmic-trigonometric tables (1910–1911) that were reissued in 1936 and 1958. He wrote articles for the Enzyklopädie der mathematischen Wissenschaften on least-squares adjustment, interpolation, astronomical constants and the rotation of celestial bodies, and his 1888 habilitation thesis dealt with the bending of meridian telescopes. His doctoral students in Berlin, Strasbourg and Leipzig included Alfred Wegener (1905) and Aurel Wintner, whose Leipzig dissertation on convergence questions in lunar theory he supervised with Leon Lichtenstein. Wintner's Johns Hopkins student Monroe H. Martin advised Simon A. Levin (Maryland, 1964), whose Cornell student Daniel Grünbaum is a University of Washington scientist with FHL-connected papers from 2010 to 2020.

name: Kaddee A. Lawrence
text:
Kaddee A. Lawrence worked on the behaviour and neurobiology of the nudibranch Melibe leonina with a University of New Hampshire group that studied the animal at Friday Harbor Laboratories. Her three census papers, from 2001 to 2004, all list the Zoology Department and Center for Marine Biology at the University of New Hampshire together with FHL. All three were written with Winsor H. Watson, and two also with James M. Newcomb. A footnote in the 2002 paper gives her a later address at Highline Community College in Des Moines, Washington. The census counts three FHL-address papers from 2001 to 2004. No public biography was found, so her position at New Hampshire and her later career are not described here, and this profile rests on the papers and their publication records.

Lawrence's papers concern the swimming behaviour of Melibe leonina and its neural control. A 2001 paper led by Watson in American Zoologist summarised the swim circuit. About 15 swim motoneurons in each pedal ganglion are driven by a central pattern generator of four interneurons, and swimming is inhibited by light and by nitric oxide donors. Her 2002 paper with Watson in the Biological Bulletin broke swimming into a fixed sequence of five movements. It showed that swimming can be set off reliably by contact with the predatory sea star Pycnopodia helianthoides, by pinching or by potassium chloride, which makes it suitable for neuroethological study. A 2004 paper led by Newcomb found that Melibe is more active at night and that constant light suppresses its locomotion. In isolated brains, light acting through the eyes quickly inhibited the swim motor program.

name: Karen Vedder
text:
Karen Vedder is a co-author of four papers on the reproduction, larvae and settlement of marine invertebrates, all carrying a Friday Harbor Laboratories address. No biography or CV was found, so this profile rests on the papers themselves. Three appeared between 1977 and 1982, with her address given as FHL. The fourth, from 2014, lists all three authors at "Friday Harbor Laboratories and Department of Biology, University of Washington." Each paper was written with Richard R. Strathmann of the University of Washington and FHL, with E. Sanford Branscomb, or with both. Her FHL-connected papers therefore span 1977 to 2014. The sources do not say what position she held at the laboratories.

The papers deal with how invertebrates provision and release their young and what happens to larvae at settlement. The 1977 Marine Biology paper with Strathmann related the size and organic content of eggs of echinoderms and other invertebrates to their developmental strategies and to egg eating. A 1981 Oecologia paper treated fatal settlement errors by barnacle larvae as a cost of dispersal and examined the influence of intertidal flora on barnacle settlement. A 1982 Crustaceana paper with Branscomb described the naupliar larval stages of three Puget Sound barnacles, Balanus glandula, B. cariosus and B. crenatus, the first two not described before. The 2014 Invertebrate Biology paper returned to B. glandula: broods ready to hatch at different times in winter all hatched within about two weeks in spring, breaking up brood masses triggered hatching, and crabs that broke open barnacles released many larvae while whelks released few.

name: Karly Elizabeth Cohen
text:
Karly E. Cohen is a comparative biologist who studies the evolution, development and mechanics of hard skeletal tissues in fishes, particularly teeth, scales and armour. She completed a Ph.D. in biology at the University of Washington in 2022 with a thesis on homodont and heterodont dentitions; the mentoring network links her to Adam P. Summers through that thesis, and to L. Patricia Hernandez of George Washington University and Gareth J. Fraser through co-authorship. She moved to Friday Harbor Laboratories in 2018. UW News described her as a doctoral student in 2019 and as a postdoctoral researcher at FHL in 2025. The Save Our Seas Foundation, which supports her work on spotted ratfish, says she developed research and mentorship programs at FHL and lists her as a postdoctoral fellow in the University of Florida Department of Biology. The census counts 25 FHL-address papers from 2019 to 2026.

Cohen combines CT scanning, histology, gene expression and mechanical testing to relate skeletal form to function. Early papers dealt with filter feeding in silver carp (2018) and tooth replacement in piranhas and pacus (2019), and during her doctoral years she examined tooth shape and replacement in wrasses and Pacific lingcod (2020-2021). Many FHL-connected papers use local species: armour, fluorescence and drag reduction in the Pacific spiny lumpsucker, adhesion in clingfishes, lumpsuckers and snailfishes, vertebral shape across habitats, poacher armour and prickleback jaws. A 2025 PNAS paper with Michael Coates and Fraser, based on spotted ratfish caught around FHL, showed that the forehead clasper (tenaculum) of male ratfish carries teeth rooted in a dental lamina, a tissue previously known only from the jaw. She has also reported a possible ratfish nursery in San Juan Channel (2025) and co-authored papers on biological armour and bioinspired design.

name: Kathryn A. McDonald
text:
Kathryn A. McDonald is a marine invertebrate biologist whose papers deal with the swimming and development of echinoderm embryos and larvae. She did graduate research in the University of Washington's Department of Biology while based at the Friday Harbor Laboratories, which her papers from 2003 to 2011 give as her address. Her graduate advisory committee was Richard R. Strathmann, Danny Grünbaum, Tom Daniel and Jennifer Ruesink. Her turbulence study was supported by an FHL Wainwright Fellowship and by a National Science Foundation grant to Strathmann. By 2010 her papers gave a present address at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) in Panama, and a 2014 paper on development in the gastropod Calyptraea lichen, with Rachel Collin and Maryna Lesoway, lists her at Humboldt State University in California and at STRI. Her later positions were not traced.

Her FHL research asked how the earliest swimming stages of sea urchins and sand dollars move in the water and respond to their surroundings. A 2004 paper measured swimming and sinking of blastulae of four eastern Pacific echinoids. Sinking speeds equalled or exceeded swimming speeds, smaller embryos swam faster, and sinking was faster at 10 °C than at 14 °C. In the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus the temperature effect disappeared in killed embryos, suggesting active density regulation. With Dawn Vaughn (2010) she found that a sudden increase in food induced cloning in D. excentricus plutei, possibly by anterior autotomy. A later paper used a grid-stirred turbulence tank and shear flows: swimming increased upward transport of D. excentricus blastulae but reduced it in the purple urchin Strongylocentrotus purpuratus. A 2003 paper with Megan N. Dethier and Strathmann compared the seaweeds and animals of an isolated Washington jetty with distant source sites.

name: Kathryn L. Van Alstyne
text:
Kathryn L. Van Alstyne is a marine chemical ecologist and phycologist. Van Alstyne received a B.S. in zoology from the University of Rhode Island in 1983 and a Ph.D. in zoology from the University of Washington in 1988. Papers from 1992 to 1994 give the University of Guam Marine Laboratory as an address, papers from 1993 and 1995 the Department of Biology at Kenyon College in Ohio, and papers from 1999 the Department of Zoology at Oregon State University. From 1997 to 2025 Van Alstyne was a marine scientist at Western Washington University's Shannon Point Marine Center. The FHL-connected papers begin in 1988-1990, from the UW Department of Zoology; the 1989 and 1990 papers give Friday Harbor Laboratories as a second address. Later census papers, from 2016 to 2023, come from collaborations on eelgrass, kelp crabs and ocean acidification with co-authors including Maya Groner, Megan Dethier and Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria.

Van Alstyne has studied how seaweeds and other attached marine organisms defend themselves against herbivores, predators and environmental stress. The FHL-era papers showed that grazing increased polyphenolic levels and induced adventitious branching in the intertidal rockweed Fucus distichus, measured how wounding by Littorina snails affects its growth and reproduction, and, with Valerie Paul, tested whether polyphenolic defenses of temperate brown algae deter tropical herbivorous fishes. Papers with Guam addresses examined chemical and structural defenses in Halimeda green algae, sea fans and soft corals. Later studies cover phlorotannins in Northeast Pacific kelps and rockweeds, DMSP cleavage as an activated defense, nutrients and DMSP in green-tide Ulva, and contaminants in edible Salish Sea seaweeds. The census papers from 2016 to 2023 deal with eelgrass wasting disease and its pathogen Labyrinthula zosterae, oysters and eelgrass in a high-CO2 ocean, and food choice between two kelps by the kelp crab Pugettia (2017).

name: Katie A. Dobkowski
text:
Katie A. Dobkowski is a marine ecologist whose work centres on bull kelp (Nereocystis luetkeana) and the crabs that graze it in the Salish Sea. She joined the Ruesink laboratory in UW Biology in 2012 to pursue a PhD and completed a dissertation in 2017 on the biological and physical factors that influence bull kelp abundance and distribution. Her doctoral fieldwork was based at Friday Harbor Laboratories, and she was a UW scientific diver. Her 2023 paper on the graceful kelp crab lists her at Bates College, FHL and Woodbury University in California, and Woodbury reported in 2023 on her talks about kelp and kelp crabs. In summer 2020 Bates College students did research projects with her at FHL. Her FHL-connected papers run from 2017 to 2024, and she appears on FHL student reports from 2011, when she wrote a course report on cormorant diving, to 2025.

Dobkowski asks how species interactions and physical conditions control the abundance of bull kelp. Her 2017 study of northern and graceful kelp crabs (Pugettia producta and P. gracilis) combined laboratory feeding trials, in which P. producta preferred fresh bull kelp but also ate snails, with field enclosures in which only protected juvenile kelp grew. Further papers compared crab preferences between two kelps (2017), examined what influences bull kelp recruitment (2018) and described the scaling and structure of juvenile kelp (2021); with Megan Dethier she also studied shore crab predation on juvenile clams (2019). Recent papers (2023–2024) test how warming affects feeding by kelp crabs and the graceful kelp crab's choice between bull kelp and the invasive Sargassum muticum. Her annual snorkel surveys in the San Juan Islands suggest that bull kelp is declining overall. Student projects she co-authored at FHL range from kelp grazing and breakage to river otter diets.

name: Kayla C. Hall
text:
Kayla C. Hall is a biologist who studies the form, movement and life history of cartilaginous fishes. Hall's first papers, in 2018, came from the Department of Biology at San Francisco State University, in work with Karen Crow, Peter Hundt, John Swenson and Adam Summers of the Friday Harbor Laboratories. Hall then completed a Ph.D. in biology at the University of Washington in 2023, with Summers as advisor. Papers from 2025 and 2026 give the Friday Harbor Laboratories and the UW Department of Biology as affiliations. Hall's FHL-connected papers in the census run from 2018 to 2026 and include fieldwork in the San Juan Channel near the laboratories, laboratory studies of sharks, skates and chimaeras, and a 2026 preprint, with Summers and others, on clingfish adhesive discs and skull shape.

Hall's research asks how skeletal design, swimming style and reproduction relate to where sharks, skates, rays and chimaeras live. Using radiography, CT scanning and dissection, the 2018 study showed that rays that swim by flapping, such as manta rays, have pectoral fin rays shifted toward the rear of the fin, and that fin-ray number and distribution are set early in development. The dissertation reviewed chondrichthyan life-history traits, compared the hydrodynamics of egg cases from several skate species, and described how spotted ratfish (Hydrolagus colliei) use their pectoral and pelvic fins in swimming. Later papers report the first identified potential ratfish nursery in the San Juan Islands, found in trawls from FHL (2025), and the shape and orientation of denticles around the nostrils of the Pacific spiny dogfish (2025). A 2026 paper used model chimaera fins to test how fin-ray diameter and packing affect fin motion.
