name: Kenneth M. Halanych
text:
Kenneth M. Halanych is an evolutionary biologist who studies the relationships and evolution of marine invertebrates. He holds a BS in biology from Wake Forest University and a PhD in zoology from the University of Texas (1994). After postdoctoral work at Rutgers University and the University of Pretoria, he was a scientist at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution from 1998 to 2002. He was then a professor at Auburn University from 2003 to 2021, where he held the Stewart Schneller Endowed Chair and was curator of marine invertebrates at the university museum from 2014. He is now executive director of the Center for Marine Science at the University of North Carolina Wilmington. He has edited the Biological Bulletin since 2016 and was elected an AAAS Fellow in 2018. He has taught at FHL several times as a visiting instructor, in courses on metazoan evolution and development and on deep-sea biology.

Halanych uses molecular systematics and genome-scale phylogenetics to work out the relationships of major animal groups. He also works on Antarctic fauna and on chemosynthetic animals. His 1995 Science paper used 18S ribosomal DNA to argue that lophophorates are protostomes. The census lists 29 FHL-connected items by him from 1995 to 2023, several written with the FHL-based Billie J. Swalla. Two papers concern hemichordate phylogeny, including deep-sea enteropneusts (2009) and a cold-water clade of harrimaniid acorn worms (2013). Two 2011 papers cover the spionid polychaete Boccardia proboscidea, whose reproduction varies along the West Coast, and the compact, fast-evolving mitochondrial genome of the ctenophore Pleurobrachia bachei. Later phylogenomic papers resolve the hemichordate–echinoderm clade (2014), major tunicate relationships (2017) and the aplacophoran molluscs (2019). Kevin M. Kocot and Johanna Taylor Cannon, linked to him in the report's network, are co-authors on several of these studies.

name: Kenneth P. Sebens
text:
Kenneth P. Sebens is a marine benthic ecologist and Professor in the Department of Biology and the School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences at the University of Washington, resident at Friday Harbor Laboratories since 2005. He received a BA from the University of Connecticut (1972) and a PhD from the University of Washington (1977). He was on the Harvard faculty from 1977 to 1985, and from 1979 a curator of invertebrates at the Museum of Comparative Zoology. He then directed Northeastern University's Marine Science Center (1985–1991) and the University of Maryland system's Marine-Estuarine-Environmental Sciences graduate program (1991–1997), and was the first dean of the College of Science and Mathematics at the University of Massachusetts Boston (2003–2005). He was Director of FHL from 2005 to 2013, holding the Dennis Willows Director's Endowed Professorship from 2011. The census counts 16 FHL-address papers by him, from 2005 to 2021.

Sebens studies subtidal populations and communities in temperate and tropical seas. He has spent six missions living in the Hydrolab and Aquarius underwater laboratories on Caribbean reefs. His coral research concerned coral nutrition and how water flow affects particle capture, nutrient uptake and growth; a 2005 paper measured nitrate uptake by a reef coral. His paper on indeterminate growth and optimal size in marine invertebrates received the Ecological Society of America's 1983 Mercer Award. In 2006 he began studying rocky subtidal communities of the San Juan Islands. His FHL-connected papers cover grazer removal and four decades of change in subtidal communities (2013), ocean warming and coral body size (2016), mussel mechanics, energetics and byssal threads (2014–2021), giant Pacific octopus along an urbanization gradient (2018) and seawater data from the FHL Ocean Observatory (2020–2025). The mentoring network lists seven of his students, including Robin Elahi and Eliza Heery.

name: Kerry J. Kim
text:
Kerry J. Kim is a biologist whose published work spans retinal physiology, computer models of gene networks and biology education research. Papers under his name from 2001 and 2003 give the Department of Physiology and Biophysics at the University of Washington as his address. From 2009 to 2011 his papers list the Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories; the census counts four FHL-address papers from those years among five FHL-connected papers. His papers from 2017 to 2023 give SimBiotic Software in Missoula, Montana, as his address. The sources found for this profile do not describe his positions or titles, and the link between his earlier, FHL-era and later papers rests on bibliographic author matching rather than a CV or staff page.

At the Center for Cell Dynamics Kim worked with computer models of gene regulatory networks, describing Ingeneue, a software tool for simulating and exploring them (2009). With Vilaiwan Fernandes he used a model of the segment polarity network, a gene network essential to development in many insects, to simulate evolution in haploid and diploid, sexual and asexual populations; robustness rose in all four, most in diploid sexual populations (2009). He wrote the 2009 Science commentary 'Sizing up the cell' with Bruce Edgar and co-authored a 2011 Nature study of how E2F and CRL4Cdt2 control endocycles in Drosophila and a 2011 Current Biology paper, with Marie-Anne Félix and Edwin Munro, on quantitative variation in signalling in the Caenorhabditis vulval network. Earlier papers with Fred Rieke studied adaptation in salamander retinal ganglion cells. His SimBiotic papers test question formats, assessments and feedback for teaching biology, including neurophysiology and experimental design.

name: Kevin H. Britton‐Simmons
text:
Kevin H. Britton-Simmons is a marine community ecologist whose published work concerns subtidal habitats of the San Juan Islands, Washington. With Timothy Wootton and support from the SeaDoc Society, he ran three years of field and laboratory experiments on the introduced brown seaweed Sargassum muticum. His papers give Friday Harbor Laboratories as an address from 2004 to 2014, and several from 2004 to 2010 also list the University of Chicago. The sources found do not give his position at FHL or his later career. His co-authors include H. L. Stewart, K. C. Abbott, T. Klinger, D. K. Padilla, D. O. Duggins and A. W. Galloway; the mentoring network links him to Duggins through co-authorship from 2008 to 2011. The census counts ten FHL-address papers by him, from 2004 to 2014.

Much of his work tested how Sargassum muticum, introduced to Washington's inland waters with oysters imported from Asia, affects native communities. A 2004 paper reported its direct and indirect effects on subtidal communities; SeaDoc's summary says the seaweed outcompetes native kelp for light and indirectly harms green urchins, and that native communities recovered within about a year of its removal. Later papers examined how disturbance and propagule supply shape invasion success (2007), invaders in marine reserves (2006) and effects on a native herbivorous snail (2010). He also studied the nonnative seagrass Zostera japonica (2010) and how tidal currents bias estimates of kelp bed size (2008). A second line of work followed seaweed drifting below the zone where it grows: drift algae as food for a deep subtidal sea urchin (2009), drift macrophytes and their invertebrates (2011), fatty-acid signatures of macrophytes (2012) and sedentary urchins below the macroalgal zone (2014).

name: Kjell Johansen
text:
Kjell Johansen was a comparative physiologist who studied respiration and circulation in a wide range of animals. His papers from 1958 to the mid-1960s carry addresses at the Institute for Experimental Medical Research and the University of Oslo in Norway. From 1962 into the mid-1970s he published from the Department of Zoology at the University of Washington, and from 1972 his papers list the Department of Zoophysiology at Aarhus University in Denmark; his publications continue to the late 1980s. His FHL-connected papers date from 1967 to 1973. A 1967 study of the hepatic veins of elasmobranchs, written with David Hanson, gives both the UW Department of Zoology and Friday Harbor Laboratories as addresses and states that its physiological experiments on dogfish and skates were made at FHL. The report's mentoring network links him to Hans Jorgen Fyhn as a student.

Johansen's research concerned how animals take up, transport and deliver oxygen, often comparing water and air breathing. His publications cover air breathing in fishes, including the African, South American and Australian lungfishes, the bowfin Amia calva and the electric eel; blood distribution in ducks during submersion; oxygen storage in pinnipeds and the sea otter; circulation and hemocyanin oxygen transport in the octopus Octopus dofleini; gravitational haemodynamics in the giraffe; and shifts in hemoglobin-oxygen affinity as an adaptation to hypoxia. His FHL-connected papers apply these questions to local marine animals: muscular sphincters that control hepatic blood flow in the Pacific dogfish and a skate (1967), oxygen uptake and responses to respiratory stress in sea urchins, with Robert Vadas (1967), and gas exchange in the sea star Pteraster tesselatus (1971) and the giant chiton Cryptochiton stelleri (1973), both with J. A. Petersen.

name: Kristian Fauchald
text:
Kristian Fauchald (1935–2015) was a Norwegian-born zoologist who specialised in polychaete worms. He took his first degrees at the University of Bergen and moved to California in 1965 for doctoral work with Olga Hartman at the University of Southern California. He became assistant professor of biology there in 1969 and was curator of marine annelids at the Allan Hancock Foundation until 1979. In 1979 he moved to the Department of Invertebrate Zoology at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History, where he stayed for the rest of his career and was latterly an emeritus research zoologist. He was a founding editor of the Polychaeta section of the World Register of Marine Species. At Friday Harbor he taught polychaete biology classes with Peter Jumars and later with Sally Woodin and Herb Wilson. The census holds three of his papers, from 2008 to 2014.

Fauchald worked on the classification of polychaetes. His 1977 definitions and keys to the orders, families and genera of polychaetes (the 'Pink Book') and his 1979 study of polychaete feeding guilds with Jumars, 'The diet of worms', had each been cited more than a thousand times by 2015. Much of his work concerned the order Eunicida, including revisionary monographs such as a 1982 revision of the onuphid genera Onuphis, Nothria and Paradiopatra based on type material, and he took part in early cladistic analyses of annelids. His census papers continue this line: a 2008 description of a new Diopatra from Belize and a 2014 study with Joana Zanol and Kenneth Halanych that reconciled taxonomy and phylogeny in the Eunicidae. The 2009 paper, with Nataliya Budaeva, described the larval development of the onuphid Mooreonuphis stigmatis from the north-east Pacific, using specimens collected and preserved with help from FHL staff.

name: L. D. Partridge
text:
L. D. Partridge, who signs most of his papers L. Donald Partridge, is a neurophysiologist. His FHL-connected papers date from 1973 to 1979. A 1976 paper with Charles F. Stevens gives his address as the Department of Physiology and Biophysics, University of Washington School of Medicine, with a present address at Friday Harbor Laboratories. His 1975 and 1979 papers in Brain Research give FHL as his address. A 1973 note in The Veliger, under the name L. D. Partridge Jr., thanks R. L. Fernald, then FHL director, for use of the laboratories. Papers under the same name, continuing the same lines of work, give addresses at the University of New Mexico School of Medicine, first in physiology from 1980 and later in neurosciences, into the 2010s. Some bibliographic databases wrongly merge his papers with those of Linda Partridge, a different scientist.

His FHL-connected papers concern the anatomy and electrical behaviour of molluscan neurons. The 1973 note described the circumesophageal ganglion complex of several dorid nudibranchs. A 1975 paper reported that bursting induced by the convulsant pentylenetetrazol can occur without a negative-conductance characteristic. In 1976 he published two papers in The Journal of Physiology. One, with Stevens, traced spike-frequency adaptation in neurons of the nudibranchs Archidoris montereyensis and Anisodoris nobilis to a slow current and added it to a model of repetitive firing. The other, with R. C. Thomas, showed that lithium injected into snail neurones raised their resting potassium permeability. A 1979 paper with S. H. Thompson, S. J. Smith and J. A. Connor analysed current-voltage relationships of repetitively firing neurons. His later New Mexico papers continued this work, then turned to calcium-activated cation channels and synaptic transmission in mammalian neurons.

name: L. Patricia Hernandez
text:
L. Patricia Hernandez is Professor of Biology in the Department of Biological Sciences at the George Washington University, where her listed field of expertise is functional morphology. She received a BS in biology from Eckerd College (1987), an MS in zoology from the University of South Florida (1994) and a PhD in organismic and evolutionary biology from Harvard University (1999). Her connection to FHL in the census comes through co-authors with FHL addresses, chiefly Karly Cohen, who came to FHL from George Washington University, and Adam Summers of FHL. The census lists six papers with her name, from 2018 to 2022, on fish feeding, teeth, attachment and development.

Hernandez studies how the fish head develops and evolves. Her group has examined craniofacial development in zebrafish, including the role of the Hedgehog pathway in the differentiation of branchial cartilages. It has also studied the proportion and distribution of muscle fibre types in cranial muscles, neurocranial shape in cyprinids, and the evolution of the Weberian apparatus in otophysan fishes. Her FHL-connected papers use anatomy, micro-CT imaging and flow measurement. They include a 2018 model of filter feeding in silver carp built from micro-CT and 3D particle image velocimetry, a 2019 study of heterodonty and tooth replacement in piranhas and pacus, and a 2020 study of the soft tissues behind the viscoelastic grip of the remora's sucker. A 2022 paper examined how shifts in developmental position and timing shaped the epibranchial organs of otocephalan fishes. She also co-signed a 2018 editorial on the aims of the journal Integrative Organismal Biology.

name: Larry R. McEdward
text:
Larry R. McEdward was a marine biologist who studied the ecology, physiology and evolution of invertebrate larvae and life histories, especially in echinoderms. He completed his PhD with Richard R. Strathmann of the University of Washington, whose CV lists him among his doctoral students. His papers from the early 1990s give his address as the Department of Zoology at the University of Florida in Gainesville. He edited Ecology of Marine Invertebrate Larvae (CRC Press, 1995), a 13-chapter review of larval diversity, feeding, mortality, behavior, dispersal, recruitment and evolution. He died unexpectedly in 2001, and the Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology held a symposium in his honor on life histories of benthic marine invertebrates. The census counts nine FHL-address papers from 1984 to 1991. Later papers appear in the FHL bibliography or mention FHL in their text.

McEdward asked how egg size, larval form and feeding shape the development and evolution of marine life cycles. His FHL-era papers measured the growth, shape and metabolism of an echinoid pluteus larva and how temperature affects its form and development rate (1984–1985). Comparative studies of echinoid larvae related egg size to larval form, feeding and metabolism (1986). With Strathmann he argued that the ciliary sieve of the cyphonautes larva breaks a biological rule of inference (1986). Other papers showed that egg volume and energy content are not correlated among sibling starfish eggs (1987), tested the developmental effects of reduced egg size with Barry Sinervo (1988), and measured eggs of echinoderms with non-feeding pelagic larvae (1991). At Florida he proposed that the starfish Pteraster tesselatus had re-evolved pelagic larval development from brooding (1992), a theme he pursued with Daniel Janies, and later modeled fecundity and development time (2003–2004).

name: Laura Newcomb
text:
Laura Newcomb is a marine biologist whose ORCID record now lists her as a program analyst in the Office of Science Support of NOAA's Oceanic and Atmospheric Research. She received a PhD in biology from the University of Washington in 2015, supported by a National Science Foundation IGERT Program on Ocean Change fellowship, FHL's Strathmann and Wainwright fellowships and UW Biology's Edmondson Award. The report's mentoring network lists Emily Carrington as her thesis advisor. Her doctoral experiments used mussels held at Friday Harbor Laboratories, which appears as an address on her papers from 2015 to 2022. Earlier co-authored papers concern the sea crossings of migrating griffon vultures (2009) and coral mortality from low-temperature stress in the Florida Keys (2011). At NOAA she has co-authored analyses of research transition and a 2023 Philosophy of Science paper on how institutional values shape the evaluation of NOAA funding proposals.

Newcomb's FHL-connected work asks how ocean warming and acidification affect mussels' byssal threads. Her dissertation combined laboratory crosses of seawater pH and temperature (10 to 25 °C) with a field study at a mussel farm. Warm water produced fewer and weaker threads in Mytilus trossulus, and low pH strengthened the plaque but not the whole thread. Above about 18 °C the warm-adapted M. galloprovincialis attached more strongly while M. trossulus attached more weakly. Papers from this work analysed thread structure under combined temperature and CO2 stress (2019) and the divergent responses of the two species to warming (2022). With Emily Roberts and others she showed that induced thread production reduces mussel growth (2021). She was first author, with Jason Hall-Spencer and others, of a 2015 study of ocean acidification and the alga called the mermaid's wineglass, and co-authored FHL student reports on tide-pool carbonate chemistry (2011) and thread production (2012).

name: Lauren Eve Simonitis
text:
Lauren Eve Simonitis is a comparative morphologist who studies the anatomy of fishes, especially the olfactory organs of sharks and their relatives. Her papers from 2018 to 2022 give the Department of Marine Biology of Texas A&M University at Galveston as her address. She then held a National Science Foundation Postdoctoral Fellowship in Biology (2022 to 2024), hosted by Florida Atlantic University and the University of Washington, and an FHL Calvin Postdoctoral Fellowship. Her papers from 2023 to 2025 list Friday Harbor Laboratories, often together with Florida Atlantic University; the census counts four FHL-address papers in those years, and the report lists her as still at FHL. These papers acknowledge the laboratories' Karl F. Liem Memorial Bioimaging Facility and micro-CT scanner. In 2022 she was co-author, with Ayi Ajavon, of an FHL student research paper comparing the olfactory organs of three intertidal gunnel species.

Simonitis asks how the structure of the olfactory organ relates to water flow and smell. She has described the microstructure of the bonnethead shark's olfactory rosette (2022) and the denticles of shark nostrils and their hydrodynamic implications (2025). Using contrast-enhanced micro-CT and scanning electron microscopy, she studied the rosettes of Pacific spiny dogfish and spotted ratfish trawled near Friday Harbor, finding larger, more folded lamellae at the centre of the rosette but no difference in sensory surface area among lamellar positions (2024). Her NSF fellowship project asked whether ink from animals such as California sea hares and common cuttlefish deters sharks, whether sharks can smell it, and how it moves through the shark nostril. Other FHL-connected papers compare the anatomy and evolution of gizzards across fishes (2023) and reconstruct the history of shell-boring polychaetes in the native oyster Ostrea lurida in the Salish Sea, to inform its restoration (2025).

name: Leon Lichtenstein
text:
Leon Lichtenstein (1878–1933) was a Polish-German mathematician, born in Warsaw, who came to mathematics from engineering. He graduated in mechanical engineering from the Technische Hochschule Berlin-Charlottenburg in 1901 and worked as an electrical engineer for Siemens & Halske from 1902 to 1920, heading its cable factory from 1906. During those years he took a doctorate in engineering at the Technische Hochschule (1908) and a doctorate in mathematics at the University of Berlin (1909), and he habilitated at the Technische Hochschule in 1910. He became professor at Münster in 1920 and held the chair of mathematics at Leipzig from 1921 or 1922 until 1933. He co-founded Mathematische Zeitschrift in 1918 and edited the Jahrbuch über die Fortschritte der Mathematik from 1919 until the late 1920s. He has no papers in the census; he appears in the report at the root of a mentoring line that reaches FHL.

Lichtenstein worked in potential theory, integral equations, the calculus of variations, differential equations and conformal mapping. He applied these methods to hydrodynamics and to celestial mechanics, especially the equilibrium figures of rotating fluids. His books include Astronomie und Mathematik in ihrer Wechselwirkung (1922), Grundlagen der Hydromechanik (1929) and Gleichgewichtsfiguren rotierender Flüssigkeiten (1933). At Leipzig his doctoral students included Ernst Hölder, Erich Kähler and Aurel Wintner. Wintner was his assistant from 1927 to 1929, helping to edit Mathematische Zeitschrift and the Jahrbuch, and wrote his Leipzig dissertation on convergence questions in lunar theory under Lichtenstein and the astronomer Julius Bauschinger. Wintner later taught at Johns Hopkins, where Monroe H. Martin was his student. Martin advised Simon A. Levin (Maryland, 1964), and Levin's Cornell student Daniel Grünbaum is a University of Washington scientist with FHL-connected papers from 2010 to 2020.

name: Leonid L. Moroz
text:
Leonid L. Moroz is a neuroscientist at the University of Florida, where he is Distinguished Professor of Neuroscience, Genetics, Biology and Chemistry, based at the Whitney Laboratory for Marine Bioscience. He received a B.S. in animal and human physiology from Belarus University in Minsk (1982) and a Ph.D. from the Institute of Developmental Biology in Moscow (1989), with Dmitry Sakharov as mentor. After research posts in Leeds, at the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, in Lund and in Calgary, including a Royal Society fellowship at Leeds (1993-94), he worked at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (1994-98). He joined UF's neuroscience faculty in 1998, becoming professor in 2006 and Distinguished Professor in 2014. His FHL connection is collaborative: with Billie Swalla he directed UW research apprenticeships at FHL in 2008, 2010 and 2012 whose students contributed to sequencing the genome of the ctenophore Pleurobrachia bachei.

Moroz studies how neurons and their chemical signals arose and evolved, working mainly on ctenophores (comb jellies), placozoans and molluscs and combining neuroscience, microchemistry and genomics. His FHL-connected work centres on the sea gooseberry Pleurobrachia bachei, many of them collected in FHL waters: a 2011 study of its compact, fast-evolving mitochondrial genome; 2012 apprenticeship reports on its Wnt, LIM-homeobox, collagen and glutamate-signalling genes and candidate secretory peptides; and the 2014 Nature genome paper, which placed ctenophores on the first branch of the animal tree and argued that their neural systems evolved independently. With Tigran Norekian he mapped neural and muscular systems in Pleurobrachia, Beroe abyssicola, Euplokamis dunlapae and the hydromedusa Aglantha digitale (2015-2019), and found that nitric oxide suppresses ciliary activity in ctenophores collected from the FHL dock (2023). Earlier census papers treat nitric oxide signalling in Clione and Aglantha and, with Andreas Heyland, thyroid hormone signalling in invertebrates (2006).

name: Linda G. Wordeman
text:
Linda G. Wordeman is a cell biologist and professor in the Department of Neurobiology & Biophysics at the University of Washington, where her ORCID record lists her employment from 1994. She received a BA in molecular biology (1982) and a PhD in zoology (1988) from the University of California, Berkeley, and was a postdoctoral fellow in pharmacology at the University of California, San Francisco, until 1993. She received a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2009, has been an adjunct professor of biology at UW since 2015, and joined the Board of Scientific Counselors of the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NIH) in 2019. Her FHL connection runs through the Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories. Four of her census papers, from 2008 to 2012, carry an FHL address, eight in all are FHL-connected, and a 2007 paper thanks centre staff for help with live imaging.

Wordeman studies how kinesin-related motor proteins control microtubules, the dynamic filaments that shape cells and separate chromosomes during division. Her work centres on the kinesin-13 microtubule depolymerisers, especially MCAK, and the kinesin-8 family, and uses single-molecule TIRF microscopy and high-resolution live-cell imaging. Her FHL-connected papers, several with George von Dassow, showed that MCAK associates with the tips of growing microtubules (2005), promotes turnover of kinetochore microtubules to aid chromosome movement (2007) and acts at microtubule tips to control spindle microtubule length and kinetochore attachment (2012). Others report a kinesin-13 mutant that depolymerises microtubules in ADP (2008), the kinesin-8 Kif18A suppressing kinetochore movements to align chromosomes (2008, with Jason Stumpff), and long astral microtubules uncoupling the spindle from the cleavage furrow (2010). A 2011 review considers MCAK as a potential cancer drug target.

name: Lyda S.T. Harris
text:
Lyda S. T. Harris is a marine biologist who works on microplastic pollution and environmental policy. She received a PhD in biology from the University of Washington in 2020, and her website adds a concentration in public policy from UW's Evans School of Public Policy. The report's mentoring network lists Emily Carrington as her thesis advisor. Her doctoral research was supported by FHL's Strathmann Fellowship, an FHL research award, an FHL travel grant and UW Biology's Edmondson Award. Her papers from 2019 to 2023 give Friday Harbor Laboratories as an address. Her website describes more than a decade of work on sustainability and marine debris prevention in academic, NGO and corporate settings. This work includes corporate sustainability strategy, international marine debris programme management and a NOAA Marine Debris Program grant. The website also lists recognition from the American Institute of Biological Sciences for emerging public policy leadership.

Harris's FHL work used the mussel Mytilus trossulus to ask how microplastics affect filter feeders and the habitats they connect. In laboratory experiments she found that high concentrations of microplastic, but not natural silt, reduced mussel clearance rates (2019). With mussels held in FHL seawater tables, she found that biodeposits from mussels fed microplastic contained fewer algal cells, sank more slowly and resuspended at lower water velocities, which could carry particles farther from mussel beds (2021). Her dissertation added a scientometric and diffusion analysis of marine microplastic research and of national plastic policies. It found that both had grown exponentially and that the amount of research was not a good indicator of national policy adoption (2021). Other papers surveyed microparticles in mussels at regional and local scales across the Salish Sea (2023) and tracked microparticles beneath the Seattle Aquarium during the COVID-19 pandemic (2021).

name: Lynn M. Riddiford
text:
Lynn M. Riddiford is an insect developmental biologist and endocrinologist and Professor Emerita of Biology at the University of Washington. She received a BA in biochemical sciences from Radcliffe College (1958) and a PhD in zoology from Cornell University (1961). After postdoctoral work, teaching at Wellesley College and a fellowship in Carroll Williams's laboratory, she joined Harvard's biology faculty in 1966. She moved to the UW Department of Zoology in 1973, became professor in 1975 and was the first Virginia and Prentice Bloedel University Professor (2000–2005). After retiring in 2007 she spent about nine years as a Senior Fellow at HHMI's Janelia Research Campus; in 2016 she set up her laboratory at Friday Harbor Laboratories. She is a member of the National Academy of Sciences (2010) and was president of the American Society of Zoologists (1991–92). The census counts 13 FHL-address papers by her, from 2017 to 2026.

Riddiford's research asks how juvenile hormone (JH) controls molting, metamorphosis and development in insects. Much of her earlier work used the tobacco hornworm, Manduca sexta, and bore on the use of JH as an insect growth regulator in pest control. At Janelia she studied hormonal control of nervous system development and behaviour in Drosophila. Her FHL-connected papers, partly from work with James Truman on the evolution of complete metamorphosis, include genetic tools for studying JH action in Drosophila (2017), JH and the developing optic lobe during metamorphosis (2018), the gene chinmo as the larval member of a three-part molecular system directing metamorphosis (2022) and the embryonic role of JH in the firebrat Thermobia domestica (2023). She has also written reviews of the evolution of insect metamorphosis (2019, 2026), a history of JH research (2020) and an autobiographical review (2019). At FHL she is extending the work to metamorphosis in crustaceans.

name: Lynn Riddiford
text:
Lynn M. Riddiford is an insect endocrinologist. She graduated from Radcliffe College in biochemical sciences in 1958, having begun work on juvenile hormone as an undergraduate in Carroll Williams's laboratory at Harvard. She earned a PhD in zoology at Cornell University in 1961, advised by Marcus Singer and Harold Scheraga, with a thesis on the structure of paramyosin. After a postdoctoral fellowship at Harvard and two years teaching at Wellesley College, she returned to Harvard in 1965 and became assistant professor in 1966 and associate professor in 1971. She joined the University of Washington's zoology department in 1973, retired from it in 2007 and became a senior fellow at HHMI's Janelia Research Campus. In 2016 she and James Truman returned to the University of Washington and set up their laboratory at FHL. Her honours include a Guggenheim Fellowship (1979) and election to the National Academy of Sciences (2010).

Riddiford studies how hormones control molting and metamorphosis in insects, especially the interplay of juvenile hormone and molting hormone. Her earlier work largely used the tobacco hornworm, Manduca sexta. Her 15 census papers date from 2017 onward, all with an FHL address, and turn largely to Drosophila and to the evolution of metamorphosis. They include genetic tools for studying juvenile hormone action in Drosophila (2017), the hormone's effects on the optic lobe during metamorphosis (2018), and a 2022 paper presenting the factor Chinmo as the larval member of a 'molecular trinity' that directs metamorphosis. A 2023 eLife study of juvenile hormone in embryos of the firebrat Thermobia domestica examined the hormone's role before it became involved in metamorphosis. She has also written reviews, a history of juvenile hormone research (2020) and an autobiographical article (2019). Most of these papers are co-authored with James W. Truman, her former graduate student.

name: M. A. R. Koehl
text:
Mimi A. R. Koehl is a biomechanist and professor in the Department of Integrative Biology at the University of California, Berkeley. She earned a B.A. in biology at Gettysburg College and a Ph.D. in zoology at Duke University with S. A. Wainwright. She then held postdoctoral fellowships at Friday Harbor Laboratories with Richard Strathmann (1976–1977) and at the University of York with John Currey. Her honours include a MacArthur Fellowship (1990), election to the National Academy of Sciences (2001) and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2002), the Borelli Award of the American Society of Biomechanics (2002) and the John Martin Award of ASLO. The census counts three FHL-address papers, all from 1977, and later papers of hers acknowledge FHL and its Helen R. Whiteley Center.

Koehl studies how the structure of organisms and their physical environment together determine mechanical function, using methods from fluid and solid mechanics and from field ecology. Her 1977 FHL papers treated sea anemones as cantilever-like sessile animals, examining the flow forces they meet and the mechanics of their body-wall connective tissue. They compared the short, wide, wave-swept Anthopleura xanthogrammica with the tall, calm-water Metridium senile. A 1977 paper with Wainwright found that high extensibility helps the kelp Nereocystis luetkeana avoid breaking in waves. A 1988 study with R. S. Alberte compared flapping and photosynthesis in undulate and flat Nereocystis blades. With Michael Hadfield she measured larval recruitment of the nudibranch Phestilla sibogae (2007) and asked whether larvae of the tubeworm Hydroides elegans must touch a biofilm to settle (2014). A 2022 study with Thomas Daniel examined flow interactions between the seaweed Mazzaella splendens and an epibiotic bryozoan at the FHL breakwater.

name: M. Patricia Morse
text:
M. Patricia Morse is a marine biologist and science educator. She spent more than thirty years as a professor of biology at Northeastern University, and her papers of the 1980s give her address as its Biology Department and Marine Science Center at Nahant, Massachusetts. Her past-presidential address to the American Society of Zoologists was published in American Zoologist in 1987. The Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology lists her as a past president and has named its award for excellence and innovation in science education after her. By 2012 she was a visiting scholar at FHL and a member of its Advancement Committee, and that year she gave FHL's Arthur Whiteley Lecture on a trip to Japan retracing the zoologist Edward S. Morse and his part in the growth of natural history there. The census lists eight of her papers, from 1985 to 2008, most found through FHL's research bibliography.

Morse combined electron microscopy with experimental methods such as injection techniques to study the structure and function of molluscan tissues, especially in bivalves. Her central subject was the bivalve excretory system. With Edgar Meyhöfer, then a co-worker at Northeastern, and William Robinson she presented morphological evidence for ultrafiltration by podocytes in bivalves (1985). In 1987 she reviewed how filtration at the podocytes of the pericardial gland, followed by secretion and reabsorption, produces the urine. With Meyhöfer she compared the heart-kidney complex in three protobranch bivalves (1990) and characterised the ultrafiltration system of the mussel Mytilus edulis, the scallop Chlamys hastata and the clam Mercenaria mercenaria (1996). With Meyhöfer and others she also reported hemocyanin in bivalves (1986) and compared it with other molluscan hemocyanins (1988). Other papers described the body wall of the priapulid Meiopriapulus fijiensis (1989) and, with John Zardus, the pericalymma larva of the protobranch Acila castrensis (1998).

name: M. R. Baker
text:
Matthew R. Baker is a fisheries ecologist who works on North Pacific fishes and their habitats. Since 2014 he has been Science Director of the North Pacific Research Board, a marine research organization in Anchorage, Alaska, created by Congress in 1997. He previously worked at NOAA's Alaska Fisheries Science Center and with the University of Washington's Alaska Salmon Program, and his ORCID record lists him as a research affiliate of the Center from 2010. At Friday Harbor Laboratories he is an instructor in Pelagic Ecosystem Function, an autumn research apprenticeship in which students study the oceanography, plankton, forage fish and predators of the San Juan Archipelago. A 2016 conference abstract gives his affiliation as UW Friday Harbor Labs. The census counts 15 FHL-address papers by him, from 2016 to 2026.

Baker's FHL research centres on the Pacific sand lance (Ammodytes personatus), a forage fish of sandy seabeds. With apprenticeship students he built a six-year time series (2010–2015) on sand lance in the San Juan Archipelago, covering abundance, diet, condition, movements and sediment association. Papers from this work report seasonal abundance and demographics (2016), feeding ecology (2017), gonad maturation (2022) and diel vertical migration (2023). In 2018 he led the sand lance team in a SeaDoc Society submersible project headed by Gary Greene of the Tombolo Mapping Laboratory, which filmed the fish over sand waves with a stereo-camera array. Papers on this sand-wave habitat followed (2019–2025). Others assess threats to the species (2024), microplastics in forage fish and sediments (2023, 2025), and climate and noise effects on condition, overwinter survival and anti-predator behaviour (2025–2026). A 2020 paper compares age and growth at the latitudinal extremes of the Gulf of Alaska.

name: M. W. Jacobs
text:
Molly W. Jacobs is a marine invertebrate biologist who studies larval development, metamorphosis and life histories, mainly in ascidians (sea squirts). Her papers of 2006 and 2008 give the Friday Harbor Laboratories as her address. There she published with Richard Strathmann of FHL and with Bernard Degnan's group at the University of Queensland. From 2010 her papers give the Department of Biology at McDaniel College in Westminster, Maryland, and a 2016 paper gives both McDaniel and FHL. Papers from 2012 to 2017 on American lobsters list the University of Connecticut and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, and a 2019 paper on long-term change in eastern Long Island Sound lists Project Oceanology in Groton, Connecticut. The census counts three FHL-address papers, all from 2006, within FHL-connected work from 2003 to 2016. No public biography was found to confirm her current position.

Jacobs's FHL research asked what happens when ascidian larvae delay metamorphosis. A 2006 study with Degnan's group found that older larvae of Herdmania momus change in shape and gene expression. A 2008 paper with Degnan, John Bishop and Strathmann found that three of six solitary species begin forming postlarval structures during the delay, and that delays of up to three days did not slow juvenile growth. With Kristin Sherrard she reported in 2010 that offspring size did not predict juvenile growth or survival in seven ascidian species. The FHL bibliography also lists a 2004 book chapter on solitary-to-colonial transitions in animal evolution. Other FHL-connected papers cover non-native species in marinas on England's south coast (2006), local adaptation in the colonial ascidian Botrylloides violaceus in the San Juan Islands (2013), and decorator crabs, Oregonia gracilis, which begin decorating at the first juvenile stage (2016).

name: Mackenzie E. Gerringer
text:
Mackenzie E. Gerringer is a deep-sea biologist who studies fishes of the abyssal and hadal (ocean-trench) zones. She earned a B.A. in biology and German studies at Whitman College, spent 2012–2013 as a Fulbright English teaching assistant in Bremen, Germany, and completed a Ph.D. in marine biology at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, where she held an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship from 2015. From 2017 to 2019 she was a postdoctoral research fellow at FHL, working on the functional morphology and physiology of fishes. She was instructor of record for FHL's Integrative Oceans course in 2017 and 2019 and for Seminars in Marine Science in 2017. She joined SUNY Geneseo as assistant professor of biology in 2019, became associate professor in 2024, and in 2026 moved to Whitman College as assistant professor of biology. The census counts three FHL-address papers from 2017 to 2022.

Gerringer studies how fishes live under the high pressure, cold and darkness of the deep sea. Her papers include species descriptions, diet studies from stomach contents and isotopes, life histories from otoliths, measurements of metabolic enzymes and micro-CT scans of skeletons. Her CV lists more than 200 days at sea, including expeditions to the Kermadec, Mariana, New Hebrides and Peru-Chile trenches and a 2022 Alvin submersible expedition to the Puerto Rico Trench. Her FHL-connected work, partly with Adam Summers, includes a 2014 FHL student report on the gelatinous tissue under the skin of a hadal snailfish, a 2017 survey of gelatinous tissues in deep-sea fishes, a 2019 review of why snailfishes dominate the fish fauna of the deepest trenches, and micro-CT studies relating bone density to habitat depth in snailfishes (2021) and rattails (2022). Later papers describe otoliths of the deepest fishes (2023) and three new abyssal snailfishes (2025).

name: Marcus Singer
text:
Marcus Singer (1914–1994) was a biologist who worked experimentally on regeneration. The institutions on his papers place him at Harvard University in the 1940s and early 1950s, at Cornell University from about 1953 into the early 1960s, and from the early 1960s at Case Western Reserve University. He held a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1966. At Cornell he and Harold Scheraga advised the doctoral work of Lynn Riddiford, who received her PhD in zoology in 1961 with a thesis on the structure of paramyosin. Singer has no papers in the census. He appears in the report as Riddiford's teacher; in 2016 she and James Truman set up their laboratory at FHL, where she has carried out her later insect research.

Singer's main question was how nerves control the regrowth of amputated limbs. In a series of papers from 1942 to 1949 on forelimb regeneration in the adult newt Triturus, he tested the roles of the sympathetic, sensory and motor nerve supplies and related regenerative ability to the number of nerve fibres in the limb. He reported that augmenting the nerve supply could induce forelimb regeneration in frogs (1951, 1954), and he reviewed the subject in The Quarterly Review of Biology in 1952. Later papers extended the question to taste buds, catfish barbels, lizard tails and mouse limbs, and measured acetylcholine and acetylcholinesterase in the regenerating newt limb. A 1964 paper set out theoretical considerations on the trophic role of the neuron. He also published histochemical studies of dye binding by tissues and works on the human brain in sagittal section (1955) and the dog brain in section (1962).

name: Matthew A. Kolmann
text:
Matthew A. Kolmann is an evolutionary biologist and functional morphologist who studies fishes. He received a BSc in biology from the University of Tampa (2008) and an MSc from Florida State University (2012), where he worked with Dean Grubbs on the feeding biomechanics and fisheries ecology of cownose rays. His PhD at the University of Toronto produced a 2016 thesis on the evolution of the feeding mechanism in stingrays. His papers from 2016 to 2020 list Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address, several jointly with George Washington University or the Royal Ontario Museum, and he held an NSF Postdoctoral Research Fellowship in Biology from 2018 to 2020. Since 2022 he has been an assistant professor of biology at the University of Louisville. The census counts 11 FHL-address papers by him, from 2017 to 2020, and also includes a 2014 report in UW ResearchWorks on stingray jaws and shell crushing.

Kolmann studies how anatomy, mechanics and ecology shape the evolution of feeding in fishes, using CT scanning, measurements of bite force and jaw stiffness, museum specimens and phylogenetic comparisons. His stingray work covers jaw curvature and shell crushing (2015), chewing of insect prey (2016) and changes in jaw stiffness with growth in mollusc-eating stingrays (2019). His FHL-connected papers range across fish groups: sexual dimorphism in Neotropical electric fishes (2018), the armored keel (2018) and tooth replacement (2019) of piranhas and pacus, diet specialization in scale-eating fishes (2018), diet and form in freshwater sculpins (2019), habitat transitions in needlefishes (2020), trade-offs between swimming and armor in poachers (2020) and a step-by-step guide to CT data with open software (2020). Later papers treat fish gizzards (2023), tooth mechanics of fruit-eating fishes (2025), stingray spines (2026) and a new freshwater stingray species (2026). The network lists Jonathan M. Huie as his student.

name: Matthew N. George
text:
Matthew N. George is a marine biologist who studies how shellfish respond to changing ocean conditions. After a B.S. in biology from Gonzaga University (2010), he worked as a research technologist at Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) in 2011–2012. He then earned a Ph.D. in biology at the University of Washington (2018) in Emily Carrington's laboratory, with a dissertation on mussel attachment from an ecomechanical perspective. He was then a research fellow in physiology and biomedical engineering at the Mayo Clinic (2018–2019), a postdoctoral fellow at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (2019–2020) and a research scientist in the University of Washington's School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences (2020–2023). In 2023 he became Coastal Shellfish Manager in the Fish Program of the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife. His FHL-address papers date from 2013 to 2022.

Most of George's FHL work concerns the byssus, the protein threads and adhesive plaques that anchor mussels to rocks and aquaculture lines. He co-authored a 2013 Nature Climate Change paper reporting that ocean acidification weakens byssal attachment, and his later papers examined how seawater conditions after secretion strengthen the adhesive (2018), how low oxygen interrupts DOPA cross-linking as plaques cure (2018), how warming and elevated carbon dioxide together affect thread structure (2019), and how pH and oxygen fluctuate within mussel clumps, with implications for raft aquaculture (2019). Experiments used mussels from San Juan Island held at FHL and mesocosms in the laboratory's ocean acidification facility. A 2022 paper found that mussels repair shell damage despite limits imposed by acidification. With Carrington he also studied how sea urchins reorient their spines to capture drifting particles (2014), and at UW he later co-authored work on heatwave mortality in triploid Pacific oysters (2023).

name: Megan L Vandenberg
text:
Megan L. Vandenberg is a doctoral student in Biology at the University of Washington, working in Adam Summers' laboratory at Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL), where she began her PhD research in autumn 2023. She earned a B.S. in Biology from UW in 2022. Her connection to FHL began in autumn 2021 with the Bio Imaging research apprenticeship led by Summers, followed the next summer by the Functional Morphology and Ecology of Marine Fishes course. In July 2022 she gave an FHL talk on poacher armour, and in 2023 she worked at FHL as a research technician in CT scanning, particle image velocimetry and SEM imaging. Her research has been supported by FHL's Stephen and Ruth Wainwright Endowed Fellowship (2023) and Research Endowment Fellowship (2025), and she wrote FHL's March 2025 Tide Bite column. Her FHL-connected papers date from 2023 to 2026.

Her research asks what the bony armour of poachers (family Agonidae), bottom-dwelling fishes covered in overlapping plates, does besides protection, testing functions such as reducing drag and adding bending stiffness. She combines CT scanning, scanning electron microscopy and histology with 3D-printed models, flume experiments, particle image velocimetry and materials testing. A 2024 paper in the Biological Journal of the Linnean Society found that larger spines on poacher armour reduce boundary-layer separation and drag; 2026 papers address the phylogenomics of poachers and the evolution of armour across cottoid fishes, and the mechanical strengths and weaknesses of poacher armour. Her first paper (2023), from her apprenticeship project, showed how the keratin plates of whale baleen break away to expose the hair-like fringe that filters food. Other work covers the neck vertebrae of plunge-diving seabirds (2026), bioinspiration research shared between biologists and engineers (2025) and FHL undergraduate research reports she co-authored (2025).

name: Megan N. Dethier
text:
Megan N. Dethier is a marine ecologist and research professor in the University of Washington Department of Biology, in full-time residence at Friday Harbor Laboratories. She received a BA in biology from Carleton College (1975) and a PhD in zoology from the University of Washington (1981), working with Robert Paine on the community structure of Washington tidepools, and held an FHL postdoctoral fellowship in 1983. After research positions at UW's Institute for Environmental Studies and in Zoology and Biology, she became research professor in 2006. At FHL she taught the spring Marine Biology (invertebrate zoology) course from 1987 to 2019, became associate director for academics and the environment in 2014, and was interim director from June 2019 and director from April 2020. She was president of the Western Society of Naturalists in 1991 and its Naturalist of the Year in 2011. The census lists 59 FHL-connected papers, 1981–2026.

Her research concerns the community ecology of Pacific Northwest shorelines, first rocky shores and later mud, gravel and salt marsh, and how physical conditions, stress, disturbance and herbivory shape them. Early work covered tidepool algae, algal crusts and the effects of desiccation on seaweeds. She later designed a marine and estuarine habitat classification for Washington, co-wrote the book Monitoring Rocky Shores (2006) and worked with the National Park Service on intertidal monitoring. In Puget Sound and the Salish Sea she has studied how shoreline armoring, and its removal, affect beach biota (2016–2024). Other FHL-connected papers examine the food value of kelp detritus and urchin feces in nearshore food webs (2014–2019), kelp crab feeding (2017), growth and predation of juvenile clams (2019), native and invasive macrophytes as nurseries for juvenile salmon (2020), kelp responses to temperature and nitrogen (2023) and the effects of the 2021 heatwave on intertidal communities (2025).

name: Megumi F. Strathmann
text:
Megumi F. Strathmann is a marine invertebrate embryologist and larval biologist associated with the University of Washington's Friday Harbor Laboratories. Her papers of 1992 and 2007 give FHL as her address, the first jointly with the UW Department of Zoology. She is the author of Reproduction and Development of Marine Invertebrates of the Northern Pacific Coast (University of Washington Press, 1987), a 670-page volume of data and methods for studying eggs, embryos and larvae, prepared with text contributions and advice from colleagues and students of Robert L. Fernald. Many of her papers are co-authored with Richard R. Strathmann. FHL's Richard and Megumi Strathmann Fellowship supports graduate students working on natural and physical science problems in the Pacific Northwest. The census counts 12 FHL-address papers by her, from 1984 to 2020.

Her papers deal mainly with how development responds to conditions and how larval life histories evolve. With co-authors she examined developmental plasticity in sea urchin larvae and its implications for the evolution of nonfeeding larvae (1992), used rates of development and form of sea urchin larvae to test whether larvae in coastal waters are food-limited (1994), and compared food effects on a molluscan veliger (1993) and across echinoderm classes (2020). Other papers concern suspension feeding in the tube worm Spirobranchus giganteus (1984), shells and pelagic development in trochoidean snails (1990), oxygen supply to masses of embryos (1995), nurse eggs, cannibalism and brood reduction in a vermetid gastropod (2005, 2018), a 4.5-year larval period in the snail Fusitriton oregonensis (2007), hatching plasticity in the nudibranch Phestilla sibogae (2010), a new brooding sea star, Henricia pumila (2010), and coelom development in a brittle star (2020).

name: Michael A. Harkey
text:
Michael A. Harkey is a biologist whose publications move from sea urchin developmental biology to transplantation research, all in Seattle. From 1980 to the early 1990s he published with Arthur H. Whiteley of the University of Washington's Department of Zoology on the cells that build the sea urchin larval skeleton; his 1988 and 1992 papers, with H. R. Whiteley as well, list the Department of Microbiology. His 1980 paper lists both the Department of Zoology and Friday Harbor Laboratories, and his census papers span 1980 to 1989. He also collaborated with R. A. Raff's group at Indiana University on skeletal genes (1987–1997). A 1995 paper lists the UW Department of Orthopaedics, and he co-authored collagen studies with D. R. Eyre's group (1997, 2007). From the early 2000s his papers are associated with the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center, which his ORCID record gives as his employer.

Harkey's FHL-connected work focused on primary mesenchyme cells, the descendants of the micromeres that secrete the skeleton of the sea urchin larva. He developed methods to isolate and culture primary mesenchyme cells (1980) and to isolate micromeres in bulk (1985), and used two-dimensional gel electrophoresis to follow cell-specific programs of protein synthesis as these cells differentiate (1982, 1983). Later papers showed that five transcripts accumulate together in primary mesenchyme during skeleton formation (1988) and that embryonic primary mesenchyme genes are also expressed in adult skeletal tissues of several echinoderms (1989). Others examined the skeletal proteins msp130 and PM27 (1992, 1995). At Fred Hutch his publications concern gene transfer into blood-forming stem cells, canine models of marrow and cord blood transplantation, and variation in the canine leukocyte antigen (DLA) genes.

name: Michael G. Hadfield
text:
Michael G. Hadfield is an invertebrate biologist and professor emeritus at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa. He earned BA and MS degrees in zoology at the University of Washington. On a Fulbright fellowship he studied with the larval biologist Gunnar Thorson at the University of Copenhagen's marine laboratory, and he completed a PhD in biological sciences at Stanford University in 1966. After teaching at Pomona College until 1968 he joined the University of Hawaiʻi faculty. There he was among the first faculty of the Kewalo Marine Laboratory, which he directed from 1996 to 2007; he retired in 2013. His FHL connection is through collaboration. The census lists nine papers from 1985 to 2018; three were written with Megumi Strathmann of FHL (two also with Richard Strathmann), and a 2014 paper thanks FHL's Helen R. Whiteley Center as a place to analyse data and write.

Hadfield studies the reproduction and development of marine gastropods and worms, and how their larvae settle and metamorphose. For about thirty years his group has examined the bacterial signals that induce larvae of the polychaete Hydroides elegans to settle. He has also worked on Hawaiian tree snails (Achatinella) and set up a captive breeding programme for them in 1989. His FHL-connected papers centre on larvae. Several concern the coral-eating nudibranch Phestilla sibogae: feeding by its yolk-supplied (lecithotrophic) larvae (1985), its recruitment in the field (2007), nitric-oxide signalling at metamorphosis (2008), and plasticity in hatching (2010). Others treat larval shells and torsion in trochoidean snails (1990, 2001), whether Hydroides larvae must touch a biofilm to settle (2014), and brood reduction in a vermetid snail (2018). In 2014 he was the first recipient of the Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology's M. Patricia Morse Award for Excellence and Innovation in Science Education.

name: Michael J. O’Donnell
text:
Michael J. O'Donnell describes himself in his ORCID record as a biomechanist, with interests in marine ecology, ocean acidification, biomechanics and translational medicine. His 2006 study of wave exposure on rocky shores lists Stanford University's Hopkins Marine Station and the Marine Science Institute of the University of California, Santa Barbara. From 2008 to 2013 he was a postdoctoral researcher with Emily Carrington at the University of Washington and Friday Harbor Laboratories. He was also key senior personnel (co-investigator) on her National Science Foundation project 'Effects of ocean acidification on coastal organisms: an ecomaterials perspective'. A 2019 paper lists him at the Department of Bioengineering, University of California, Berkeley. Carrington's 2020 CV gives him as executive director of the Master of Translational Medicine program of UC Berkeley and UCSF. The census counts nine FHL-address papers from 2008 to 2022.

O'Donnell applies mechanics and physiology to how marine invertebrates fare as seawater warms and acidifies. A 2008 study with Gretchen Hofmann's group found that elevated CO2 alters the response of sea urchin larvae to heat stress, and a 2010 paper described a system for rearing larvae under controlled pCO2. Co-authored FHL studies showed that acidification changes the shape of sand dollar larvae, affecting swimming and feeding (2011), and delays early development of Pacific oyster larvae (2012). As lead author of a 2013 Nature Climate Change paper, he found that bay mussels (Mytilus trossulus) from San Juan Island held at low pH made weaker byssal threads, which most often broke at the adhesive plaque; at pH 7.5 they lost up to 40 percent of their attachment strength. Later papers examined temperature and pCO2 together on mussel attachment (2019), shell repair under acidification (2022) and, by radio tracking, thermoregulation in snails (2017).

name: Michael LaBarbera
text:
Michael LaBarbera is a biologist who works on biomechanics and functional form. A University of Chicago Press author note describes him as professor emeritus in the Department of Organismal Biology and Anatomy at the University of Chicago. OpenAlex links his papers of the mid-1970s to Duke University and his later papers to Chicago from 1979 to 2010; his papers of the mid-1980s give the university's Department of Anatomy. He is not in the report's table of FHL scientists, but a 2004 editorial in Palaios, written with Michał Kowalewski, says he had returned to FHL every two to three years for about 30 years to do research, to teach a course, or both. The census holds seven of his FHL-connected papers, from 1985 to 2008. In the mentoring network he is linked by co-authorship to Kristin Sherrard, whose two 2005 papers with him give FHL as her address.

LaBarbera's census papers all concern mechanics and form in marine animals. With Drew Harvell (1985) he examined flexibility as a way for hydroid colonies to control local water velocities, and a 1985 study with Richard Satterlie and Andrew Spencer, much of it carried out at FHL, described swimming behaviour and morphology in the pteropod Clione limacina. With Elizabeth Boulding (1986) he showed that repeated loading, which causes fatigue damage, lets crabs open larger bivalves, and with Rachel Merz (1992) he measured how gastropod shells lose strength after death, with consequences for hermit crabs, snails and their predators. With Sherrard (2005) he studied how the form of newly settled ascidians affects their performance and how their pumping rates scale with growth. With Adam Tomašových and Sandra Carlson (2008) he related the loss of rotation ability in the brachiopod Terebratalia transversa to allometric growth.

name: Michael T. Brett
text:
Michael T. Brett is a limnologist and professor in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of Washington. He studied fisheries at Humboldt State University (BSc 1983) and zoology at the University of Maine (MSc 1985), and earned a PhD in limnology at Uppsala University in Sweden. He was a research associate at the University of California, Davis, from 1991 to 1997 and joined the UW department as an assistant professor in December 1997; a 2019 department news item names him its associate chair. He is not in the report's table of FHL scientists. His three FHL-connected papers, from 2012 to 2014, came from collaborations with researchers based at the laboratories. In the mentoring network he is linked by co-authorship (2011 to 2014) to Aaron Galloway, an FHL scientist who completed a UW thesis in 2013 under Kenneth Sebens.

Brett's research follows nutrients and food quality through aquatic food webs: eutrophication and the regulation of algal biomass and secondary production in lakes, nutrient bioavailability, the production and bioaccumulation of essential fatty acids such as omega-3s, zooplankton ecology, and links between aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. His FHL-connected papers use fatty acids as dietary markers. A 2012 study led by Galloway, with Kevin Britton-Simmons and David Duggins of FHL and Paul Gabrielson of the University of North Carolina Herbarium, showed that fatty acid profiles separate marine seaweeds and seagrasses at the level of order and family. A 2013 paper led by Sami Taipale profiled 37 strains of freshwater microalgae as fatty acid biomarkers, and a 2014 study with Galloway, Morgan Eisenlord and Megan Dethier at FHL and Gordon Holtgrieve used a Bayesian fatty acid mixing model to estimate what marine isopods eat.

name: Michael T. Nishizaki
text:
Michael T. Nishizaki is a marine physiological ecologist who studies how temperature and water flow affect intertidal invertebrates. His first papers (2005, 2007), on how juvenile red sea urchins associate with adults, are linked in the census to the University of Northern British Columbia, and in 2008 and 2011 he co-authored mathematical models of swarming and helical swimming with Daniel Grünbaum. He received a PhD in biology from the University of Washington in 2013, with a thesis on barnacles in Emily Carrington's group, based on work at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 2010 to 2013. He then worked at Bowdoin College (visiting instructor, 2012–2013), the University of Guelph (postdoctoral researcher, 2013–2015), Williams College (visiting assistant professor of maritime studies, 2015–2017) and Harvard University (teaching fellow, 2018), and became an assistant professor of biology at Carleton College in 2018. His census papers and datasets with an FHL address span 2014 to 2026.

Nishizaki uses the acorn barnacle Balanus glandula and intertidal mussels to study how environmental stressors combine. His thesis and 2014–2015 papers with Carrington measured how water temperature and flow speed alter barnacle feeding, respiration and growth; modelling suggested that respiration is limited by mass transfer in slow, warm water and by uptake kinetics in fast, cold water. The barnacle data, from Cantilever Point at FHL, are archived at BCO-DMO. A 2022 Carleton study, also listing FHL, tested how temperature and pH affect sperm swimming and fertilization in sand dollars and sea urchins. As principal investigator of a collaborative project on mussels and their fluid environment, he recorded temperatures inside a mussel bed at Argyle Creek on San Juan Island from 2019 to 2024 and measured mussel respiration in experiments at FHL from 2020 to 2023. A 2026 paper showed that realistic temperature fluctuations alter mussel respiration and thermal performance.

name: Michael W. Hart
text:
Michael W. Hart is an evolutionary biologist who works on marine invertebrates, chiefly echinoderms. The addresses on his papers trace his career. His first papers, of 1987 and 1988, give the University of Alberta's Department of Zoology with the Bamfield Marine Station, and Dalhousie University. From 1989 to 1996 they give the University of Washington's Department of Zoology and Friday Harbor Laboratories, and the census counts four FHL-connected papers from these years. Papers of 1996 and 1997 give the Institute of Molecular Biology and Biochemistry at Simon Fraser University, and those of 1997 to 1999 the University of California, Davis. From 2000 to 2005 his papers give Dalhousie's Department of Biology, and from 2004 the Department of Biological Sciences at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia, which OpenAlex lists as his most recent institution.

At FHL Hart studied how echinoderm larvae feed and how larval form evolves. A 1989 paper with Lauren Dickie and Richard Helling found that the time Strongylocentrotus sea urchin larvae take to begin feeding is not correlated with egg size. A 1991 paper examined how echinoderm larvae capture particles when suspension feeding, and a 1994 study with Richard R. Strathmann tested the functional consequences of phenotypic plasticity in echinoid larvae. With Richard L. Miller and Laurence P. Madin he described the form and feeding of a living specimen of the hemichordate Planctosphaera pelagica (1994). A 1996 paper treated the facultatively feeding larva of the echinoid Brisaster latifrons as a case of evolutionary loss of larval feeding. His later work turned to molecular evolution: life-history evolution in asterinid sea stars, speciation, and selection on sperm-egg recognition genes in sea stars and in mammals, including humans and other primates.

name: Miles D. Lamare
text:
Miles D. Lamare is a marine biologist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, where his ORCID record lists him as professor and head of the Department of Marine Science. He received a PhD from Otago's Department of Marine Science in 1997 with a thesis on the population biology and recruitment of the sea urchin Evechinus chloroticus. A 1998 paper on its larvae in a New Zealand fiord gives his address as Otago's Portobello Marine Laboratory, with a present address at Friday Harbor Laboratories. His papers published from 1999 to 2004 give FHL as an address. Most report New Zealand studies, written with co-authors including M. F. Barker, Paul E. Brewin, Philip V. Mladenov and Stephen R. Wing; the last, from 2004, concerns sea urchins of the genus Strongylocentrotus. OpenAlex links nearly all of his later work to the University of Otago.

Lamare's research centres on sea urchins and other echinoderms: their reproduction, larval biology and responses to environmental stress. His FHL-connected papers trace the origin and transport of Evechinus chloroticus larvae in a fiord (1998) and estimate their development and mortality in situ (1999). Two 2000 papers compare four years of reproductive variation among habitats and model the urchin's growth. A 2001 paper with Wing measured the calorific content of New Zealand marine macrophytes. A 2004 study with Jennifer R. Hoffman examined natural variation of carotenoids in the eggs and gonads of Strongylocentrotus and their possible role in protection from ultraviolet radiation. That theme continued in his later work on ultraviolet damage to the DNA of Antarctic sea urchin embryos, including the protection given by sea ice, and in studies of the effects of ocean acidification and warming on echinoderm larvae from Antarctica to the tropics.

name: Miles Lamare
text:
Miles D. Lamare is a marine biologist at the University of Otago in New Zealand. Wikidata records his appointment there as associate professor from 2015 and professor from 2020, and his ORCID record lists him as professor and head of the Department of Marine Science. His 1998 paper on sea urchin larvae in a New Zealand fiord gives his address as Otago's Portobello Marine Laboratory, with FHL as his present address. His papers of 1999 to 2001 give FHL as his address, and a 2004 paper with Jennifer Hoffman also carries an FHL address. He is not in the report's table of FHL scientists. Wikidata lists six of his doctoral students who appear in the mentoring network: Anja Studer, Khalid Alqaisi, Kate Sparks, Samuel Karelitz, Danilo Pecorino and Gert-Jan Jeunen.

Lamare studies echinoderms and other marine invertebrates, especially their reproduction, early development and larval ecology, and how these respond to ultraviolet radiation, warming and ocean acidification. His work ranges from New Zealand fiords to Antarctica and the tropics, covers sea urchins, sea stars including the crown-of-thorns, brachiopods and Antarctic fishes, and now uses environmental DNA. Marsden Fund grants on his ORCID record cover sea star pigments, the vulnerability of Antarctic coasts to colonisation, and whole-body regeneration in a chordate. His FHL-connected papers centre on the New Zealand sea urchin Evechinus chloroticus: larval origin and transport in a fiord (1998), larval development and mortality in the field (1999) and four years of reproductive variation across habitats (2000, with Paul Brewin and colleagues). Later papers measured the energy content of New Zealand seaweeds (2001, with Stephen Wing) and carotenoids in Strongylocentrotus eggs and gonads as possible ultraviolet protection (2004, with Hoffman).

name: Monroe H. Martin
text:
Monroe Harnish Martin (1907–2007) was an American mathematician who spent most of his career at the University of Maryland. He graduated from Lebanon Valley College in 1928 and earned a PhD at Johns Hopkins University in 1932 under Aurel Wintner, with a dissertation on infinite orthogonal matrices. After a National Research Council fellowship at Harvard and, from 1933, an instructorship at Trinity College in Hartford, he joined Maryland in 1936, became full professor in 1942, and headed the mathematics department from 1943 to 1954. In 1949 he became the first director of the university's Institute of Fluid Dynamics and Applied Mathematics, and he became emeritus in 1972. He has no FHL papers; he appears in the report as an early link in an academic lineage.

Martin's research centred on fluid dynamics, and he also worked on partial differential equations, including a 1952 study with J. B. Diaz of Riemann's method for equations of hyperbolic, parabolic and elliptic type, and a 1969 paper on inequalities for Hermitian functionals. He held a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1959, when he lectured at the University of St Andrews and the University of Rome, and the University of Maryland later named the Monroe H. Martin Prize after him. The Mathematics Genealogy Project lists three Maryland doctoral students: Simon Levin (1964), Dennis Dunninger (1966) and Jim Cushing (1968). The tie to FHL runs through the ecologist Simon Levin, whose own student Daniel Grünbaum is in the report's table of FHL scientists; both links in this lineage come from Wikidata.

name: Nicholas J. Gidmark
text:
Nicholas J. Gidmark is a comparative biomechanist who studies how fishes capture and process food. He received a B.A. from the University of Minnesota in 2006 and a Ph.D. from Brown University in 2012. He has taught at Knox College in Galesburg, Illinois, since 2016 and is associate professor of biology there. His papers from Brown were co-authored with Elizabeth Brainerd, who appears as his teacher in the report's mentoring network. His FHL connection runs from 2011 to 2020. A 2011 study of sand lances had FHL co-authors, including Adam Summers. He co-authored a series of FHL student research papers in 2014 and 2015, and his papers of 2016 to 2020 give FHL as an address, from 2018 alongside Knox. The census counts three FHL-address papers in that period. No public source found gives a formal FHL title.

Gidmark links the properties of muscles to skeletal mechanics and whole-animal performance. His methods include CT scanning, 3D biomechanical modelling, electromyography, high-speed light and X-ray video, and XROMM (X-ray reconstruction of moving morphology). His Brown-era work examined how sand lances move from water into sand (2011) and how the throat (pharyngeal) jaws of grass carp chew food and those of black carp crush hard prey (2014, 2015). At FHL he turned to local sculpins and Pacific salmon. Student papers he co-authored, with Nina Finley and others, compared jaw muscles, bite and suction forces and jaw leverage in Salish Sea sculpins and in salmon. Published results include a 2016 paper with Daniel Geldof on developmental timing in two Psychrolutes sculpins, a 2018 study of jaw-closing muscles and bones across sculpins and their relatives, and a 2020 paper with Elska Kaczmarek on the bite force–gape relationship in two salmonid fishes.

name: Nicole E. Phillips
text:
Nicole E. Phillips is a marine ecologist in the School of Biological Sciences at Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand. Her work centres on the early life stages of marine invertebrates. Her papers of 1996 and 1997 give the Friday Harbor Laboratories and the University of Washington Department of Zoology as her address. There she co-authored a study of polychaete larvae with Bruno Pernet and studies of molluscan neuropeptides with A. O. Dennis Willows. She completed a Ph.D. in ecology, evolution and marine biology at the University of California, Santa Barbara, in 2002. A paper of that year gives Victoria University's School of Biological Sciences as her new address, and from 2008 her papers also name its Coastal Ecology Laboratory. The census records three FHL-address papers from 1996 and 1997, and a 2009 paper co-authored with Richard Strathmann of FHL.

Her FHL-era papers cover two different subjects. With Pernet she showed that larvae of the scaleworm Arctonoe vittata, which lack the feeding structures most polychaete larvae use, capture particles up to 60 micrometres across (1996). With Willows and colleagues she helped purify and sequence neuropeptides from identified neurons of the sea slug Tritonia (1996), and a 1997 follow-up showed that these peptides speed the beating of the cilia that drive crawling. The 2009 paper with Douglas Bertram and Strathmann found that larger eggs did not speed development of the juvenile rudiment relative to the larval body in Strongylocentrotus sea urchins. Her later work, listed on her ORCID record, follows larvae through settlement into juvenile life: larval nutrition and size at settlement in mussels, maternal provisioning in whelks, ultraviolet and low-tide stress on egg masses, copper effects on sea urchin larvae, and recruitment on New Zealand shores and reefs.

name: Nicole Phillips
text:
Nicole E. Phillips is a marine and freshwater biologist in biological sciences at Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand. She earned a PhD in ecology, evolution and marine biology at the University of California, Santa Barbara, completed in 2002. In the mid-1990s her papers give FHL as her address: her 1996 paper with Bruno Pernet lists her at the laboratories, and the 1996 and 1997 neuropeptide papers with Dennis Willows carry FHL addresses. A later collaboration with Douglas Bertram and Richard Strathmann, published in 2009, was supported by FHL and thanks its staff for facilities. She is not in the report's table of FHL scientists. Wikidata lists three of her doctoral students who appear in the mentoring network: Wan Fatma Zuharah, Sonja Lee Miller and Andrea Glockner Fagetti.

Phillips studies the early life of marine invertebrates: egg size and maternal provisioning, larval nutrition and settlement, juvenile performance, and how stressors such as copper, ultraviolet light and temperature carry over from one life stage to the next. Her early work dealt with intertidal mussels in California; in New Zealand she has studied whelks, limpets, mussel and barnacle recruitment and the sea urchin Evechinus chloroticus, and she has also worked on vermetid gastropods on coral reefs in Moorea, French Polynesia. Her first FHL-connected paper showed that suspension-feeding scaleworm larvae can capture large particles (1996). With Philip Lloyd, Willows and colleagues she helped purify and sequence neuropeptides from identified neurons of the sea slug Tritonia (1996), and with Willows and Galina Pavlova showed that these peptides modulate ciliary beat frequency (1997). The 2009 paper examined how changes in egg volume shift the timing of larval and juvenile development in echinoderm plutei.

name: Osamu Shimomura
text:
Osamu Shimomura (1928–2018) was a Japanese organic chemist who studied bioluminescence. He graduated from the pharmacy course of Nagasaki Medical College in 1951 and received his PhD from Nagoya University in 1960 under Yoshimasa Hirata, working on the luciferin of the sea firefly Cypridina. From 1960 he worked with Frank H. Johnson at Princeton University, returned to Nagoya as an associate professor in 1963, and was a senior research associate at Princeton from 1965 to 1982 and at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole from 1982 to 2001; he was also a visiting professor at Boston University. With Johnson he collected the jellyfish Aequorea victoria over many summers at Friday Harbor Laboratories, where in 1962 they discovered aequorin and green fluorescent protein (GFP). He shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien for the discovery and development of GFP.

The census lists four papers with an FHL address, from 1962 and 1963, written with Johnson and Yo Saiga. They describe the extraction and purification of aequorin from Aequorea, a related photoprotein, halistaurin, from the hydromedusa Halistaura, and the use of aequorin's light emission to measure small amounts of calcium (Science, 1963). Later census papers mention FHL in their text or are listed in its research bibliography: work with Johnson on the chemistry of coelenterate bioluminescence (1975) and on peroxidized coelenterazine as the active group of aequorin (1978), the structure of the GFP chromophore (1979), and a series in the Biochemical Journal (1981 to 1990) on the stability and molecular forms of aequorin, the effect of calcium chelators on its luminescence, and semi-synthetic and recombinant aequorins, made with Yoshito Kishi and colleagues, as improved calcium indicators for cells. He recounted the work in 'A short story of aequorin' (1995).
