name: Pamela Roe
text:
Pamela Roe is an invertebrate zoologist who works on nemerteans (ribbon worms). Her 1970 and 1976 papers on the nemertean Paranemertes peregrina give the Department of Zoology at the University of Washington as her address. The 1976 paper acknowledges support from FHL. From 1981 to at least 2001 her papers give the Department of Biological Sciences at California State College (later California State University), Stanislaus, in Turlock. Papers of 1981 and 1982 written with John and Lois Crowe and Daniel Wickham also list FHL, and the 1982 paper lists the University of California, Davis and the Bodega Marine Laboratory. The census counts three FHL-address papers from 1976 to 1982. A 2020 column, first published in FHL's Tide Bite newsletter, lists a Pamela Roe Graduate Student Endowed Fund among the awards supporting graduate students' summers at FHL.

Roe's research concerns the feeding, life histories and reproduction of nemerteans. Her first papers described the food and feeding behaviour of Paranemertes peregrina (1970) and its life history and predator–prey interactions on Washington mud flats (1976). There it feeds only on polychaete worms and returns to its burrow by following its own mucus trail. She also wrote on territorial behaviour in young nereid polychaetes (1975). With the Crowes and Wickham she showed that juveniles of Carcinonemertes errans, an egg-eating nemertean that lives on crabs, take up dissolved amino acids (1981, 1982). Later papers dealt with transmission between crab hosts, mating and parthenogenesis in Carcinonemertes, and the high-intertidal Pantinonemertes californiensis. With Jon Norenburg she studied pelagic nemerteans off California and Hawaii, and with Norenburg and Svetlana Maslakova she wrote the Nemertea chapter of the Light and Smith Manual (2007).

name: Patrick T. Martone
text:
Patrick T. Martone is a phycologist and professor in the Department of Botany at the University of British Columbia, where his lab studies the biomechanics, evolution and ecophysiology of marine macroalgae. He received a BS from Duke University in 1998 and a PhD from Stanford University in 2007, followed by a year as a postdoctoral scholar at Stanford. He joined UBC as an assistant professor in 2008, became associate professor in 2013 and professor in 2019. He is not in the report's table of FHL scientists; his FHL connection comes through collaborators. Several of his coralline papers note work done while co-author Paul Gabrielson was a visiting professor at FHL, and others came from projects with Emily Carrington and colleagues at the laboratories. In the mentoring network he is linked by co-authorship (2014 to 2018) to Katharine Hind.

Martone's lab asks how intertidal seaweeds withstand wave forces and other stresses, using flumes and breakage tests. It uses DNA barcoding to sort out coralline algal diversity and evolution, including cryptic species, and studies kelp development, the evolution of algal cell walls and seaweed physiology on the British Columbia coast. Most of his FHL-connected papers are coralline systematics with Gabrielson and Hind: two species of Calliarthron (2011), Chiharaea and Yamadaia as reduced, recently derived articulated forms (2012), sequencing of type specimens (2014, 2023), cryptic Bossiella species resolved with historical DNA (2015), the new crustose genus Crusticorallina (2016), and Bossiella as a genus with both jointed and unjointed species (2018). Others treat the hydrodynamic performance of foliose red algae (2011), ocean acidification delaying and weakening spore adhesion (2017), and whether calcification protects corallines from urchin grazing (2021) or lowers their caloric value (2023).

name: Patsy S. Dickinson
text:
Patsy S. Dickinson is a neurobiologist and is Josiah Little Professor of Natural Sciences Emerita and adjunct professor of biology at Bowdoin College. She received a BA from Pomona College and MS and PhD degrees from the University of Washington. From 1979 to 1981 she was a postdoctoral researcher at the Laboratoire de Neurobiologie Comparée (CNRS and Université de Bordeaux I) in Arcachon, France. Her FHL-connected work falls into two periods. Her single-authored papers of 1978 to 1980 list FHL as an address. From 2006 to 2010 she co-authored papers on crustacean neuropeptides, mostly with Andrew E. Christie and Elizabeth A. Stemmler, that are linked to FHL through an author address or the text. The census lists ten FHL-connected papers by her from 1978 to 2014, including a multi-author 2014 BioScience article on synthesis in organismal biology.

Dickinson studies how the nervous system produces flexible patterned movements, such as the change between walking and running. Her Bowdoin laboratory uses two simple neural circuits in the lobster, combining recordings of neuronal activity and heart contractions with immunohistochemistry and molecular methods. Her first FHL paper described the conduction systems that control expansion and contraction in the sea pen Ptilosarcus gurneyi (1978). Papers in 1979 and 1980 examined the neurons that control gill movements in nudibranchs, Pleurobranchaea and several Aplysia species, and proposed that they are homologous across these groups. Her later FHL-connected papers identified crustacean neuropeptides, among them a SIFamide peptide in the stomatogastric nervous system of the American lobster (2006) and a C-type allatostatin-like peptide that acts on both neural circuits and the heart (2009). A 2008 paper found that the pyloric circuit of the herbivorous crab Pugettia producta responds only weakly to several neuromodulators that act strongly in more opportunistic feeders.

name: Paul K. Dayton
text:
Paul K. Dayton is a benthic marine ecologist and emeritus member of the Integrative Oceanography Division at Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego, where he spent a 35-year career. He earned a BS at the University of Arizona in 1963 and a PhD in zoology at the University of Washington (1970, per Wikidata) under Robert T. Paine. His FHL connection rests on subtidal work in the San Juan Islands from his Washington years: a 1982 paper with Charles Birkeland and Norman Engstrom gives FHL as the authors' address, thanks Robert Fernald for facilities there and credits a National Science Foundation grant to the UW Department of Zoology. He is not in the report's table of FHL scientists, but Wikidata lists Terrie Klinger, who is, as his doctoral student. His honours include the Ecological Society of America's Mercer (1974) and Cooper (2000) awards and the first Ramon Margalef Prize in Ecology.

Dayton's research covers benthic ecology, natural history and marine conservation, including coastal Antarctic habitats, Washington's rocky shores, and the effects of overfishing and El Niño on coastal ecosystems; a 1971 paper treated competition and disturbance in a rocky intertidal community. The 1982 FHL paper describes a subtidal food web in the San Juan Islands, where the small sea cucumber Cucumaria lubrica lives at about 4,400 per square metre. Seven sea star species eat it, yet together they take only about 3% of the population each year. The authors argued that the top predator, Solaster dawsoni, probably keeps the sea cucumber's most abundant predator, Solaster stimpsoni, from building up, while refuges in size and behaviour let S. stimpsoni persist. None of the three trophic levels changed significantly from 1965 to 1976. His other census paper (1999) is a multi-author case for networks of no-take marine reserves.

name: Paul M. Anderson
text:
Paul M. Anderson, a biochemist, published from the University of Minnesota Duluth from the 1970s into the 2000s; his 1989 paper gives its Department of Biochemistry and his 1998 paper its Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology in the School of Medicine. He is not in the report's table of FHL scientists. The census holds twelve of his papers from 1985 to 1998. Most are listed in FHL's research bibliographies, including the laboratories' list of publications resulting from research conducted at FHL, and the texts of the 1989 and 1998 papers mention Friday Harbor. Eleven of the twelve concern the spiny dogfish Squalus acanthias. In the mentoring network he is linked by co-authorship (1994 to 1995) to Jin Hong, first author of their papers on dogfish carbamoyl phosphate synthetase III and the multifunctional CAD protein.

Anderson's research concerns enzymes of nitrogen metabolism, above all the carbamoyl phosphate synthetases that begin urea and pyrimidine synthesis, and the urea cycle in fishes. Working largely with dogfish liver mitochondria, he located arginase and other urea-cycle enzymes within mitochondria (1985), tested how urea, trimethylamine oxide and osmolality affect respiration and citrulline synthesis (1986), and traced ketone body and phosphoenolpyruvate formation and purified related enzymes (1990 to 1996). A 1989 study suggested that the first three pyrimidine-pathway enzymes of dogfish spleen are separate polypeptides, unlike the single CAD protein of mammals; in 1995 Hong, Wilmar Salo and Anderson found that dogfish testes express the three as a single CAD-like transcript. With Hong and colleagues he sequenced dogfish carbamoyl phosphate synthetase III, proposing it as an evolutionary intermediate between the glutamine- and ammonia-dependent forms (1994). He also reviewed the fish urea cycle (1995) and studied N-acetylglutamate in Gulf toadfish (1998).

name: Paul R. Benjamin
text:
Paul R. Benjamin is a neuroscientist at the University of Sussex, England, whose research centres on the nervous system of the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis. OpenAlex links his publications to Sussex from 1968 to 2023, and a 2012 review gives his address as the university's School of Life Sciences. He is not in the report's table of FHL scientists, and the sources found here do not record any time at Friday Harbor. His place in the census rests on four papers from 1998 that appear in FHL's own research bibliography; the census did not check their text for an FHL link. In the report's mentoring network he is linked, as doctoral advisor at Sussex, to Kevin Staras, first author of two of those papers. Europe PMC lists 16 papers the two wrote together between 1997 and 2023.

Benjamin uses Lymnaea, whose feeding is controlled by a small network of identifiable neurons, to ask how circuits generate rhythmic behaviour and how they change with learning. His 2012 review argues that feeding arises from a distributed network in which neurons often take on more than one role, among them rhythm generation, the decision to feed, modulation, and hunger and satiety, with about 100 neurons doing work that takes millions in vertebrates. The four 1998 papers share this focus. Two, with Staras and G. Kemenes, showed that feeding motoneurons help maintain and set the phase of the feeding rhythm rather than simply following it, and recorded neural correlates of a conditioned feeding response to lip touch paired with sucrose. The others describe how myomodulin peptides and acetylcholine control foregut contractions, and use mass spectrometry to identify the peptides made in single neurons from alternatively spliced FMRFamide gene transcripts.

name: Pedro Verdugo
text:
Pedro Verdugo is a biophysicist and professor emeritus of bioengineering at the University of Washington. He studied chemistry and medicine at the University of Chile, trained in pediatric cardiology in Santiago, and came to the University of Washington as an NIH Fogarty International senior postdoctoral fellow (1969-1973). He joined UW Bioengineering in 1974, chaired its graduate curriculum committee and, from 1982, as assistant director, led the development of a pilot undergraduate program. He later moved his research to Friday Harbor Laboratories, where he launched a research program in 2001 with a grant from the National Science Foundation; over the following 17 years more than 80 undergraduates worked in his laboratory. His honours include a fellowship of Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge (1988) and a UW award for contributions to undergraduate education (2004). The census counts 26 FHL-address papers from 2003 to 2022.

Verdugo's research applies polymer physics to biological gels. His group found that secreted mucus is stored in vesicles as a condensed polymer network that undergoes a gel phase transition on release, a model since used to study airway disease, and that intracellular calcium is released in periodic pulses; FHL-connected papers on mast-cell granules, airway ciliated cells and mucus continue this line (2003-2012). In 1998, with graduate student Wei-Chun Chin and postdoctoral fellow Monica Orellana, he reported in Nature that dissolved organic matter in seawater can assemble spontaneously into polymer gels, and proposed a role for these microgels in ocean carbon cycling. His FHL papers develop this idea: regulated secretion in the phytoplankter Phaeocystis globosa, effects of ultraviolet light and lower pH on gel formation, bacterial exopolymers that promote assembly, and reviews of marine microgels (2011, 2021). Iván Quesada and Yong-Xue Ding are also among his students in the mentoring network.

name: Peter A. Jumars
text:
Peter A. Jumars is a marine benthic ecologist. He received a BA in biological sciences from the University of Delaware in 1969 and a PhD from Scripps Institution of Oceanography in 1974. OpenAlex links his papers to the University of Washington mainly from the mid-1970s to the late 1990s and to the University of Maine from the late 1990s; papers from 2001 and 2003 give his address as Maine's Darling Marine Center. He is now professor emeritus in Maine's School of Marine Sciences; his teaching of biological fluid dynamics at the Darling Marine Center was the basis of his 2019 book on viscous flow environments. He is not in the report's table of FHL scientists. The census lists 22 FHL-connected papers by him from 1986 to 2003; most appear in FHL's research bibliography, and a few mention FHL in the text or give the FHL address of his co-author Robert Self.

Jumars has studied how animals that live in sediments obtain food, and how water flow and sediment transport shape that supply. His 1979 review with Fauchald of polychaete feeding guilds was updated in 2015. With Deborah Penry, linked to him as a doctoral student in the report's network, he modelled animal guts as chemical reactors (1986, 1987) and related gut architecture to diet in polychaetes (1990). Other FHL-connected papers measured bacterial growth and chemical conditions inside deposit-feeder guts (1989, 1992), the availability of sedimentary amino acids and contaminants to digestion (1995 to 1997), and particle selection by deposit feeders (1988). Flume studies with Arthur Nowell examined suspended sediment, the erosion and deposition of grains, and flow in eelgrass beds (1988 to 1990). Later papers used acoustics, including field manipulations in West Sound, Orcas Island (2001), and a record of mysids rising nightly from the seabed (2003).

name: Peter D. Ward
text:
Peter D. Ward is a paleontologist at the University of Washington in Seattle; his ORCID record lists him as a professor in Biology and Earth and Space Sciences since 1985. He received his PhD from McMaster University in 1976. He has also held teaching posts and other connections with Ohio State University, the University of California, Caltech and the NASA Astrobiology Institute, and is associated with the Sprigg Institute of Geobiology at the University of Adelaide. He was elected a fellow of the California Academy of Sciences in 1984, and his book On Methuselah's Trail (1992) received the Paleontological Society's Golden Trilobite Award. He is not in the report's table of FHL scientists. The census lists four FHL-connected papers by him from 2012 to 2016, and the 2016 paper gives his address as FHL and the university's Biology Department.

Ward's research centres on mass extinctions, especially the Cretaceous-Paleogene and Permian-Triassic events. He wrote In Search of Nautilus (1988) about the living cephalopod and published on Late Permian land vertebrates of South Africa's Karoo Basin (2005). He co-wrote Rare Earth (2000) with Donald Brownlee and proposed the Medea hypothesis, that multicellular life may be self-destructive. His FHL-connected papers are experimental and genetic. A 2012 study led by Loren Ballanti, which thanks FHL staff, compared oxygen consumption in the brachiopod Terebratalia transversa and two bivalves for clues to survival through mass extinctions. Frederick Dooley's 2015 University of Washington doctoral thesis on seagrasses and hydrogen sulfide is recorded in the census with Ward as advisor. Papers led by Dooley in 2012 and 2015 tested how seedlings of the seagrasses Zostera marina and Phyllospadix scouleri tolerate hydrogen sulfide. A 2016 paper revisited the phylogeography of Nautilus pompilius.

name: Petra Ditsche
text:
Petra Ditsche is a biologist trained in Germany who studies how aquatic animals attach to surfaces and cope with water flow. She earned undergraduate degrees in biology and hydrobiology at the University of Düsseldorf and the Technical University of Dresden and a PhD at the University of Bonn on how surface roughness affects attachment in running-water insects. Postdoctoral work followed at Bonn with Wilhelm Barthlott on air-retaining superhydrophobic surfaces and at the University of Kiel with Stanislav Gorb on underwater attachment and biomimetics. She came to Friday Harbor Laboratories in 2012 on a German Academic Exchange Service postdoctoral scholarship and returned a year later to work with Adam Summers on an NSF project on sticky intertidal fishes. Some 2017 papers also list the University of Alaska Anchorage. By 2019 she was based in Germany, where she founded ClingTech Bionics to develop a bionic suction cup.

Ditsche's research asks how organisms hold on in wet, moving environments and how engineers can borrow their solutions. At FHL she worked mainly on the northern clingfish, Gobiesox maeandricus, whose suction disc attaches to rough and fouled surfaces. Papers measured its attachment on fouled and rough substrates (2014) and described its intertidal habitat (2017). A 2019 paper with Summers used the disc as a model for artificial suction cups, the best of which outperformed the fish in pull-off tests on every surface. Related papers examined how biofilm affects attachment of mayfly larvae (2013), compared attachment in water and on land (2014) and tested harbor seal skin and blubber for direction-dependent properties (2017). A 2023 paper showed that the widened legs of stream mayfly larvae work like hydrofoils that hold them on the bottom. She also co-authored 2014 FHL student reports on attachment in chitons, anemones, sculpins and clingfish.

name: Rachel A. Merz
text:
Rachel A. Merz is an invertebrate biomechanist and the Walter Kemp Professor Emerita of Natural Science at Swarthmore College. OpenAlex associates her early papers with the University of Chicago and Northeastern University in the 1980s and her later work with Swarthmore from 1991. She is not in the report's table of FHL scientists, but her FHL-connected work runs from 1984 to 2023. Her 1984 paper on the feeding currents of a sabellid worm thanks FHL's director and staff, and a 2023 paper lists her at FHL. From 2011 to 2014 she co-wrote project reports with undergraduates in FHL's Blinks/BEACON/NSF REU summer internship program; the census includes these reports. One of those interns, Rachel Crane, became her co-author on a 2017 paper funded through FHL's REU program.

Merz's laboratory borrows theory and techniques from engineering to address ecological and evolutionary questions about invertebrates. Much of her work concerns the chaetae (bristles) of polychaete worms. With Sarah Woodin she tested whether hooked chaetae anchor tube-dwelling worms (1987, 2000) and reviewed the mechanical functions of chaetae (2003). With Deirdre Edwards she examined the role of jointed chaetae in locomotion and gait changes (1998). She has also studied how flow shapes feeding posture and predator avoidance in black fly larvae, and the strength of empty snail shells used by hermit crabs (1992). Later FHL-connected papers showed that overturned sand dollars orient in flow to help them right themselves (2013) and examined how tube textures give polychaetes traction (2015). Others related sediment mechanics to lugworm burrowing and distribution (2017), work that began as a 2012 intern project in False Bay, and to eelgrass seed burial (2023).

name: Rebecca L. Maher
text:
Rebecca L. Maher is a microbiologist who studies microbial communities associated with hosts and habitats, including the eelgrass microbiome and its role in disease. Her ORCID record lists her as a graduate fellow in microbiology at Oregon State University from 2016 and as a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Oregon's Institute of Ecology and Evolution. She then held FHL's William Calvin Postdoctoral Fellowship, which is credited in her 2025 and 2026 eelgrass papers. FHL is also her address on 2024 training materials and presentations for the National Microbiome Data Collaborative's ambassador program, and on her other papers from 2025 and 2026. The census lists eleven FHL-connected items by her from 2024 to 2026, including datasets and preprints.

At FHL she studied eelgrass (Zostera marina) and wasting disease, which is caused by Labyrinthula zosterae. Her 2025 paper with C. Drew Harvell and others infected eelgrass in the laboratory with two local pathogen strains at ambient and raised temperatures. It also sampled blades at Fourth of July Beach on San Juan Island around unusually hot low tides in May 2024. Heat increased disease severity and lowered microbiome diversity in the laboratory, and in the field the heat event damaged blades, slowed growth and reduced microbiome diversity. A 2025 Biology Letters paper links wasting disease to community interactions, and a 2026 paper examines the distribution of L. zosterae and the emergence of a new seagrass pathogen. Her other recent work covers the genomics of predatory Pseudobdellovibrionaceae bacteria (2025 preprint), microeukaryotes in the coral Acropora hyacinthus during an extreme bleaching event (2025), and microbial patchiness in stream beds at a subcontinental scale (2025–2026).

name: Richard A. Cloney
text:
Richard A. Cloney, of the Department of Zoology at the University of Washington, used electron microscopy to study the fine structure of marine invertebrate cells, tissues and larvae. His papers run from 1961 to 1996. The census lists ten of them, from 1973 to 1996. Those with an FHL address include a 1973 study of ascidian metamorphosis and five papers from 1981 to 1983, and a 1983 paper gives both the UW Department of Zoology and Friday Harbor Laboratories as addresses. Two of his co-authors appear as his students in the report's mentoring network. Stephen A. Stricker was his co-author on nemertean worms from 1981 to 1985, and Christopher G. Reed on brachiopod tentacles (1977) and bryozoan larvae (1982). Other frequent co-authors included Michael J. Cavey, on ascidian muscle and the larval tunic.

Cloney's main subject was the metamorphosis of ascidian (sea squirt) tadpole larvae. Papers from 1961 into the early 1970s examined tail resorption and the role of cytoplasmic filaments in the epidermis and notochord, and a 1973 study tested the effect of cytochalasin B on tail resorption and metamorphosis in ten ascidian species. Later papers covered larval adhesive papillae, sensory neurons, sperm and the larval tunic, the effect of tunichrome on tunic and fin formation in Ascidia callosa embryos (1986), and the role of test cells in keeping larvae from becoming hydrophobic (1996). He also studied cephalopod chromatophores and reflector cells, polychaete setae and chiton sensory hairs. His FHL-address papers from 1981 to 1983 describe the nemertean Paranemertes peregrina, its stylet apparatus and role in prey capture (1981), stylet formation (1982) and venom-producing cells (1983), and the larval structure, settlement and metamorphosis of the bryozoan Bowerbankia gracilis (1982).

name: Richard A. Satterlie
text:
Richard A. Satterlie is an invertebrate neurobiologist who studies the neural and muscular control of swimming in marine animals. His papers from 1993 to 1997 give his address as the Department of Zoology at Arizona State University, and those from 2000 to 2004 as the university's Department of Biology; from 2005 they give the Department of Biology and Marine Biology and the Center for Marine Science at the University of North Carolina Wilmington. His FHL connection came through summer fieldwork on the pteropod mollusc Clione limacina: an ASU outreach article notes that he went to Washington State every summer to collect the animals, and papers with Tigran P. Norekian in 1993 and 1994 carry a Friday Harbor Laboratories address. The census credits him with 17 FHL-connected papers between 1985 and 2010, and the report's mentoring network links him to Norekian and Thomas J. Pirtle, frequent co-authors on the Clione work.

Satterlie's work asks how simple nervous systems generate and adjust rhythmic locomotion. In Clione, which swims by beating a pair of wings, he described swimming behavior and wing musculature (1985, 1989-1991), showed that reciprocal inhibition and postinhibitory rebound produce reverberation in the swim pattern generator (Science, 1985), and found two types of striated muscle that suggest two-geared swimming (1990). Later papers analyzed fast-strike prey capture, in which buccal cones are inflated hydraulically by co-activated antagonistic motoneurons (1992-1995), serotonergic and nitric oxide modulation of swim speed (1996-2001, 2020), startle and escape swimming (1997), and a hyperpolarization-activated current that alters swim frequency (2010). A second line of work examines how jellyfish nerve nets and pacemakers control swimming, from the hydromedusa Aequorea (1985, 2008) to box jellyfish (2001) and scyphomedusae (2014-2015).

name: Richard B. Emlet
text:
Richard B. Emlet is a marine invertebrate biologist and professor emeritus of biology at the University of Oregon, based at the Oregon Institute of Marine Biology (OIMB) in Charleston, Oregon. He received a BS in zoology from Duke University in 1977 and a PhD in zoology from the University of Washington in 1985. His FHL-connected papers from 1982 to 1986 give the UW Department of Zoology and Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address, and they include a 1985 Science paper with Richard Strathmann. He later joined the University of Oregon faculty at OIMB, where his research group studied marine invertebrate larvae and how larval history affects juveniles. From 2022 to 2025 he was a research associate of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute. FHL is also named in the text of several of his later papers, up to 2025.

Emlet studies the functional morphology, biomechanics, ecology and evolution of marine invertebrates, especially echinoderm larvae. His methods include video micrography, motion analysis, dynamically scaled mechanical models, and laboratory and field experiments. His early FHL-connected papers examined the mechanics of calcite in sea urchin larval spicules (1982) and showed that crystal axes in living and fossil adult sea urchins indicate whether their larvae fed (1985). Others analysed how gravity and drag shape the feeding currents of small zooplankton (1985) and followed larvae of the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus in a fjord, including their vertical migrations (1986). Later papers in the census cover swimming in nonfeeding echinoderm larvae (1994), offspring size in a marine snail (2001, with Amy Moran), barnacle survival after settlement along an estuarine gradient (2006) and chiton eggs and larvae (2015). With Nicole Nakata he described brittle star larvae of the northeast Pacific (2023, 2025).

name: Richard E. Norris
text:
Richard Earl Norris (1926–2013) was a phycologist who studied marine algae, especially small flagellates, in the Pacific Northwest and South Africa. The Harvard University Herbaria's Index of Botanists associates him with the University of Washington, the University of Natal and the University of Hawaii. It records him as a collector of algae mainly in the Puget Sound area from 1948 to 1955 and in Minnesota from 1956, with specimens in herbaria including FHL's. His census papers with an FHL address date from 1977 to 1984. The 1977 to 1979 papers give Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address, and the 1978 paper also lists the Department of Botany of the University of Natal in Pietermaritzburg, South Africa. A biography with a photograph appeared in Phycologia in 2001.

Norris's FHL-connected papers use electron microscopy to work out the structure, life histories and classification of small marine algae. A 1977 paper described flagellate cells in the life history of the chrysophyte Stichogloea. With Richard N. Pienaar of the University of Natal he compared the fine structure of five marine species of the green flagellate Pyramimonas (1978) and described scale production in the flagellate Chrysochromulina spinifera (1979). An earlier study with Barbara R. Pearson (1975) followed cell division in Pyramimonas parkeae, a species named by the two of them. With Terumitsu Hori and Mitsuo Chihara he revised the prasinophyte genus Tetraselmis (1980). With David J. Hibberd he described the cytology and ultrastructure of the amoeboid alga Chlorarachnion reptans and placed it in a new division and class, the Chlorarachniophyta and Chlorarachniophyceae (1984). Names he authored include Gelidiocolax lyndae.

name: Richard Lloyd Miller
text:
Richard L. Miller worked on sperm chemotaxis, the guidance of swimming sperm by substances released from eggs; his 1983 paper gives his address as the Department of Biology at Temple University in Philadelphia. His earlier papers dealt with chemotaxis during fertilization in the hydroids Campanularia (1966) and Gonothyrea (1970), and a 1975 paper in Nature reported sperm chemotaxis in the ascidian Ciona intestinalis. A 2012 review of the field in the Journal of General Physiology states that his experiments of the late 1960s and 1970s firmly established chemotaxis in animal sperm. His papers connected with Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) run from 1979 to 1994. Most give FHL as an address, and the 1983 paper, written with Kenneth King of the University of Washington's Department of Oceanography and FHL, thanks the FHL staff for their hospitality during the authors' residence.

Miller's FHL papers extend sperm chemotaxis studies across the local fauna. Two 1979 papers on hydromedusae covered the species-specificity of sperm attraction, sperm behaviour and the attractants' chemical properties. Hybridization tests with the medusa Sarsia (1982) revealed at least three species within the 'Sarsia tubulosa complex' at Friday Harbor, and work with Gary Freeman showed that hydrozoan eggs can be fertilized only at the site of polar body formation. With King he showed chemotaxis in the larvacean Oikopleura dioica, collected at the FHL dock (1983). Later papers showed sperm chemotaxis in sea stars, sea cucumbers and brittle stars (1985), detected sperm attractant in the FHL seawater system in the spring and summer of 1986 (1989), and partially purified the attractant of the sunflower star Pycnopodia helianthoides (1992). He also co-authored papers on a ctenophore eating a medusa (1984, with Claudia Mills) and on a living Planctosphaera pelagica, a hemichordate (1994).

name: Richard R. Strathmann
text:
Richard R. Strathmann is a marine invertebrate biologist and professor emeritus in the University of Washington Department of Biology, based at Friday Harbor Laboratories. He earned a BA in zoology and chemistry at Pomona College (1963), then an MS in oceanography (1966) and a PhD in zoology (1970) at the University of Washington, advised by K. Banse and A. J. Kohn. After postdoctoral work at UCLA and the Hawaii Institute of Marine Biology and two years as an assistant professor at the University of Maryland, he joined the UW Zoology Department in 1973 and was professor from 1982 to 2008. From 1973 to 2008 he was also Resident Associate Director of FHL, facilitating research and instruction by visitors from many institutions. He was a Guggenheim Fellow in 1980–81 and received the Western Society of Naturalists' Lifetime Achievement Award in 2012. The census lists 86 FHL-connected papers by him, 1975–2025.

His research asks why patterns of development evolved as they did, by working out the functional demands and limits on marine embryos, larvae and juveniles. He has studied how larvae capture food with cilia, trade-offs between feeding and swimming, plasticity of larval feeding structures, how long embryos and larvae spend in the plankton and the risks they face there, and limits on brooding and on benthic egg masses. His subjects include echinoderm and bryozoan larvae, gastropod veligers, and annelid, brachiopod and ascidian larvae. FHL-connected papers report a 4.5-year larval period in the snail Fusitriton oregonensis (2007), predator-induced cloning in echinoderm larvae (2008), a new brooding sea star, Henricia pumila (2010), kelp detritus as food for urchin larvae (2017) and hazards to drifting periwinkle embryos (2022). He has also written reviews on multicellularity, dispersal and the origin of feeding larvae. His PhD students include Richard Emlet, Larry McEdward and Michael Hart.

name: Robert A. Andersen
text:
Robert A. Andersen is a phycologist who works on the systematics and culture of algae. He holds a BS in botany from North Dakota State University, an MA in aquatic biology from St. Cloud State College and a PhD in botany and phycology from the University of Arkansas. He directed the Provasoli-Guillard National Center for Culture of Marine Phytoplankton (CCMP) at Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences until he retired from the post in 2009, and is emeritus director of the center, now the National Center for Marine Algae and Microbiota. He edited Algal Culturing Techniques (Elsevier, 2005), sponsored by the Phycological Society of America. He is listed as a senior research scientist at the University of Washington and an adjunct professor at Michigan Technological University, and Wikispecies gives Friday Harbor Laboratories as his affiliation. The census lists 43 FHL-connected papers, 2011–2026.

His listed research interests are chrysophyte algae, algal systematics and algal culturing, and in 1987 he named the class Synurophyceae. His FHL-connected papers combine cultures, microscopy and multigene or plastid-genome data to describe new taxa and revise old ones, mostly among heterokont algae (chrysophytes, pelagophytes, xanthophytes and related classes) and haptophytes. Examples include a re-examination of the haptophyte Chrysotila from its type locality (2014–15), new pelagophytes from the Bahamas (2014) and the Great Barrier Reef (2025), a new class, Phaeosacciophyceae (2020–21), the perforated theca that defines the Pelagophyceae (2022) and a revised classification of the Cyanidiophyceae (2023). He also co-authored work on alkenone-producing haptophytes used in paleoclimate reconstruction (2015, 2019), a study placing the origin of brown algae in the Ordovician (2024), and reports of the Nomenclature Committee for Algae (2018–2023).

name: Robert C. Terwilliger
text:
Robert C. Terwilliger is a comparative biochemist whose papers, from 1964 to 1988, concern the oxygen-binding proteins of marine invertebrates and fishes. His papers of 1966 to 1972 give Boston University as his address, several also the New England Aquarium. Three 1970 papers written with Kenneth R. H. Read of Boston University list FHL and deal with sea cucumbers, chitons and marine snails. From the early 1970s through 1988 his papers give the University of Oregon's Department of Biology and its Oregon Institute of Marine Biology at Charleston. The census records these three FHL-address papers, all from 1970. It also includes papers of 1987 and 1988 on chiton and bivalve respiratory proteins that are listed in the FHL bibliography. In 1988 he also wrote on teaching and research at marine stations. No biography was found, so his career is traced here from the addresses on his papers.

Terwilliger described the structure and oxygen binding of hemoglobins, myoglobins, chlorocruorins and hemocyanins across many animal groups. His earliest papers concern fiddler crab responses to ionizing radiation (1964) and, with Frank Belamarich, neurosecretory substances and a heart-stimulating peptide in crabs (1966, 1970). His 1970 FHL papers characterized the hemoglobins of the sea cucumbers Cucumaria miniata, C. piperata and Molpadia intermedia, and the radular muscle myoglobins of chitons such as Katharina tunicata and of gastropods including a limpet, an abalone and Tegula. At Oregon he and co-authors, often Nora B. Terwilliger, studied giant extracellular hemoglobins of polychaetes and clams, hemoglobins of hydrothermal-vent animals and vestimentiferan tubeworms, changes in crab hemocyanin during development, and maternal–fetal oxygen transfer in the viviparous seaperch Embiotoca lateralis. The FHL-listed papers of 1987–1988 cover Katharina hemocyanin, bivalve hemocyanins and tissue hemoglobins in a lepidopleurid chiton.

name: Robert G. Chuinard
text:
Robert G. Chuinard appears in the census as a co-author, with Sefton R. Wellings, of three papers on skin tumours in flatfishes published in 1964 and 1965. The papers give a joint address: the Department of Pathology, University of Oregon Medical School, Portland, and Friday Harbor Laboratories. No source was found that describes his training, his career or his role at FHL. The bibliographic database behind the census links the same name to later papers on orthopaedic surgery, with addresses at the University of California, Davis (1976) and Louisiana State University, including its Health Sciences Center in New Orleans (from 1977). The census's Louisiana State University destination comes from these records, but it has not been confirmed that they are by the same person.

Their FHL-connected papers, from 1964 and 1965, concern epidermal papillomas in the flathead sole, Hippoglossoides elassodon, from waters around the San Juan Islands. A 1964 paper in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute, with R. T. Gourley and R. A. Cooper, reported tumours in 281 of 4,364 flathead sole collected between July 1963 and July 1964. The growths began in first-year fish as small nodules, some of which later became papillomas, and similar neoplasms appeared occasionally in other pleuronectid flatfishes. A 1964 report in Science described virus-like particles, and granular bodies that may also be viral, in the tumour cells but not in normal epidermis. A 1965 paper with M. Bens in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences compared skin neoplasms in four pleuronectid species.

name: Robert W. Meech
text:
Robert W. Meech is a neurophysiologist at the University of Bristol, England. His ORCID record lists him as a senior research fellow in the School of Physiology, Pharmacology and Neuroscience from 1982, and the university now lists him as an honorary research fellow in the School of Psychology and Neuroscience. He holds BSc, PhD and DSc degrees from the University of Southampton, and OpenAlex links earlier papers to Scripps Institution of Oceanography (1969), Caltech (1972) and Cambridge (1974 to 1980). He is not in the report's table of FHL scientists. However, his 2015 review states that his work on cnidarians was done at FHL, and his 2022 review that much of his work on the jellyfish Aglantha digitale was done there. The census lists 11 of his papers from 2001 to 2026.

Meech studies the ion channels that underlie electrical impulses, using patch- and voltage-clamp methods on potassium, sodium and calcium channels. He has also studied calcium signals at mouse inner hair cell synapses (2002). His FHL work centres on swimming in jellyfish and siphonophores, some collected at the laboratory dock. In Aglantha, two swimming modes arise from two separate impulses, a fast sodium-dependent action potential and a low-amplitude calcium spike. Meech reviewed its impulse conduction (2004). With Leonid Moroz, George Mackie and others he studied how nitric oxide regulates its swimming (2004), and with Mackie he described nerves in the endodermal canals of hydromedusae that inhibit swimming (2008). A 2021 paper with FHL's Claudia Mills examined bell kinematics and giant axons in trachymedusae. Papers with Tigran Norekian described nervous systems of the siphonophores Nanomia bijuga (2020) and N. septata (2026), and the 2015 and 2022 reviews traced the evolution of excitability and giant axons.

name: Robin B. Kodner
text:
Robin B. Kodner is a biologist whose work spans algal evolution, microbial ecology and geobiology. Her first papers (2000–2002) give the Department of Botany at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and concern fossil fungi and early land plants. From 2004 to 2008 her papers give Harvard University's Department of Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, where she published with Andrew Knoll and Roger Summons. Her papers of 2009 and 2010 give FHL, and those of 2009 to 2013 the University of Washington School of Oceanography, where she published with E. Virginia Armbrust. A 2011 news report gave her affiliations as FHL and the Beam Reach Marine Science and Sustainability School. Her ORCID record lists her as professor in the Department of Environmental Science at Western Washington University from 2012. It also lists a visiting researcher post at the Laboratoire d'Écologie Alpine, Université Grenoble Alpes, for 2026–2028.

Kodner studies how algae and other single-celled eukaryotes evolved and how their communities respond to the environment. With Knoll and Summons she traced sterols (2008) and the resistant biopolymer algaenan (2009) across algal lineages, to help interpret molecular fossils in ancient rocks. Her other FHL-connected work includes a 2009 PNAS paper with Phoebe Cohen and Knoll interpreting large spiny Ediacaran microfossils as resting stages of early animals, and pplacer (2010), software developed with Frederick Matsen and Armbrust that places DNA sequences on a fixed reference tree. A 2011 FHL student report she co-authored dealt with growth and domoic acid (toxin) production by the diatom Pseudo-nitzschia, and in 2011 she presented work on toxin-producing Pseudo-nitzschia blooms in East Sound, Washington. At Western Washington University she studies snow algae in the Cascade Mountains, including through the Living Snow Project, a citizen-science program, and has worked on plankton in Bellingham Bay.

name: Robin J. Fales
text:
Robin J. Fales is a marine ecologist who studies how kelps and other intertidal organisms respond to climate change. Fales earned a B.S. at the University of California, Irvine (2016) and an M.S. in biology at California State Polytechnic University, Pomona (2019), while working as a technician for the Multi-Agency Rocky Intertidal Network (MARINe). Fales then completed a Ph.D. in the University of Washington Department of Biology (2019–2023), with Emily Carrington as committee chair, and held a position in UC Irvine's Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology in 2023–2024. Since 2024 Fales has been Assistant Professor of Marine Ecology in Environmental Studies at Soka University of America. Fales's FHL-connected papers date from 2021 to 2026. Several list FHL as an affiliation, the doctoral experiments used FHL facilities, and the dissertation thanks reading-committee member Megan Dethier for supporting the work at FHL.

Fales's dissertation asked how warming and nutrient supply affect kelp physiology across habitats, species and populations in the Salish Sea, measuring growth, bleaching, photosynthesis, respiration and nutrient uptake. It used the 2021 Western North American heatwave to study how Hedophyllum sessile survives through self-shading and protection of its meristem, and found that eight bull kelp (Nereocystis luetkeana) populations shared a critical thermal maximum of 22 °C. A 2023 paper with Brooke Weigel, Carrington, Helen Berry and Dethier, run in FHL's Ocean Acidification Environmental Laboratory, crossed three temperatures with two nitrogen levels in bull kelp and Saccharina latissima: high temperature, not low nitrogen, was the main stressor. Other FHL-connected work covers warming and the bull kelp microbiome (2025), size-dependent mussel survival on the high and low shore at Cattle Point after the 2021 heat dome (a 2026 data set), and a 2021 analysis of microplastic research and national plastic policies.

name: Roger D. Longley
text:
Roger D. Longley is a neurobiologist who has studied the nervous systems of gastropod molluscs at Friday Harbor over several decades. A 2020 island newspaper item calls him a marine neurobiologist and a long-time researcher at FHL. In a 1984 paper in the Journal of Experimental Biology his address was the Pacific Sciences Institute in Friday Harbor, and he thanked the director of FHL for the use of its facilities. His papers from 2008 to 2014 give FHL as his address, and most are single-authored. No faculty page or CV was found, so this profile rests on his published record. The census matches six papers from 1997 to 2014 to his full name, and lists earlier work under 'R. D. Longley', from 1981 to 1993, that has an FHL address or appears in FHL's research bibliography.

His research asks how gastropod nervous systems are organized and how they control behaviour. The earlier census items describe mating behaviour in the nudibranch Aeolidia papillosa (1981, 1984, 1993), agonistic or mating behaviour in Hermissenda (1982) and variation in a ganglion of the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea (1991). The 1984 paper related axon surface infolding to axon size in Tritonia and other gastropods. His later FHL papers focus on the ciliated sole of the foot. He traced the development of a serotonin-like immunoreactive nerve plexus in the foot of the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis appressa (2008), compared the neural control of pedal cilia in Lymnaea and Helisoma trivolvis (2010, 2012), and mapped immunoreactive axons in the sole of the land pulmonates Limax, Arion and Helix (2014). A 2011 paper measured neurogenesis in the procerebrum of the snail Helix aspersa. A 1997 co-authored paper on numerical least-squares methods also gives an FHL address.

name: Roger deRoos
text:
Roger McLean deRoos (1930–2015) was a comparative endocrinologist at the University of Missouri. He earned a bachelor's degree in wildlife conservation at the University of California, Berkeley, a master's degree in wildlife management at Utah State University and a doctorate in zoology at Berkeley, where he studied under the endocrinologist Howard Bern. He joined the Missouri faculty in 1961, taught undergraduate biology and graduate courses in anatomy, histology and endocrinology, and received the Purple Chalk award, given by students for teaching. After retiring in 1992 he taught biology at Skagit Valley Community College. His obituary records that he spent most summers at Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL), studying glucose regulation in the spiny dogfish with his research partner and co-author Carolyn C. deRoos; their papers with an FHL address appeared from 1967 to 1992.

The deRooses' FHL work asked how the pituitary–adrenal axis and other hormones regulate blood sugar in sharks and their relatives, using the spiny dogfish, Squalus acanthias, as the experimental animal. A 1967 paper reported corticotropin (ACTH) activity in the pituitary glands of chondrichthyan fishes. Later papers, all in General and Comparative Endocrinology, reported that mammalian ACTH (1973) and catecholamines (1978) raise plasma glucose in dogfish, described severe hypoglycaemia induced by insulin (1979), and found that plasma glucose rises after partial removal of the pituitary and also after sham surgery (1980). Papers in 1985, with Carole and Harold Werner, and in 1992 measured glucose, alanine, lactate, β-hydroxybutyrate and other potential fuels and gluconeogenic substrates in the plasma of unfed dogfish after surgery, insulin infusion or ACTH treatment.

name: Rudolf A. Raff
text:
Rudolf A. Raff (1941-2019) was an evolutionary developmental biologist at Indiana University. He received a BS from Pennsylvania State University and a PhD in biochemistry from Duke University (1967). He then held postdoctoral posts at the National Naval Medical Center and, from 1969, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He joined Indiana's Department of Biology as an assistant professor in 1971 and was named James H. Rudy Professor in 2000 and Distinguished Professor in 2002. He directed the Indiana Molecular Biology Institute and retired in 2018. He founded and edited the journal Evolution & Development. His honours include a Guggenheim Fellowship (1987), the A. O. Kovalevsky Medal (2001), the Sewall Wright Award (2004) and election to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2000). He is not in the report's table of FHL scientists; his five census papers, from 1991 to 2013, connect to FHL mainly through co-authors.

Raff studied how changes in development produce evolutionary change, working mainly with sea urchins. A 2017 tribute from his department credits him with arguing early that changes in form require changes in developmental processes, using DNA sequence data to show that genes and developmental pathways are conserved across distantly related animals, and showing that embryos evolve as readily as adults. His books include Embryos, Genes, and Evolution (1983, with Thomas Kaufman), The Shape of Life (1996) and Once We All Had Gills (2012). Two 1991 papers with Gregory Wray, then at FHL, described the wrinkled blastula of the sea urchin Heliocidaris erythrogramma and reviewed the evolution of developmental strategy in marine invertebrates. Later papers with Kirk Zigler, whose NSF postdoctoral fellowship (2002 to 2005) Raff co-hosted and who also held FHL fellowships, examined egg energetics and fertilization in echinoids with facultatively feeding larvae (2008) and germ-layer allocation in Clypeaster rosaceus (2013).

name: Russell C. Wyeth
text:
Russell C. Wyeth is a neuroethologist and professor in the Department of Biology at St. Francis Xavier University (StFX) in Antigonish, Nova Scotia. His earliest papers, on feeding in the glass sponge Rhabdocalyptus dawsoni (1996, 1999), began at the University of Victoria. From 1999 to 2006 his papers give the University of Washington as his address. By 2008 he was in the Department of Physiology and Biophysics at Dalhousie University, and his StFX papers begin in 2010. His six FHL-connected papers, from 2002 to 2008, were all co-authored with A. O. Dennis Willows, starting with a 2002 paper on micro-fabricated probes for recording inside neurons. A 2006 press release described Wyeth and Willows as biologists at the University of Washington's Friday Harbor Laboratories. In 2026 he received a five-year NSERC Discovery Grant for research on chemical and flow-based navigation in aquatic gastropods.

Wyeth studies how gastropod molluscs use sensory cues, especially odours and water flow, to find their way. His FHL-connected work centred on the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea, a sea slug much used in studies of how nervous systems control behaviour. With Willows he used SCUBA and time-lapse video to record its behaviour in the field near Vargas Island, British Columbia, and in southern Puget Sound (2006). The slugs crawled upstream to feed and mate, and swam up into currents to escape predators. Related 2006 papers adapted underwater video to measure currents near the seabed, analysed orientation to flow, prey, other slugs and predators, and showed that odours sensed by the rhinophores guide orientation to flow. A 2008 paper identified 1-phenoxy-2-propanol as a useful anaesthetic for gastropod neurophysiology. His later work includes navigation in the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis and the use of ultraviolet-C light against marine biofouling.

name: Ryan S. Littlefield
text:
Ryan S. Littlefield is a cell biologist who studies the structure of muscle and has been an assistant professor of biology at the University of South Alabama since 2013. He received a BA in biophysics from Johns Hopkins University in 1994 and a PhD in cell biology from The Scripps Research Institute in La Jolla, California, in 2001. His papers from 2006 to 2010 give the University of Washington's Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address. He was corresponding author of a 2009 paper written there. His co-authors in this period included Velia Fowler, Richard Lieber and Ju Chen. The census does not record a teaching role or other formal position at FHL.

Littlefield's research asks how the lengths of the actin thin filaments in the sarcomeres of striated muscle are set and maintained. His FHL-connected papers centre on nebulin, a protein proposed to act as a ruler for thin filament length. A 2006 study of nebulin-deficient mice found shorter thin filaments and reduced contractile function in skeletal muscle. A 2008 review with Fowler argued that dynamics at the filaments' pointed ends go beyond a simple nebulin ruler, and the 2009 Biophysical Journal paper reported that a nebulin ruler does not dictate thin filament lengths. Related papers examined nebulin's role in actin-myosin interactions (2009), tropomodulin isoforms that cap filament ends (2010) and the length-tension relationship of the external anal sphincter muscle (2008). A 2024 preprint on his record concerns actin assembly by FHOD-1 and profilin in the sarcomeres of the nematode C. elegans.

name: SEFTON R. WELLINGS
text:
The research of the pathologist Sefton R. Wellings joined the study of the mammary gland in mice and humans with the study of tumours and disease in fishes. The addresses on his papers of the late 1950s and early 1960s are the Department of Pathology of the University of California School of Medicine in San Francisco and the Department of Zoology and its Cancer Research Genetics Laboratory at the University of California, Berkeley. From 1962 to 1969 they give the Department of Pathology of the University of Oregon Medical School in Portland, and from 1969 into the late 1980s the Department of Pathology of the University of California, Davis, School of Medicine. His four FHL-connected papers, from 1964 to 1969, give the Oregon department together with Friday Harbor Laboratories; the 1969 paper also lists UC Davis.

At Friday Harbor, Wellings and his co-workers, chiefly Robert G. Chuinard, studied epidermal papillomas of the flathead sole, Hippoglossoides elassodon. They reported virus-like particles in the tumours (1964), described similar growths in other flatfishes of the family Pleuronectidae (1964) and compared skin neoplasms in four pleuronectid species (1965). A 1969 paper with G. A. Brown described the larval skin of the flathead sole. Later papers treat skin tumours of English sole and starry flounder from Puget Sound (1968), flathead sole tumours in East Sound, Orcas Island (1971), fish diseases in the Bering Sea (1977) and liver tumours in fish from an urban estuary (1977-78). His earlier electron-microscope studies dealt with milk secretion in the mouse mammary gland and with human melanoma. At Davis he studied the human breast, including a 1975 atlas of its subgross pathology and a 1980 hypothesis tracing breast cancer to the terminal ductal lobular unit.

name: Sandy Wyllie‐Echeverria
text:
Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria is a seagrass biologist whose work centres on eelgrass (Zostera marina) in the northeast Pacific. A 1994 Alaska Sea Grant report on research needs for managing seagrass systems in western North America, begun while Wyllie-Echeverria was a graduate student at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, lists the author as a visiting scholar in the University of Washington School of Marine Affairs and a member of its Interdisciplinary Seagrass Working Group. Later School of Marine Affairs pages and a newspaper notice give the titles seagrass research coordinator and research scientist there. A 2022 Seacology article says Wyllie-Echeverria has worked at Friday Harbor Laboratories since the early 2000s, with students in the laboratories' Seagrass Lab. The census counts 28 FHL-address papers from 2007 to 2023, and the mentoring network lists Brian S. Ort and Ryley S. Crow as students.

Wyllie-Echeverria's research covers seagrass population biology, genetics, disease and restoration. FHL-connected papers compare native eelgrass with the introduced Zostera japonica, including desiccation tolerance and vertical zonation (2007), the role of climate in the distribution of Z. japonica in North America (2008) and how small-scale topography lets the two coexist (2014). Others treat the genetic structure of eelgrass beds in the San Juan Archipelago, San Francisco Bay and Alaska; seed size, long-term seed storage and seedling tolerance of hydrogen sulfide; water flow through eelgrass canopies; and eelgrass wasting disease, including its relation to host demography and whether migratory waterfowl carry seagrass pathogens (2020). A 2015 disturbance experiment modelled on traditional Indigenous harvesting of eelgrass, and the reseeding of Westcott Bay since 2020 with Seacology and the San Juan Islands Conservation District, connect the research to restoration.

name: Sara M. Rolfe
text:
Sara M. Rolfe is an engineer who develops software for analysing three-dimensional biological shape. She studied electrical engineering at Seattle Pacific University (BS, 2005) and electrical and computer engineering at the University of Washington (MS, 2007; PhD, 2014). She worked as a clinical research engineer at NeuroVista from 2007 to 2009. After a postdoctoral fellowship at the Center for Developmental Biology and Regenerative Medicine of Seattle Children's Research Institute (2014 to 2018), she became a research scientist there in 2021. Her ORCID record also lists a research scientist position at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 2018, and her FHL-connected papers, from 2021 and 2022, give FHL as an address. SlicerMorph, the platform whose software development she led, was funded by NSF Advances in Biological Informatics grants whose recipients included Adam Summers of FHL.

Rolfe's work applies image analysis and computer vision to morphometrics, the quantitative study of shape. She led software development for SlicerMorph (2021), an open extension of the 3D Slicer imaging platform. It lets biologists import image stacks, retrieve open-access 3D models, place landmarks, and run geometric morphometric analyses. With Arthur Porto and Murat Maga she developed ALPACA (2021), a fast computer-vision method for automatically placing landmarks on 3D specimens, and a 2022 paper extended it to multiple templates. A 2021 paper compared semi-landmarking approaches for 3D cranial morphology, and a 2022 study applied computational anatomy to craniofacial phenotypes in zebrafish. Her earlier work produced landmark-free tools for quantifying shape variation and asymmetry, including a 2019 study of facial skeletal asymmetry during fetal development. Later papers use deep learning to segment organs in mouse embryos (2023).

name: Sarah A. Woodin
text:
Sarah A. Woodin is an ecologist of marine soft-sediment communities and Carolina Distinguished Professor Emerita at the University of South Carolina. She received a BA in biology from Goucher College in 1967 and a PhD in zoology from the University of Washington in 1972. She was an assistant professor of zoology at the University of Maryland (1972 to 1975) and of earth and planetary sciences at Johns Hopkins University (1975 to 1980). At South Carolina she rose from research associate professor in 1980 to professor in 1987 and was Carolina Distinguished Professor of Biology and Marine Science from 1999 to 2013. She is an elected fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. She is not in the report's table of FHL scientists. The census lists 15 FHL-connected papers by her from 1984 to 2012, several of which thank FHL or report experiments run there.

Woodin has studied how animals living in soft sediments interact, and how those interactions and sediment cues shape where larvae settle. A 1984 paper, which thanks FHL's then director Dennis Willows, examined how infaunal animals change their activity after browsing predators remove tissue. She continued this theme with Sara Lindsay, her doctoral student in the report's network, in work on feeding-mode switching and sediment disturbance by browsed spionid polychaetes (1995, 1996). With Rachel Merz she tested whether hooked chaetae anchor worms in their tubes (1987, 2000) and reviewed chaetal mechanics (2003). Other papers reported brominated compounds in soft-bottom animals (1987) and sediment disturbance by the lugworm Abarenicola pacifica (1993). Others examined chemical and disturbance cues that inhibit or guide recruitment (1993, 1995, 1998), including experiments run at FHL in 1990. Later collaborations covered decorating by the spider crab Oregonia gracilis with Sarah Berke (2008, 2009) and intermittent bioirrigation by tellinid bivalves (2012).

name: Sarah Cohen
text:
C. Sarah Cohen is a marine biologist and professor of biology at San Francisco State University, where her ORCID record dates her appointment from 2003. Her papers since 2006 give the university's Romberg Tiburon Center for Environmental Studies and, from 2019, its Estuary and Ocean Science Center. ORCID lists studies in biology at Swarthmore College, a PhD in zoology from the University of Washington and a fellowship of the California Academy of Sciences. Her papers of 1988 to 1996 give the UW Department of Zoology and, from 1990, Friday Harbor Laboratories. Later addresses are Stanford University's Department of Developmental Biology and Hopkins Marine Station (1998) and Harvard University's Department of Organismic and Evolutionary Biology (2001-02). Her FHL-connected papers span 1988 to 2014. A 1996 study was written with Richard R. Strathmann, and the eelgrass papers of 2012 and 2014 with Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria of FHL.

Cohen uses genetic tools to study mating systems, population structure and self-recognition in marine invertebrates and plants. Her early FHL work concerned genetic differentiation in the brooding sea cucumber Leptosynapta clarki (1988, with several co-authors) and outcrossing in field populations of two self-fertile ascidians (1990). Two 1996 papers examined levels of inbreeding under contrasting modes of fertilization in the marine invertebrate genus Corella, and how environment and the structure of egg masses affect the supply of oxygen to embryos. Later papers address allorecognition and phylogeny in botryllid ascidians, a histocompatibility gene in an estuarine fish under pollution stress, the invasive tunicate Didemnum vexillum, and population genetics and wasting disease in brooding Leptasterias sea stars. The eelgrass studies measured genetic diversity among Zostera marina beds and depths in San Francisco Bay (2012) and its conservation in a mesocosm restoration experiment (2014).

name: Sarah E. Gilman
text:
Sarah E. Gilman is an intertidal ecologist at the Claremont Colleges in California. ORCID lists a B.S. in Earth Systems from Stanford University, a PhD in population biology from the University of California, Davis, an associate professorship of biology at Scripps College from 2016 and a professorship of biology at Pitzer College. Her first papers, of 1995 and 1999, give Stanford's Hopkins Marine Station and the Center for Population Biology at UC Davis, and those of 2005 and 2006 the University of South Carolina. A 2017 paper acknowledges a postdoctoral fellowship from Friday Harbor Laboratories, and papers from 2006 to 2010 give FHL as her address. From 2009 her papers give the Joint Science Department of the Claremont Colleges and, from 2014, the W. M. Keck Science Department of Claremont McKenna, Pitzer and Scripps Colleges. She continued FHL-connected work with Hilary Hayford and Emily Carrington into the 2020s.

Gilman studies how temperature and other conditions on rocky shores shape the performance, distribution and interactions of intertidal animals under climate change. Her first papers documented climate-related change in a California intertidal community (1995, 1999). FHL-connected papers test the northern range limit of the limpet Collisella scabra (2006), evaluate effective shore level as a measure of wave exposure (2006) and, with many co-authors, map mosaic patterns of thermal stress on rocky shores (2006). A 2009 paper with Lauren Yamane found opposite responses of an intertidal predator to rising water and air temperatures, and a 2010 review with Mark Urban and others proposed a framework for community interactions under climate change. Work with Hayford and Carrington showed that a marine snail's foraging limits its heat exposure, aided by tidal cues (2014, 2021). Later studies concern the barnacle Balanus glandula and the effects of ocean and terrestrial warming on an intertidal crustacean (2024-2025).

name: Sasha K. Seroy
text:
Sasha K. Seroy is an oceanographer whose work combines marine community ecology with oceanography education. As an undergraduate at Stony Brook University, Seroy was mentored by Dianna Padilla, who later also helped with Seroy's summer research at FHL. Seroy completed a Ph.D. in oceanography at the University of Washington in 2021, with Daniel Grünbaum as committee chair. Much of the experimental work was done at FHL, including its Ocean Acidification Environmental Laboratory, with support from FHL fellowships. Seroy's FHL-connected research papers run from 2018 to 2024 and list both FHL and the UW School of Oceanography as affiliations. Education papers from 2019 to 2025 describe student-built pH and acoustic sensors, an interactive 3D model of thermohaline circulation for introductory courses, and the Student Seaglider Center, a student-run laboratory.

Seroy's research uses inducible traits, such as defences that prey grow when predators are present, to follow how species interactions shape responses to ocean acidification and warming. A 2018 paper with Grünbaum, from experiments at FHL, tested the bryozoan Membranipora membranacea and its nudibranch predator Corambe steinbergae across pH 7.0 to 7.9. Defensive spines still formed at every pH, and a model showed that competition for space amplifies the cost of defence at the population level. The dissertation also showed that the snail Lacuna vincta moves often between eelgrass and macroalgae, which shapes its response to warming. In later work with Katie Dobkowski and colleagues, graceful kelp crabs (Pugettia gracilis) preferred native bull kelp to the invasive Sargassum muticum and ate more at about 19.5 °C than at 11.5 °C (2023). In a 2024 study, warming did not change the feeding rate or diet of the omnivorous Pugettia producta.

name: Scott Smiley
text:
Scott Smiley's research began with sea cucumber reproduction at the Friday Harbor Laboratories and later turned to seafood and aquaculture-feed science in Alaska. Smiley's papers from 1985 to 1988 give FHL and the University of Washington Department of Zoology as addresses; the first was written with Richard A. Cloney. The 1986 paper also gives an address in the Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics at the University of California, San Francisco, where Smiley co-authored a 1992 study of cytoskeleton reorganization during Drosophila oogenesis with William Theurkauf, Mei Lie Wong and Bruce Alberts. A 1990 review of echinoderm oogenesis carries addresses at the Institute of Arctic Biology and the Department of Biology and Wildlife of the University of Alaska Fairbanks. Papers from 2003 to 2013 place Smiley at the university's Fishery Industrial Technology Center in Kodiak, part of its School of Fisheries and Ocean Sciences.

The FHL-connected papers describe the reproductive biology and development of the sea cucumber Stichopus californicus (now Apostichopus californicus). A 1985 paper with Cloney described the fine structure of the ovarian tubules and ovulation. A 1986 paper described metamorphosis and discussed where it places holothurians among the echinoderms, and a 1988 paper traced oogenesis through the annual ovarian cycle. Two further census papers from the FHL bibliography concern classification: a 1987 study with V. S. Levin and colleagues of triterpene glycosides in two stichopodid species, and a 1988 cladistic analysis of holothurian relationships. In Kodiak the work turned to fishery byproducts: fish meals, hydrolysates, oils and testes meals tested as feeds for trout, tilapia, Pacific threadfin and shrimp, and salmon-based infant foods. A 2012 paper returned to the same sea cucumber, under the name Parastichopus californicus, analysing the chemical composition of animals harvested commercially in Alaska.

name: Sebastian Kruppert
text:
Sebastian Kruppert is a zoologist whose work concerns the biomechanics of predators and prey. He received his doctorate from Ruhr University Bochum, with a 2016 dissertation on the form, function, structure and plasticity of the carapace of the water flea Daphnia, and his earlier papers dealt with predator-induced defences and carapace mechanics in Daphnia. His papers from 2019 to 2022 give Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) as his address, and several were written with Adam Summers. His FHL work on poacher fishes was supported in part by the German Research Foundation (DFG). Papers from 2022 also give the Plant Biomechanics Group at the University of Freiburg's Botanic Garden as an address, and his later papers, listed on his ORCID record, deal with latex coagulation in Campanula, a biomimetic speaking valve (2024) and the transfer of animal strides to a biomimetic soft walker (2025).

At FHL, Kruppert studied the bony armour of poachers (Agonidae). A 2020 paper in the Journal of Morphology used CT scans of 27 poacher species to compare the mineral invested in armour and skeleton, and recorded abrasion and impact damage, worsening with age, on the plates of the northern spearnose poacher, Agonopsis vulsa. A 2021 conference abstract with Summers and others used feeding trials and machined crab claws to test whether red rock crabs cause such damage. He also co-authored a 2021 study of swimming, body stiffness and vertebral counts in four elongate fishes of the genera Anoplarchus and Xiphister, and a 2019 Nature commentary with Summers on a paradox in fish feeding. With colleagues from Bochum and Freiburg he worked on carnivorous aquatic plants: prey spectra and prey capture of the waterwheel plant Aldrovanda vesiculosa (2019) and the defences of the water flea Ceriodaphnia dubia against a bladderwort (2022).

name: Shaun D. Cain
text:
Shaun D. Cain is a neurobiologist and professor of biology at Eastern Oregon University (EOU). He holds a BS in biology with a marine biology concentration from Florida Atlantic University, an MS in biology from the University of North Carolina Wilmington and a PhD in biology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. His 2004 and 2005 papers give Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address, and he joined EOU's biology faculty in 2005. A 2010–2011 EOU program report says he specializes in cellular and organismal neurobiology and teaches anatomy and physiology, cell biology, neurobiology and neuroethology. It adds that he involves undergraduates in research on neurotransmission in the slug. At FHL he has co-taught the summer Neuroethology course with James Murray. The census counts eight FHL-address papers from 2004 to 2011, plus later papers that mention FHL in their text.

Cain studies how invertebrate nervous systems detect sensory cues and control behavior. With Kenneth Lohmann's group at Chapel Hill he worked on the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea, in which three pairs of identifiable pedal neurons respond to magnetic fields of Earth strength. His FHL-address papers identified a pair of neurons that such fields inhibit (2004) and analyzed the neurochemistry and electrophysiology of the responsive cells (2005). He also co-wrote reviews of magnetic orientation in sea turtles, lobsters and molluscs (2005) and of the neural bases of orientation and navigation (2006). With Andrew Christie and colleagues he co-authored anatomical and mass-spectrometry studies of neuroendocrine sites in the crab Cancer productus (2004–2005). Later work traced a network of Tritonia pedal peptides across gastropods (2011). A 2014 study he co-authored, run in FHL's magnetic coil, found that four chiton species headed north-northwest in the natural field but at random in a rotated field.

name: Shawn M. Luttrell
text:
Shawn M. Luttrell received a PhD from the University of Washington in 2017 with a dissertation on regeneration in the acorn worm Ptychodera flava. The supervisory committee was chaired by Billie J. Swalla, then director of Friday Harbor Laboratories. Luttrell's papers from 2012 to 2018 give the UW Department of Biology and FHL as addresses. They include a 2012 conference paper with Swalla and others and a 2014 book chapter with Swalla; a 2011 abstract with Swalla and others concerned neural organization in the hemichordate Saccoglossus bromophenolosus. For the larval experiments, P. flava larvae were carried from Taipei, Taiwan, to FHL, and a 2018 paper on larval regeneration was written with Yi-Hsien Su and Swalla.

Luttrell's research asks how hemichordates, a sister group to the echinoderms that shares some features with chordates, build and rebuild their nervous system and anterior structures. The 2012 conference paper described neurulation in a ptychoderid hemichordate that lacks a notochord. The 2014 chapter reviewed genomic and evolutionary evidence on chordate origins. A 2016 paper in Developmental Dynamics, with Kirsten Gotting, Eric Ross, Alejandro Sanchez Alvarado and Swalla, concluded that head regeneration in hemichordates is not a strict recapitulation of embryonic development. The dissertation followed anterior regeneration over time and compared transcriptomes at eight stages. It and the 2018 paper extended the work to larvae, which regenerate after being cut in several planes and re-form serotonin-positive cells in the region of the eyespots and larval brain within two weeks. New cells are added both at the cut site and throughout the regenerating tissue.

name: Shigeki Mizuno
text:
Shigeki Mizuno, a molecular biologist, wrote four FHL-connected papers, from 1973 to 1981, that report work with Arthur H. Whiteley and Helen R. Whiteley in the University of Washington's Departments of Microbiology and Zoology and at Friday Harbor Laboratories. A 1968 paper with Helen Whiteley on RNA synthesis in Bacillus subtilis gives his address as the Department of Microbiology of the UW School of Medicine. Papers in one OpenAlex record under his name give the University of Tokyo's Institute of Applied Microbiology in the 1960s and early 1970s, and the University of Leicester's Department of Zoology, in work with Herbert C. Macgregor, from 1974 to 1976. From 1984 to 2001 they give the Faculty of Agriculture of Tohoku University, and from 2001 to 2007 Nihon University. These later attributions rest on one bibliographic database record and are less certain than the UW and FHL papers.

Mizuno's research concerned how RNA populations, chromosomes and chromatin relate to gene expression and development. With the Whiteleys he studied embryos of the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus. They reported an enrichment of egg-type RNA in cleavage-stage embryos (1973) and examined how RNA populations are distributed among the cells of the 16-cell embryo (1974). A 1975 paper discussed transcripts of repeated DNA sequences in the determination of blastomeres and early differentiation of echinoid larvae. A 1981 paper with Arthur Whiteley used electron microscopy to visualize giant polysomes in sea urchin embryos. Earlier papers in the same OpenAlex record deal with RNA synthesis in bacteria, the silk gland of the silkworm and the salmon brain. Later ones cover repetitive DNA in salamander chromosomes, the chicken W sex chromosome and a protein that binds its repeated DNA, the silk fibroin genes of Bombyx mori, and DNA-based sexing of birds.

name: Shigeko Ooishi
text:
Shigeko Ooishi is a taxonomist of copepods that live in ascidians (sea squirts). She was a professor at Mie University in Japan: the Japanese research database KAKEN lists her as a professor in the Faculty of Fisheries in 1986, and the E. S. Morse Institute at Friday Harbor Laboratories describes her as a professor on Mie's faculty of biosciences. According to the Morse Institute, she spent many summers at FHL working with Paul Illg on the systematics and biology of parasitic copepods, and after retiring she continued her copepod work at FHL for many years. She was inducted into the Morse Institute in 2013. Her 2006 description of a new copepod genus from Okinawa gives FHL as her address and thanks the laboratories for facilities and equipment. The census counts 29 FHL-address papers by her from 1994 to 2014.

Ooishi's research is the descriptive taxonomy of cyclopoid copepods of the families Ascidicolidae and Notodelphyidae, which live inside colonial and solitary ascidians, some of them in the host's intestine. The earliest papers in the census, from 1977 and 1980, treat haplostomine copepods from compound ascidians of the San Juan Archipelago and the larval development of these copepods, and mention FHL in their text. Later papers describe new species and redescribe little-known ones, often treating both females and males, from hosts collected in Hawaii, Florida, the Gulf of California, Vancouver Island, New Zealand, Okinawa, Madagascar and European sites such as Roscoff, Strangford Lough and the Clyde estuary. A series on species from Madagascar ran from 2008 to 2014. Most of this work appeared in the Journal of Crustacean Biology and the Proceedings of the Biological Society of Washington.
