name: Simon A. Levin
text:
Simon A. Levin is an ecologist trained in mathematics. Since 1992 he has been James S. McDonnell Distinguished University Professor in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at Princeton University, where he directs the Center for BioComplexity. He received a BA from Johns Hopkins University and a PhD in mathematics from the University of Maryland; Wikidata names Monroe H. Martin as his doctoral advisor. From 1965 to 1992 he was at Cornell University. There he chaired the Section of Ecology and Systematics, directed the Ecosystems Research Center, and was Charles A. Alexander Professor of Biological Sciences from 1985. He has been president of the Ecological Society of America and of the Society for Mathematical Biology. His honours include the Kyoto Prize (2005), the Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement (2014), the National Medal of Science, membership of the National Academy of Sciences and election as a Fellow of the Royal Society (2026).

Levin's research combines mathematical modelling with empirical study. It asks how large-scale patterns and processes in ecosystems and the biosphere are maintained by ecological and evolutionary mechanisms acting mainly at the level of organisms. He has also worked on infectious diseases and on links between basic and applied ecology. He is not in the report's table of FHL scientists. The census lists two of his papers. One is a 2002 model, with William McFarland of FHL, of how water currents affect prey capture by plankton-feeding fishes. The other is a 2008 article with Jane Lubchenco on resilience, robustness and ecosystem-based management of marine systems. It thanks FHL's director and staff for use of the laboratories' Helen R. Whiteley Center. Wikidata lists many doctoral students for him, among them Daniel Grünbaum, who appears in the report's table of FHL scientists for papers from 2010 to 2020.

name: Sophie B. George
text:
Sophie B. George is a marine biologist who studies the reproduction and larval biology of echinoderms. Her doctoral thesis (Université Paris 6, 1990, supervised by Paul Nival) examined how food affects reproduction and larval development in the sea urchins Arbacia lixula and Paracentrotus lividus and the sea star Luidia clathrata, and her first papers came from the Station Zoologique at Villefranche-sur-Mer. Later papers list the University of South Florida (1991), Friday Harbor Laboratories (1994) and Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution in Florida (1996-97); since the late 1990s she has published from the Biology Department of Georgia Southern University. Her FHL-connected census papers run from 1994 to 2025. Seven are reports from FHL's summer Blinks/NSF REU/BEACON internship program with student first authors, among them Sam Bashevkin (2012), whom she mentored as a fellow. In 2023 she was first author of a note in Oryx announcing the new IUCN Marine Star Specialist Group.

Her research asks how a parent's diet and condition, and the conditions larvae meet in the plankton, affect egg quality, larval growth and metamorphosis. At Georgia Southern she has also worked on diets for rearing the sea urchin Lytechinus variegatus and on shell use by juvenile fiddler crabs (2010). Her FHL-connected papers began with maternal size and offspring quality in populations of the sea star Leptasterias epichlora (1994). Papers from 2006 to 2008 examined how food and dietary lipids affect growth and fatty acid composition of sand dollar (Dendraster excentricus) larvae, and how short-term salinity fluctuations speed their development. Since 2012 most concern larvae of the ochre star Pisaster ochraceus: shape changes and vertical position in low-salinity layers (2012), the use of larval arms in swimming (2019, with Richard Strathmann of FHL), feeding under fluctuating temperature and salinity (2021), and development during temperature spikes and marine heatwaves (2025).

name: Stacy C. Farina
text:
Stacy C. Farina is a comparative biologist who studies the functional morphology and evolution of fishes. She earned a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology at Cornell University in 2015; William E. Bemis chaired the committee, which included Adam Summers of the Friday Harbor Laboratories. In summer 2012 she took Summers's course in functional morphology and ecology of marine fishes at FHL and used her course project data as the basis for a doctoral dissertation improvement grant proposal. The dissertation's sculpin ventilation study was carried out at FHL that summer, and she returned to the Summers lab for many later visits. Her FHL-connected work, from 2014 to 2023, includes student reports from the FHL fish course (2014) and the Blinks–NSF REU–BEACON internship program (2015) on which she is a co-author. Farina is on the biology faculty at Howard University in Washington, D.C.; her 2023 dogfish paper gives both Howard and FHL addresses.

Farina's research centres on how fishes pump water over their gills and how breathing is tied to feeding and locomotion. The dissertation found that restricted gill openings evolved at least 11 times among ray-finned fishes, described very slow ventilation in the goosefish Lophius americanus, and proposed adding a third pump, formed by the branchiostegal rays, to the usual two-pump model. A 2019 paper followed the coupled evolution of suction feeding and gill ventilation in sculpins. Other FHL-connected work covers burial by flatfishes (2015) and by English sole (2018), dynamic testing of shark teeth (2016), overland walking by the tidepool sculpin Oligocottus maculosus (2018), the evolution of sculpin jaw bones and muscles (2018), skeletal reduction with depth in snailfishes (2021), and a ventilatory shunt in the flatfish Isopsetta isolepis (2022). A 2023 paper measured pressures in the gill chambers of the Pacific spiny dogfish, Squalus suckleyi.

name: Stephanie B. Crofts
text:
Stephanie B. Crofts is a biomechanist and functional morphologist and an assistant professor of biology at the College of the Holy Cross in Worcester, Massachusetts, where she has worked since 2020. She completed her PhD at the University of Washington in 2015, working with Adam Summers on the functional morphology of teeth that crush hard prey. She then studied swimming in living and extinct reptiles with Brooke Flammang at the New Jersey Institute of Technology. Her papers from 2018 to 2020 give the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign as her address. The census lists sixteen FHL-connected items by her from 2011 to 2025. Besides her doctoral papers, they include student research reports she co-authored in FHL's autumn research courses (2012, 2014), a 2014 summer fish course and its summer internship programmes (2014, 2023), and later papers with FHL-based colleagues.

Crofts uses physical specimens, CT data and models to study how organisms match their structures to their ecology, with a particular interest in the evolution of specialised dentitions. Her FHL-era papers deal with durophagy, the eating of hard-shelled prey. A 2014 study measured how tooth shape affects the load needed to crush snail shells. Other papers built finite element models of occlusal variation in crushing teeth (2015), tested jaw curvature and prey crushing in stingrays (2015) and analysed tooth shape in the extinct marine reptiles Placodontia (2016). She also contributed to studies of chiton morphology under ocean acidification (2015) and of harbour seal skin and blubber (2017). Later FHL-linked papers treat the scaling and structure of juvenile bull kelp (2021, with Katie Dobkowski) and tooth indentation in fruit-eating fishes (2025). At Illinois her papers turned to biological puncture, including snake fangs and cactus spines.

name: Stephen A. Stricker
text:
Stephen A. Stricker is a cell and developmental biologist and professor emeritus of biology at the University of New Mexico (UNM). He received his PhD in zoology from the University of Washington in 1983. His early papers give the UW Department of Zoology and Friday Harbor Laboratories as addresses. They include a 1982 study of stylet formation in nemertean worms co-authored with Richard A. Cloney, and a 1983 study of maturing starfish oocytes with Thomas E. Schroeder. Papers from 1985 list the University of Calgary and one from 1988 the University of Wisconsin–Madison; by 1990 he was in UNM's Department of Biology. The census counts eight FHL-address papers from 1981 to 1984, and later papers through 2016 that appear in the FHL bibliography or mention FHL. UNM lists his research as calcium dynamics during oocyte maturation, fertilization and early development, and the roles of kinases and cyclic nucleotides in eggs.

Stricker's early studies used electron and polarization microscopy to show how nemertean worms build the calcified stylets of their proboscis armature, and described venom-producing cells in Paranemertes peregrina (1982–1985). He described two new nemerteans from Washington: Paranemertes sanjuanensis (1982) and a Tetrastemma from San Juan Island (1985). Related work examined shell and pedicle formation in the brachiopod Terebratalia transversa (1984–1985) and calcareous ossicles of sea cucumbers (1985–1986). Other papers covered gametogenesis in nemerteans, including a crab symbiont (1986), and the cyphonautes larva and metamorphosis of the bryozoan Membranipora membranacea (1988). His later papers, largely on nemerteans such as Cerebratulus, imaged calcium signals at fertilization by confocal microscopy. They also tested the roles of cAMP, serotonin, MAP kinase, protein kinase C, Src-family kinases and AMP-activated kinase in oocyte maturation and aging, with comparative reviews in 1999, 2013 and 2015.

name: Steven B. Roberts
text:
Steven B. Roberts is a Professor in the School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences (SAFS) at the University of Washington, where his laboratory studies the genomics, epigenetics and physiology of marine invertebrates. Earlier papers place him in the Department of Biological Sciences at the University of Notre Dame (about 1999-2001), working on genes involved in fish ovulation and muscle growth, and at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole (about 2003-2007), where he worked on aquaculture species and marine pathogens, including the hard clam parasite QPX; his SAFS papers begin in 2007. His FHL-connected census papers, from 2012 to 2026, draw on oysters spawned and held at Friday Harbor, a graduate course taught there and FHL-based co-authors. He chaired the doctoral committee of Emma Timmins-Schiffman (UW SAFS, PhD 2014), first author of his oyster papers in the census.

The Roberts lab studies how marine organisms carry a memory of past environmental conditions, linking molecular regulation to physiology across life stages and generations, in oysters, corals and sunflower sea stars. His FHL-connected papers follow two lines. The first concerns the Pacific oyster Crassostrea gigas and ocean acidification: a 2012 paper with FHL's Michael O'Donnell found that larvae from wild adults spawned at Friday Harbor developed more slowly under elevated carbon dioxide, a 2013 paper on oysters held at FHL tested shotgun proteomics of the gill, and a 2014 paper used it to describe responses to four weeks in acidified water. The second concerns disease. A 2013 genome-browser dataset for QPX came largely from a graduate course at Friday Harbor; a 2015 paper measured immune and nervous system gene expression in sunflower sea stars with wasting disease, and 2026 papers with FHL's C. Drew Harvell compare juvenile and adult responses.

name: Stuart H. Thompson
text:
Stuart H. Thompson is a neurobiologist and Professor of Biology at Stanford University's Hopkins Marine Station in Pacific Grove, California, and a member of Stanford's Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute. Thompson's papers carry the Hopkins address from 1983 onward, and Thompson teaches courses on marine animal physiology and the sensory ecology of marine animals. The earliest FHL-connected papers date from the 1970s. A 1973 chapter on bursting mechanisms in mollusc locomotion, written with A. O. Dennis Willows and Peter Getting, carries FHL and UW Department of Zoology addresses, and a 1979 Brain Research paper with L. Donald Partridge, Stephen Smith and John Connor carries an FHL address. Later FHL-connected papers, from 2002 and 2005, came from a collaboration with Winsor Watson of the University of New Hampshire on the nudibranch Melibe leonina.

Thompson studies ion channels and the electrical behaviour of nerve cells, mostly in marine animals. Work from the 1970s and 1980s on molluscan neurons identified three pharmacologically distinct potassium channels (1977), examined the slow currents behind bursting pacemaker activity in Tritonia and Aplysia, and used patch methods to map the uneven distribution of potassium and calcium channels over the cell body. In the 1990s Thompson used fura-2 imaging to study calcium signalling in neuroblastoma cells. Later work includes vision in juvenile rockfish, measured by electroretinogram, the spectral sensitivity of box jellyfish eyes (Tripedalia cystophora), bluefin tuna heart cells and the nervous system of the colonial tunicate Botryllus schlosseri. The FHL-connected Melibe papers link cell properties to behaviour: a 2002 study showed that isolated Melibe brains still produce the swim rhythm, and a 2005 paper identified the two pairs of interneurons that form the swim central pattern generator.

name: Susan Lynn Williams
text:
Susan Lynn Williams (1951–2018) was a marine ecologist who studied seagrasses, seaweeds and coral reef algae. She received a B.S. in biology from the University of Michigan (1972), an M.S. in biological oceanography from the University of Alaska (1977) and a Ph.D. in botany and marine biology from the University of Maryland (1981). Several papers from 1983 to 1985 came from the Smithsonian Institution's Marine Systems Laboratory, and she was later science director of NOAA's National Undersea Research Program in the Virgin Islands. Her papers from 1988 to 1990 carry FHL addresses, with the UW Department of Botany in 1989 and San Diego State University in 1990. At San Diego State she was a professor of biology and directed the Coastal and Marine Institute. From 2000 she was at the University of California, Davis, where she directed the Bodega Marine Laboratory until 2010 and was Distinguished Professor of Evolution and Ecology.

Williams studied how light, nutrients, grazing and physical stress shape coastal seagrass and seaweed communities, and how human activity affects them. Her FHL-connected papers from 1988 to 1990 cover grazing by green turtles on the seagrass Thalassia testudinum in a disturbed bed, the photosynthetic response of nitrogen-starved brown algae (Petalonia fascia and Laminaria saccharina) to ammonium resupply (with Stephen Herbert), and photosynthesis-light relationships among components of coral reef algal turfs (with R. C. Carpenter). Later FHL-connected papers (2004–2008), with Megan Dethier and colleagues, concern the rockweed Fucus gardneri on San Juan Island: the performance of embryos, juveniles and adults across tidal heights and seasons, variation in net photosynthesis, and the effects of manipulated stress and herbivory. With Dianna Padilla she identified aquarium and ornamental trades as sources of aquatic invasive species (2004). She was president of the Coastal and Estuarine Research Federation (2009–2011) and a fellow of the AAAS (2006).

name: T E Schroeder
text:
Thomas E. Schroeder is a cell and developmental biologist whose papers from 1972 to 1991 give the Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address. The census lists some of them under the name T. E. Schroeder; the report's fuller record for him appears under Thomas E. Schroeder. His first papers, from 1967 to 1970, give the University of Washington Department of Zoology. They concern cytoplasmic filaments in the folding of the amphibian neural tube and filaments in the cleavage furrow of dividing cells. Papers of 1970 and 1971 come from the Department of Anatomy at the Stanford University School of Medicine. A 1981 study of the development of a cidaroid sea urchin, Eucidaris tribuloides, also lists the Discovery Bay Marine Laboratory of the University of the West Indies. Under this name the census holds three FHL-address papers from 1973 to 1982.

Schroeder studied how animal cells divide and how the egg cortex, the layer beneath the egg surface, is organized. In 1972 he described the contractile ring, the band of microfilaments under the cleavage furrow of sea urchin eggs. In 1973 he showed that these filaments in dividing HeLa cells bind heavy meromyosin, evidence that they are actin. Mostly with sea urchin and starfish eggs and oocytes, he studied cleavage forces, egg polarity, microvilli, surface changes at fertilization, and actin and microtubule assembly during oocyte maturation. Papers under this census name cover peristaltic constrictions in fertilized eggs of the stalked barnacle Pollicipes polymerus (1973, with Fu-Shiang Chia), calcium and contractility in frog eggs (1974), and actin polymerization in starfish sperm (1982). Clara F. Asnes co-authored his 1979 paper on cell cleavage. With Gary Conrad he wrote the preface to a 1990 Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences volume on cytokinesis.

name: Tamara M. McGovern
text:
Tamara M. McGovern is a marine biologist whose papers concern reproduction and population genetics in marine invertebrates, seagrasses and sharks. McGovern's 2002 and 2003 papers on brittle stars give the Department of Biological Science at Florida State University as an address. A 2003 paper with Michael Hellberg gives the Department of Biological Sciences at Louisiana State University as an address and the Friday Harbor Laboratories as a present address. FHL also appears on a 2002 brittle star paper and on a 2004 coral study, so the FHL-connected work falls between 2002 and 2004. Later papers give addresses at the Dauphin Island Sea Lab in Alabama (2007, 2009) and in Clemson University's Department of Biological Sciences (2009, 2010). A 2010 paper gives a present address in the Natural Sciences Division of Limestone College in South Carolina.

McGovern's work at Florida State concerned the brittle star Ophiactis savignyi, which reproduces both sexually and by dividing in two. Two 2002 papers described sexual and asexual reproduction in Florida Keys populations and showed that males divide more often than females, enough to explain the excess of males. A 2003 study found that individuals divide less often when mates are present. With Hellberg, McGovern used mitochondrial COI sequences to show that regional differences in the chemical defences of the western Atlantic bryozoan Bugula neritina follow two cryptic species; the bryostatin-producing bacterium Endobugula sertula was found only in the southern species (2003). A 2004 study led by Don Levitan, with McGovern as co-author, examined reproductive isolation among broadcast-spawning corals of the Montastraea annularis complex. Later papers address seagrass reproduction in the northern Gulf of Mexico, lemon shark phylogeography and rocky-shore phylogeography, and, with Levitan, Allee effects in the sea.

name: Teresa Audesirk
text:
Teresa Audesirk is a neurobiologist and an author of biology textbooks. Her papers of 1975 to 1978 give the University of Southern California, including its Catalina Marine Science Center, and the California Institute of Technology. Her four FHL-connected papers, of 1979 and 1980, give Friday Harbor Laboratories. Her papers of 1982 to 1984 give the University of Missouri-Columbia, and those of 1985 to 2004 the biology department of the University of Colorado at Denver. The FHL papers form two two-part series in the Journal of Comparative Physiology on the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea. The first is single-authored and the others were written with Gerald J. Audesirk, whose own FHL papers of 1978 and 1979 concern the neurons that control Tritonia's locomotory cilia. With Gerald Audesirk and Bruce E. Byers she is an author of the textbook Biology: Life on Earth (from 1986; eleventh edition 2016).

Her research has used molluscs and, later, cultured vertebrate neurons to study how animals sense their surroundings and how toxic substances affect nerve cells. Early papers examined distance chemoreception and evidence for pheromones in the sea hare Aplysia californica, and a 1979 field study followed its growth and reproduction. At FHL she recorded from oral mechanoreceptors of Tritonia, describing their electrophysiological properties, receptive fields and role in feeding (1979). The 1980 papers described complex mechanoreceptors, their responses to mechanical and chemical stimuli, and neuronal correlates of a change in the animal's behavioural responsiveness. Later work with freshwater snails, chiefly the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis, dealt with rapid and one-trial reward conditioning and with the effects of chronic lead exposure on identified neurons. From about 1990 she and her colleagues studied how inorganic lead, nicotine and estradiol affect calcium channels, neurite growth and dendritic branching in cultured hippocampal and neuroblastoma cells.

name: Terrie Klinger
text:
Terrie Klinger is a marine ecologist whose work spans seaweed biology, marine conservation and ocean governance. She received a BA from the University of California, Berkeley (1979), an MSc from the University of British Columbia (1984) and a PhD from the University of California, San Diego (1989). Her doctoral advisor was Paul K. Dayton. Wikidata records postdoctoral work at the University of California, Riverside (1989 to 1992), lecturing for Northeastern University (1991 to 1999) and a visiting position at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 1992 to 2001. She joined the University of Washington faculty in 2001 as an assistant professor and became an associate professor in 2008. Her papers from 1993 to 2003 give FHL as an address. A 2018 ocean acidification study, papers on the San Juan Islands and a 2021 student report also name FHL.

Klinger's early FHL-connected work concerned algae: a 1993 review of why haplodiploid life cycles persist in algae, and 1999 studies with David Garbary, David Duggins and others of kelp gametophytes living inside red algae. With Duggins she did field work on how small grazers and current flow together affect kelp survival (2001), and on three understory kelps along a gradient of water motion (2003). With Jennifer Hoffman and Lara Hansen she showed that UV radiation and temperature interact, limiting what single-factor experiments can show (2003). She also wrote on biosafety assessment of genetically engineered organisms (1998, 1999). Later papers turned to marine reserves and ecosystem-based management: invaders in reserves (2006), the San Juan Archipelago (2007), dispersal among reserves (2007) and governance (2008). Her experiments on pteropod shell dissolution under ocean acidification were done at FHL during a graduate summer course (2018).

name: Thomas E. Schroeder
text:
Thomas E. Schroeder, a cell biologist, studied cell division and the egg cortex using the eggs and oocytes of marine invertebrates. According to an FHL centennial timeline, he first came to Friday Harbor in 1965 as a University of Washington graduate student of Richard Cloney, to take the Comparative Invertebrate Embryology course. In 1971 he joined the UW Zoology Department and took up year-round residence at FHL, bringing an American Cancer Society grant with which he set up a transmission electron microscopy facility at the laboratories. His earliest papers (1970-1971) analyzed neurulation in the frog Xenopus laevis and the fine structure of dividing HeLa cells. The census credits him with 25 FHL-connected papers from 1972 to 1991, and his papers of those years give Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address.

Much of Schroeder's work concerns the contractile ring, the band of filaments that pinches a dividing cell in two. His 1972 electron-microscope study of Arbacia sea urchin eggs found that the ring exists only from shortly after anaphase to the end of furrowing, that its volume decreases as it constricts, and that cytochalasin B removes its filaments and halts cleavage; a 1973 paper showed that ring filaments in dividing HeLa cells bind heavy meromyosin, indicating that they are closely related to muscle actin. From the late 1970s he turned to the egg surface and cortex: microvillus elongation after fertilization (1978), markers of egg polarity such as the jelly canal (1980), the "primitive" sea urchin Eucidaris (1981), actin and microtubule arrays in maturing starfish oocytes (1983-1985, several with J. J. Otto), unequal fourth cleavage in sea urchins (1987), and a periodic cytokeratin network in the starfish oocyte cortex called "snoods" (1991).

name: Thomas F. Mumford
text:
Thomas F. Mumford Jr. is a phycologist whose publications, from 1980 to 2024, deal mostly with seaweeds and seagrasses in Washington State. He received an A.B. in botany from Wabash College in 1966 and a Ph.D. in botany from the University of Washington in 1973. Papers from 1990 and 1997 give his address as the Washington State Department of Natural Resources, and papers from 2015 to 2023 list Marine Agronomics LLC. His ORCID record lists him as a visiting lecturer at Friday Harbor Laboratories since 1984, and his census papers with an FHL address date from 2016 to 2024. He co-authored FHL student papers, including a 2014 project with Megan Dethier on haptera growth in two kelps and a 2020 report with Chiko Meng on blade growth and erosion in the sugar kelp Saccharina latissima, based on a spring class project run at FHL over six years.

Mumford's work joins seaweed biology with resource management and aquaculture. Earlier publications deal with field cultivation of the red algae Iridaea cordata and Gigartina exasperata (1980), shellfish and seaweed harvests in Puget Sound (1988), the growth of nori farming in North America (1990), underwater video for estimating seagrass cover (1997), and kelp and eelgrass in Puget Sound (a 2007 report). Later papers report an introduced population of the brown alga Chorda asiatica (2015), reconstruct 145 years of bull kelp (Nereocystis luetkeana) records in South Puget Sound, finding 63% less kelp in 2017 than in 1878 (2021), and model free-floating offshore seaweed farms (2019-2022). His FHL-connected papers are collaborations in red algal genetics and systematics: the organelle genomes of Mastocarpus papillatus (2016), DNA sequencing of the coralline genus Lithothamnion in the Arctic and Subarctic (2021), and the chloroplast genome of Rhodochorton tenue from San Juan Island (2024).

name: Thomas J. Pirtle
text:
Thomas J. Pirtle is a biologist whose research interests include comparative physiology, developmental biology and neuroethology. He earned a B.S. (1990) and an M.S. (1992) in biology at Abilene Christian University and a Ph.D. in biology at Arizona State University (2003). He taught at Abilene Christian University and Grand Canyon University before joining the biology faculty of The College of Idaho in 2014. His courses there include anatomy and physiology, developmental biology, and regional anatomy and histology for a physician assistant program run with Idaho State University. The census lists eight FHL-connected papers from 2000 to 2022, written from Arizona State, Abilene Christian, Grand Canyon and The College of Idaho, several also giving an FHL address. His 2022 review says the work depended on the continued support of the Friday Harbor Laboratories. Richard A. Satterlie, a co-author of six of the papers, is linked to him in the report's network.

Much of his research concerns the swimming pteropod mollusc Clione limacina and how its locomotor central pattern generator, the neural circuit that sets the swimming rhythm, speeds up. In 2000, with Satterlie and Tigran P. Norekian, he reported that serotonin narrows the spikes of the circuit's interneurons, permitting faster cycling. A second 2000 paper, led by Leonid L. Moroz, mapped NADPH-diaphorase reactivity, a putative marker of nitric oxide synthase, in the Clione nervous system and found that nitric oxide activates neurons in feeding and locomotor circuits. Later papers examined the pleural type 12 interneuron in swim acceleration (2006), postinhibitory rebound (2007) and a hyperpolarization-activated current that alters swim frequency (2010). A 2020 study of Pd-7 swim interneurons found that cGMP mediates acceleration induced by nitric oxide but not by serotonin, and a 2022 review brought the work together. His newer projects use chick embryos and the water flea Daphnia magna.

name: Thomas Kleinteich
text:
Thomas Kleinteich is a zoologist whose published research, from 2006 to 2022, concerns functional morphology and biomechanics, much of it in amphibians. He completed a doctoral dissertation at the Universität Hamburg in 2009 on the evolution of intrauterine feeding in caecilians (Gymnophiona). It compared the morphology, function and development of cranial muscles in egg-laying and live-bearing species. He then worked at Friday Harbor Laboratories as a postdoctoral researcher, a role named in a 2011 student report. His papers from 2010 to 2013 give FHL as an address, and several were co-authored with Adam Summers. From 2012 his papers also give the Functional Morphology and Biomechanics group of the Zoological Institute at Kiel University (Christian-Albrechts-Universität zu Kiel) as his address, and many of his Kiel papers were co-authored with Stanislav Gorb.

His research combines anatomy, micro-CT imaging, finite element analysis and performance testing. His FHL-connected papers extended his caecilian work: feeding biomechanics in egg-laying and live-bearing species (2010), the female cloaca (2011), larval throat muscles compared with those of salamanders (2011) and cranial performance in solid and fenestrated skulls (2012). At FHL he also took part in a finite element study of scorpion pincer shapes (2012) and a study of the filter pads of devil rays (2013). A 2011 report by Dylan Wainwright, an undergraduate in FHL's summer internship programme, was followed by a 2013 paper with Kleinteich and Summers showing that the northern clingfish adheres about equally well across a wide range of surface roughness, while artificial suction cups hold only on the smoothest. Kiel papers treat adhesion by frog tongues and octopus suckers, insect mouthparts and legs, and, in 2021 and 2022, head shape, bite force, burrowing and vertebral shape in caecilians.

name: Tigran P. Norekian
text:
Tigran P. Norekian is a neurobiologist who studies the nervous systems and behaviour of marine invertebrates. His 2020 and 2023 papers give joint affiliations with the Whitney Laboratory for Marine Bioscience of the University of Florida and Friday Harbor Laboratories, and the 2020 paper also lists the Institute of Higher Nervous Activity and Neurophysiology in Moscow. Much of his ctenophore work is co-authored with Leonid L. Moroz of the Whitney Laboratory, and the animals for his 2020 siphonophore study and 2023 ctenophore study were collected at the FHL dock. The census counts 27 FHL-address papers from 1993 to 2024, and the mentoring network links him to Richard A. Satterlie through co-authorship from 1993 to 2019.

Norekian's earlier work, much of it with Satterlie, used the swimming pteropod mollusc Clione limacina to study how identified neurons produce behaviour. These papers traced the cerebral neurons and motoneurons behind the hydraulic inflation of prey-capture appendages (1993-1995), control of startle and escape swimming (1997), serotonergic modulation of swimming speed, the roles of GABA, nitric oxide and peptides in feeding circuits, and control of heartbeat (1999, 2008). From 2014 he turned to ctenophores and cnidarians, contributing to the 2014 ctenophore genome paper and describing the neuromuscular systems of the ctenophores Pleurobrachia bachei, Beroe abyssicola and Euplokamis dunlapae and the trachymedusa Aglantha digitale (2015-2019). Later studies, one with Robert W. Meech, describe the nervous system of the siphonophore Nanomia (2020), nervous system development in larvae of Mnemiopsis leidyi (2021), the suppression of ciliary beating in ctenophores by nitric oxide (2023) and sensory networks in the sea slug Pleurobranchaea (2024).

name: Victoria E. Foe
text:
Victoria E. Foe is a cell and developmental biologist and Research Professor Emerita in the Department of Biology at the University of Washington. She earned a BS (1966) and PhD (1975) at the University of Texas at Austin, where she worked with Hugh Forrest on the induction of transcription during embryogenesis, and she also worked with Charles Laird at UW on the functional organisation of chromatin. With Bruce Alberts at the University of California, San Francisco, she then studied how the cell cycle relates to the shaping of embryos. She joined the UW Zoology Department in 1991 and was a founding member of the Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories, where she held a research professorship. Her honours include a Senior Postdoctoral Fellowship from the American Cancer Society, a Guggenheim Fellowship (1990) and a MacArthur Fellowship (1993). Her FHL-connected papers span 1989 to 2022.

Foe's research asks how cell-cycle biochemistry coordinates reorganisation of the cytoskeleton, as in cell division and cellularisation of fly embryos, and how progress through the cell cycle relates to gene activity and cell fate. From detailed descriptions of fruit fly embryos she found that groups of cells in different regions divide on distinct schedules; these "mitotic domains", reported in 1989 papers, one with Garrett Odell, reveal early commitment of cell fates. A 1985 paper with Alberts used oxygen deprivation to visualise nuclear organisation between divisions, and a 2000 paper showed how microtubules and cell-cycle phase pattern actin and myosin in early fly embryos. Later she worked with echinoderm embryos: a light microscopy chapter (2004), paired experimental and computer-modelling studies of how microtubules position the cleavage furrow (2008), and the behaviour of two protein complexes during furrow specification (2012). A 2022 paper asked whether a meiotic checkpoint promotes adaptive speciation.

name: Vikram K. Iyengar
text:
Vikram K. Iyengar is a Professor of Biology at Villanova University in Pennsylvania, where the department lists him as assistant chair, and studies sexual selection and animal behavior. His early papers, published from Cornell University's Department of Neurobiology and Behavior between 1998 and 2002, many with Thomas Eisner, concerned sexual selection and chemical defense in the arctiid moth Utetheisa ornatrix. A 2004 paper lists the College of Wooster, and his ORCID record dates his Villanova appointment from 2004. His FHL-connected papers, from 2013 to 2026, report studies of the maritime earwig on San Juan Island that used FHL's laboratory facilities and field sites. Five are reports from FHL's summer Blinks/NSF REU/BEACON internship program with student first authors, including Nicole L. Hack (2013) and Jessica M. Kendall-Bar (2014), whose projects became journal papers; the report's network records him as research mentor to both.

His research uses insects and other arthropods to ask how mate choice, competition and body size shape reproductive success. The moth work examined female preference and offspring fitness, the heritability of body mass, male courtship pheromones and the sperm of sons of multiply mated females; at Villanova he has also studied harem mating in an amphipod (2008) and contests between moth larvae (2015). At FHL he turned to Anisolabis maritima, an earwig that lives under beach debris at or above the high-tide line and whose males carry curved, asymmetric forceps. Student reports and papers ask when earwigs share shelters (2013; 2017, with Hack), how body size and forceps affect mate choice and male competition (2014; 2017, with Kendall-Bar), how density and form differ among populations (2017), how sex affects nest intrusion and egg defense against cannibalism (2022; 2026), and how sex ratio in pairs and trios alters aggression and mating (2026).

name: Volker Schmid
text:
Volker Schmid is a cell and developmental biologist whose published research, from 1984 to 2007, centred on hydrozoan jellyfish at the University of Basel, Switzerland. His papers from 1984 to 2005 give his address as the Zoological Institute (Institute of Zoology) of the University of Basel. A 2007 paper on jellyfish opsins, written with Hiroshi Suga and Walter J. Gehring, gives the Department of Cell Biology at Basel's Biozentrum. No faculty page or biographical notice was found, so no positions or dates are given beyond these addresses. Three of his papers, from 1988 to 1992, list Friday Harbor Laboratories alongside Basel, and Basel co-authors such as Andreas Bally also give FHL addresses. A fourth paper (1995) appears in FHL's research bibliography. He is not the statistician of the same name at LMU Munich, whose ORCID record is attached to some of his papers in bibliographic databases.

Schmid's research uses hydrozoan medusae, including Podocoryne carnea, to study how specialised cells can change fate and how cells interact with the surrounding extracellular matrix. A 1984 paper reported that isolated, single-nucleus striated muscle cells can transdifferentiate and form a complex regenerate. His FHL-connected papers examined the mesoglea, the jellyfish's extracellular matrix. A 1988 study with Bally found that muscle and endoderm attach to and spread on mesoglea in a highly species-specific way, through an extractable factor that appeared to be mainly a collagen. A 1991 paper extended this work on cell adhesion and spreading, and a 1992 review in International Review of Cytology surveyed transdifferentiation in medusae. A 1995 study in Podocoryne carnea identified a fibrillin-like matrix protein that forms different fibrils at different life stages. His later work dealt with life-cycle reversal in Turritopsis, the origin of striated muscle and mesoderm, the germ-line gene Cniwi and jellyfish opsins.

name: Wendel W. Raymond
text:
Wendel W. Raymond is a nearshore ecologist who works on seagrass, kelp and intertidal communities in the Pacific Northwest and Alaska. He earned a BS in biology at Oregon State University in 2012 and first came to Friday Harbor Laboratories as a Research Experience for Undergraduates participant in 2011. His PhD at the University of Alaska Fairbanks (2020) examined sea otters in Southeast Alaska, including their subsistence harvest and their effects on seagrass communities, and his fieldwork there included food webs in eelgrass meadows on Prince of Wales Island. From 2021 to 2023 he was a nearshore ecology research scientist at FHL, where he helped develop and co-taught the Biodiversity and Monitoring of Estuarine Ecology research apprenticeship. Since 2023 his ORCID record lists him as a nearshore ecology research scientist with the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife. His census papers with an FHL address run from 2014 to 2026.

Raymond studies how nearshore habitats respond to predators, food supply, and human and climate stresses. A 2011 student report from his time at FHL tested red sea urchin feeding preferences among drift kelps, and a 2014 paper led by M. N. Dethier, with Aaron W. E. Galloway among the co-authors, showed that the food quality of decaying kelp changes differently among species. Other papers concern shelter competition between invasive lionfish and Nassau grouper (2015) and shoreline armoring in the Salish Sea (2016). His dissertation found sea otters positively associated with seagrass across Southeast Alaska, but no evidence of a link between crabs and seagrass epifauna. After the June 2021 heat wave he led a survey of shellfish die-offs that gathered 203 observations from 108 locations (2022), followed by studies of intertidal bivalves (2024) and rocky shores (2025). Recent papers concern nutrient pollution and green tides and a kelp stressor metric (2026).

name: Willem Weertman
text:
Willem Lee Weertman studies how octopuses use their arms and chemical senses to find food. He earned a BS in oceanography at the University of Washington in 2018 and an MS in environmental science at Alaska Pacific University's Institute of Culture and Environment, with a thesis on how octopuses use odor plumes to find food (2023). Since 2022 he has been a PhD student in psychology (behavioural neuroscience) at the University of Washington, in David H. Gire's Laboratory of Comparative System Neuroscience; the department names Gire as his mentor. His census papers with an FHL address run from 2023 to 2025, and his recent papers list Friday Harbor Laboratories alongside the UW Department of Psychology. A 2018 UW report described his design of a diver-deployed stereo underwater video camera, lit with deep red light, for recording octopus den behaviour.

Weertman combines behavioural experiments, video tracking and modelling to study octopus foraging. A 2025 PLoS ONE paper (preprinted in 2024, after a 2021 conference abstract) showed that octopuses tested in darkness moved upstream toward baited targets, with odor-gated pauses, switchbacks and cross-stream turns and fast lunges aligned with an arm; the authors argue that the suckers are the main chemosensory organs. A 2023 study with Dominic M. Sivitilli and Gire tracked arms in visually occluded, 3D-printed foraging tasks and used a simulated arm to show a contact-based search arising from local sucker coordination. With David Scheel he used DeepLabCut pose estimation on video of Octopus rubescens to show that males hold the hectocotylus, the arm modified for mating, closer to the body than their other arms (2024). He also co-authored a 2025 FHL study showing that early life stages of the endangered sunflower star tolerate current and near-future warming.

name: William B. Stickle
text:
William B. Stickle is a comparative physiologist of marine invertebrates whose career has been based at Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge. He published from its Department of Zoology and Physiology from 1973 and later from the Department of Biological Sciences, with papers into the 2020s. Papers of 1970 and 1971 list the University of North Dakota and Slippery Rock State College, and several from the 1980s the Institute for Marine Environmental Research in Plymouth, England. His doctoral thesis for the University of Saskatchewan, Regina Campus, advised by Frederick Duerr, used FHL: the snail Thais lamellosa was collected at Turn Island about monthly from 1968 to 1970 and kept at the laboratories, and he thanked director Robert L. Fernald for facilities. His FHL-connected census papers run from 1973 to 2016, including work in the 2000s with Eugene N. Kozloff of FHL.

His research asks how temperature, salinity, low oxygen and season affect the energy budgets, body fluids and survival of intertidal and estuarine animals. In Louisiana he studied the southern oyster drill, oysters and blue crabs, including responses to tidal salinity change, hypoxia, crude oil and cadmium. His FHL-connected papers began with seasonal changes in metabolism and body composition over the reproductive cycle of Thais lamellosa (1973, 1975). A 1985 paper with Richard A. Roller, probably his doctoral student (LSU, PhD 1987), measured salinity effects on larvae of four echinoderm species, and a 1990 paper compared salinity tolerance and allozymes of sea urchins from Alaska and near Friday Harbor. With Kozloff he described infection of the testes of Leptasterias sea stars by the ciliate Orchitophrya stellarum (2001-2008), and a 2016 paper with FHL's Emily Carrington and Hilary Hayford examined seasonal changes in snail tolerance of temperature and desiccation stress.

name: William M. Bement
text:
William M. (Bill) Bement is a cell biologist and professor of integrative biology at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, where he is also a member of the Center for Quantitative Cell Imaging. Publication records place his early work at Arizona State University in 1991–1992, on the cortical cytoskeleton and cell-cycle control of Xenopus eggs with D. G. Capco, followed by work at Yale University with M. S. Mooseker on unconventional myosins and wound closure (1993–1996); his papers from Wisconsin begin in the mid-1990s. His FHL connection is through the Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories, which his 2005 Journal of Cell Biology paper gives as his address. All six of his census papers, from 2005 to 2009, were written with George von Dassow of that centre, and the 2005 and 2009 cytokinesis studies used echinoderm embryos alongside frog eggs and embryos.

Bement's research asks how cells coordinate signalling and the cytoskeleton at the cell cortex during cell division and cell repair, with the frog Xenopus laevis as the main model. His lab's topics include cytokinesis, spindle assembly, wound healing, exo- and endocytosis, and cortical excitability. The FHL-connected papers centre on the small GTPase RhoA. A 2005 study used four-dimensional microscopy in four echinoderm species and Xenopus to show that microtubules direct the formation and placement of a sharply bounded zone of active RhoA that precedes cytokinesis. A 2009 study led by von Dassow, using sea urchin and frog embryos, showed that a furrow-inducing signal can reach the cortex from the spindle without transport along microtubules, and that astral microtubules refine where the furrow forms. Other papers from this period introduced fluorescent actin-filament probes based on the actin-binding domain of utrophin (2007) and reviewed Rho GTPase activity zones (2006, 2008).

name: William N. McFarland
text:
William N. "Mac" McFarland, who died in 2004, was a biologist who studied the vision and behavior of fishes. A tribute by Ellis Loew in Visual Neuroscience records that, after posts at Cornell University and the University of Southern California, he was at his death in a second post-retirement professorship, at the Friday Harbor Laboratories. The tribute also mentions his studies at the West Indies Laboratory on St. Croix and the Wrigley Marine Science Center on Catalina Island. He was the first-named author of the textbook Vertebrate Life (Macmillan, 1979). A volume of Visual Neuroscience was dedicated to him and two other vision researchers who had recently died. The census counts nine FHL-address papers from 1996 to 2008, the last published after his death.

McFarland's research linked the light environment under water to the visual pigments and behavior of fishes. A 1973–1975 series of papers with his longtime collaborator Fred Munz built a database of visual pigments in reef and open-ocean fishes and tested ideas about how pigments suit underwater light. He proposed a "twilight hypothesis" for why most rod pigments absorb near 500 nm, and studied twilight and nocturnal behavior of California near-shore fishes with Ted Hobson (1980). His FHL-connected papers continue these themes: visual limits on the migrations of juvenile French grunts (1996), reviews of ultraviolet vision in fishes and of twilight behavior on coral reefs (1999), and visual pigments in young Pacific Northwest marine fishes (2001) and yellowfin tuna (2002). Others cover polarization sensitivity in damselfishes and vision in Hawaiian reef fishes (2003), a planktivore feeding in a current (2005) and opsin expression shifts that tune visual sensitivity (2008).

name: Winsor H. Watson
text:
Winsor H. "Win" Watson III is a neurobiologist and professor emeritus of biological sciences at the University of New Hampshire (UNH). He received a BA in biology from Wesleyan University and a PhD in zoology and neurobiology from the University of Massachusetts Amherst. His UNH laboratory studies the neurobiology, behavior and physiology of marine animals, including American lobsters, horseshoe crabs, nudibranchs and fishes, with interests in biotelemetry and biological rhythms. The census counts eight FHL-address papers from 1988 to 2004. The earliest, a 1988 study with David Prior of how a neuropeptide affects the feeding motor program of the slug Limax maximus, lists both UNH and FHL. A 1992 paper on nudibranch neurons was co-authored with A. O. Dennis Willows of FHL. Later papers on the nudibranch Melibe leonina, through 2022, mention FHL in their text.

Watson's Melibe research asks how a nervous system with large, identifiable neurons produces and adjusts rhythmic behaviors such as feeding and swimming. Papers from 1992 quantified Melibe feeding and its change with prey density, examined the role of the buccal ganglia in feeding, and identified apparently homologous peptide-containing neurons across nudibranch species. With James M. Newcomb and others he mapped neurons that make nitric oxide (2001) and showed that nitric oxide modulates swimming (2002). Other studies described swimming behavior and its neural correlates (2002), the effect of light on locomotion (2004) and the central pattern generator for swimming (2005). Later papers documented circadian rhythms of crawling and swimming (2014), clock-gene transcripts in the brain (2018), the distribution of small cardioactive peptide (2020), and nerve signals from stomach distension that inhibit feeding (2022). His lobster work uses ultrasonic telemetry and underwater video to study behavior in natural habitats.

name: Yo Saiga
text:
Yo Saiga co-wrote, with Osamu Shimomura and Frank H. Johnson, the 1962–1963 papers that first described the light-emitting protein aequorin from the jellyfish Aequorea, which the Princeton group collected at Friday Harbor. No biography was found, so this account rests on the author lines of Saiga's papers. In the four FHL-connected papers, all from 1962 and 1963, Saiga's address is Princeton University's Department of Biology or its Moffett Biological Laboratory, listed together with the Friday Harbor Laboratories. Saiga's other papers from 1961 to 1963 give a Princeton address, one also naming the Bermuda Biological Station. Papers from 1967 list a Yo Saiga in the chemistry department of Tokyo Kyoiku University with Noboru Sugiyama, who had co-written two 1961 papers with the Princeton group. The sources do not confirm that this is the same person, or record Saiga's position at Princeton.

The work concerned the chemistry of animal light. With Johnson and Shimomura, Saiga co-wrote papers on the luciferin and luciferase of the ostracod Cypridina and on crystalline luciferin from the luminous fish Parapriacanthus (1961), and on the luminescence system of the polychaete Odontosyllis (1963). The 1962 FHL paper reported the extraction, purification and properties of aequorin, a protein that gives off light in the presence of calcium. A footnote in it mentioned a green protein found during the purification, later known as green fluorescent protein. In 1963 the three authors published further data on aequorin, described a similar luminescent protein, halistaurin, from the hydromedusa Halistaura, and showed in Science that aequorin luminescence can be used to measure very small amounts of calcium. Shimomura later shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for green fluorescent protein.
